Sources indicate that for adventurers and outdoor enthusiasts who want more than the average smartwatch, Garmin sets the standard with its industry-leading features and durability. But while the brand is on many wishlists, its high price tags stop many shoppers from making the splurge. Fortunately, with Amazon’s early Black Friday sale, you can get one of its bestsellers, the 44mm Garmin Instinct 3 AMOLED, for 44% off at $249.99 (originally $449.99).

According to recent reports, the 1.2-inch color AMOLED display makes the screen more readable in bright daylight conditions, and battery life is best-in-class, lasting up to 18 days (even longer when you’re not using it regularly), which reduces the need for weekly charging, a must for those going off-grid. The Garmin Pay feature is another bonus for those who don’t want to have their wallet on them at all times.

It has been revealed that if you want to log your activities, whether that’s skiing the slopes, heading out on a long trail run, or going on a camping trip in the woods, the 44mm Garmin Instinct 3 AMOLED is a rugged option with plenty of useful tools for those who love the outdoors. And you can’t forget its wildly impressive battery life. At $200 off, it’s a powerful entry into the Garmin world that can accomplish a lot and won’t set you back nearly as much as the brand’s more loaded watches.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple Home is kicking off a upcoming era with Siri AI-driven products like HomeView, making it a great time to upgrade your smart home with Apple Home-compatible accessories. Here are my top five picks.

iOS 27 upgraded Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video service (included with iCloud+) in several key ways. You’ll now get searchable videos, highlighted clips, 4K support, and more.

I have two recommendations for HomeKit Secure Video-compatible cameras. The main difference is video quality, and whether they’re designed for outdoor use or only indoors.

Smart locks have always offered convenience, but with the advent of Ultra Wideband-supported locks, they’re better than ever.

In a recent development, aqara’s U400 smart lock was among the first to introduce Ultra Wideband, which enables your door to lock and unlock automatically when it senses your presence. Unlike prior smart lock automations that relied on Bluetooth, Ultra Wideband offers excellent reliability and precision for a great overall experience.

Want to open your garage door with a quick Siri command, or via CarPlay or the Home app on iPhone? Smart garage door openers with Apple Home support can deliver that, and my recommendation is the meross MSG150HK.

meross notes the MSG150HK is compatible with “the vast majority of Chamberlain, Lift-Master, and Craftsman brand openers.” And it supports security features like automatic notifications when your door is left open, or every time it opens and closes.

Sources indicate that smart plugs are often a gateway to building out a smart home. And my favorite option, both for cost and convenience, is Tapo’s multipack of smart plugs.

According to recent reports, tapo sells its smart plug in a 2-pack at a great price—at the moment only $8 per plug. These plugs are compact and offer seamless, quick setup through the Home app without needing a separate app.

It has been revealed that controlling your thermostat entirely from your iPhone or a HomeView can prove extremely convenient. That convenience can also save you money by making it easier to stay on top of your electricity usage.

Aqara’s W200 smart thermostat is a beautifully designed, easy-to-use accessory that comes with a bonus Apple feature that’s hard to find: Adaptive Temperature, which can remove lots of the need to manually update the thermostat.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that scroll through Amazon for five minutes and you’ll find dozens of $10–20 cases that look, through a thumbnail, almost identical to $50+ aramid fiber ones. Same dark weave, same slim profile, same pitch.

Once you actually snap one onto a phone, the differences are obvious. You handle your phone for hours every day, so rough seams around the charging port, awkward cutouts, low-quality materials will make you regret your purchase instantly. With PITAKA’s Black Friday sale taking up to 30% off selected cases, it’s worth breaking down what actually separates a real aramid case from a cheap lookalike, why you should spent the extra money on PITAKA’s high-quality cases.

This post is sponsored by PITAKA.

Plenty of budget cases get the woven look by printing a pattern onto plain plastic. If you’re looking for that style, go for it, but it won’t behave like woven aramid fiber, which lets a case stay rigid and thin without adding much weight.

According to recent reports, even genuine aramid cases aren’t all made the same way. The weave, resin, thickness, and surface finish all change how a case feels in use. PITAKA uses woven aramid fiber in two main weights: 600D and 1500D. Those numbers measure yarn density; the finer 600D weave feels a bit smoother and produces a slightly thinner shell than 1500D. Whatever case you choose, look past the word “premium” and check whether the maker actually spells out what the case is made of.

Sources indicate that most aramid cases stick to plain black and gray. PITAKA’s Fusion Weaving method blends colored fibers and multiple weave styles directly into the shell instead of printing a graphic on the outside. PITAKA claims the process requires tight control over fabric tension and how fibers cross between layers. In practice, it means you can pick something colorful like the Sunset colorway without giving up the feel of woven fiber, or stick with classic Black & Grey if you prefer a quieter look.

Online listings spend almost all their time showing off the back of a case, even though your fingers spend just as much time on the sides, buttons, and bottom edge. An awkward camera cutout makes quick shots annoying, a tight port opening fights bulkier charging cables, and sharp edges dig into your hand on a long call.

Rather than selling one shell in ten colors, PITAKA splits its lineup into three builds:.

It has been revealed that if you use a magnetic charger, wallet, or grip, how the magnets are built into the case matters just as much as the outer material. Sticking a separate magnet ring inside a shell usually adds extra layers and thickness.

Sources indicate that PITAKA’s Amber Magnet Film process bonds coated magnets directly with the aramid fiber and resin under heat and pressure. That keeps the magnets enclosed without bulking up the case, which is the kind of detail you won’t spot in a photo but will notice in your pocket.

Spending more on a case doesn’t guarantee it’s better, and plenty of $20 cases are completely fine. Genuine aramid fiber by itself doesn’t guarantee better drop protection either. A thin shell like Edge is made for people who hate bulky cases. If drop protection is your main concern, look at a cushioned option like Cairn or Summa, and compare actual edge coverage and model-specific testing instead of judging by price or material alone.

What you’re really paying for with a higher-end aramid case is how it feels and fits every time you pick up your phone.

If you already want a thinner, better-finished case, Black Friday takes some of the sting out of the price. PITAKA’s Amazon offers run November 19–30, with discounts varying by device and colorway:.

According to recent reports, buying directly from the PITAKA official website? Code PTKPR12 takes an extra 5% off from November 10 through December 31. It’s separate from the Amazon sale, so double-check eligible products and your final total at checkout.

It's available in a few space configurations — 1TB, 2TB, 4TB and 8TB. I use the 2TB version, which is down to $569 at PlayStation. If you want double that, the 4TB version is reduced to $899 at Amazon, too.

In a recent development, with sequential read speeds up to 7,300 MB/s, load times are extremely short, and 6,600 MB/s write speed means copying games from discs to the SSD is supremely speedy. This is a must-have for PS5 owners.

According to recent reports, "Why do we fall, sir? So that we can learn to pick ourselves up. Batman begin," is what Michael Caine tweeted a couple years ago. He forgot the "s" at the end, and every time I think of the tweet, I laugh out loud. The tweet naturally went viral, and it even made its way into Lego Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight.

That's enough reason to buy the game this Black Friday, which is down to $49 at Amazon.

In a recent development, oh, you need more reasons? Fiiiiine. Lego Batman is extremely fun. It takes everything folks know about Batman from popular culture and filters it through the tried-and-true Lego formula. You'll love it.

Recent findings suggest that I'll be honest: I didn't expect to love Cyberpunk 2077 as much as I do when I first started playing it. No, I didn't play it when it was broken at launch — I played it once everything was fixed. I'm not a huge fan of first-person games, but man, Cyberpunk 2077 blew me away. It's a must-play for everyone, and right now, the Ultimate Edition with the Phantom Liberty DLC is 50% off (down to $35).

This open-world action RPG is set in Night City, a neon-drenched metropolis obsessed with power, glamor, and body modification. You take control of V, a mercenary outlaw hunting a one-of-a-kind cybernetic implant that holds the key to immortality, forcing tough choices that shape your story and survival.

It has been revealed that I can't say more without giving away spoilers, so I'd recommend you experience this marvel for yourself. Trust me, you won't regret it.

Recent findings suggest that baldur's Gate 3 is the greatest game of all time. Not of the year (which it won 2023, by the way). Not of the decade. Of all time. Period. You may argue with the wall. No, wait, don't go right now! Hear me out first. Please, I've played this game for 1,000 hours, I guarantee you this is worth your time.

Industry observers note that BG3 is a story-rich, party-based role-playing game set in the Dungeons & Dragons universe, and no, you don't need to have played the prequels or be well-versed with D&D to play it. Your customizable character is infected with a Mindflayer parasite and you must get rid of it. Recruit memorable companions, make choices that permanently reshape the world, participate in deep tactical turn-based combat determined by dice rolls and skill checks, and more.

This is an extremely fun game. Every playthrough is different from the last (take it from someone who's done at least six of them). Your actions have consequences. And you can choose to be good or evil, it's up to you. Like Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, I'd recommend BG3 even at its full price, but you can get the Digital Deluxe Edition for $55 today!

Recent findings suggest that ghost of Yotei is fantastic, but Ghost of Tsushima is what started it all — and now's a great time to pick up the game if you've never played it (what are you doing?!). It's $40 off right now, so you can get the Director's Cut Edition for just $29 at Amazon.

Recent findings suggest that in this open-world action-adventure game, you play as samurai Jin Sakai as he fights to liberate his island from invading Mongol forces. Forced to abandon his strict honor code, Jin adopts lethal stealth tactics as the mythical "Ghost" while exploring a vibrant, wind-guided feudal Japan.

GoT's world is beautiful, with gorgeous graphics, an emotional soundtrack, and compelling characters, both playable and NPCs alike. The game makes excellent use of the DualSense controller, too.

According to recent reports, ghost of Yotei is one of the best PS5 exclusives of all time, and if you're a fan of Ghost of Tsushima, you need to play the sequel. In GoY, you play as Atsu, a female mercenary hunting down the Yōtei Six to avenge her family in 1603 Ezo.

In this highly cinematic single-player game, you embark on a visually beautiful journey with a compelling storyline. The massive open-world is stuffed full of activities, like petting foxes and defending wolf dens, and the music is just as gorgeous.

Right now, you can get the Complete Edition (including the Most Wanted DLC and Sekigahara story expansion) for just $49 at Amazon.

Oh man. I am so excited to talk about this deal. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 won the Game of the Year Award last year, and it deserved every other accolade it picked up, too. It's a game unlike any other, and Sandfall Interactive's debut is a triumph that's worth grabbing even at full price. But right now, you can get it for just $39 at PlayStation.

You play as a group of Expeditioners trying to take down the mysterious Paintress. With extremely fun reactive turn-based combat, perhaps the best soundtrack in recent years, and stunning visuals that transport you to another world, Expedition 33 will move you to tears with its compelling story.

Industry observers note that if you love RPGs, it should be at the top of your list. I really can’t recommend it enough. Take it from someone who's played it for 200 hours, done three playthroughs and achieved the Platinum trophy!

Industry observers note that as someone who has played every single Assassin's Creed game, Syndicate is the one I had some of the most fun in — and I think it's highly underrated. Right now, you can get the base game and all of the DLCs as the Gold Edition is down to just $14 at PlayStation.

In AC Syndicate, you roam the streets of Victorian England and plays as twins Evie and Jacob Frye to uncover the Templar plot. Parkour is smooth, the world-building is fantastic, and the background score feels whimsical at times. There are plenty of side activities, such as kidnapping gang leaders, stealing horse carriages, and running street races.

Sources indicate that both Evie and Jacob are compelling characters, as are the various historical figures you encounter on your adventures. Think Charles Dickens, Florence Nightingale, Queen Victoria, and more. This is a treat for fans of the franchise and English history!

Assassin's Creed is one of my favorite franchises, and I've played every single entry in the series. Right now, many of them are down to their lowest ever prices across Amazon and the PlayStation Store. If you've been meaning to sink your teeth into one, now's the time.

For example, Assassin's Creed Origins (set in ancient Egypt) is down to just $8 at PlayStation — it usually costs $59!

It's great that lots of AAA games are discounted for Black Friday, but if you want a cozy, easy-to-play game, I've got a fantastic recommendation for you. Neva is at the moment 50% off at the PlayStation Store right now, so you can get it for just $9.

Neva is a puzzle-platformer with barely any dialog, where the beautiful art design and stunning music do the talking for the game. It conveys a lovely story which you only understand when you reach the end, and it may drive you to tears — I sobbed like a baby.

In a recent development, happy Black Friday! Nikita here, taking over from Lloyd. I've been a PlayStation gamer for nearly 20 years... I still have and use the PSP my parents gifted me for one of my birthdays! For the next four hours, I'll be bringing you the best Black Friday deals on PS5 games, accessories and, if we're lucky to see them, consoles.

Let's start then, shall we? Lloyd talked about picking up Control Resonant in his last post — and everyone should get this game, I highly recommend it — but he also mentioned Alan Wake 2. The Deluxe Edition (which includes the Night Springs and Lake House DLCs) is available for just $29 at Amazon right now.

It has been revealed that alan Wake 2 weaves together two compelling protagonists across a unique, multi-dimensional, narrative that is often seriously strange but still surprisingly engrossing. You solve various puzzles, take down different kinds of enemies with your flashlight and guns, and untangle the Dark Place's mystery.

I’ve been lucky enough to work in games for a few years, but there’s always a title every year or two that sneaks past me while I’m playing something else.

This year, that’s Control Resonant, with Remedy moving from Alan Wake II’s survival horror for a more action-focused romp through a Manhattan that looks to have ‘Inceptioned’ in on itself.

It’s up for a bunch of awards this year, and Amazon has knocked 17% off the price.

Last year’s overly futuristic Call of Duty: Black Ops 7 was divisive to say the least, but the franchise is back on blockbuster form this year.

Closing out the Modern Warfare reboot series, Modern Warfare 4 takes the battle to Korea and includes an excellent campaign, endlessly moreish multiplayer, and a return to the extraction shooter DMZ mode.

We gave it 4 stars out of 5 in our review, but I’ve been coming back to it almost every day since launch.

Sources indicate that looking for something that wraps both horror and action together in one package? Resident Evil: Requiem is one of the best games of 2026, and it’s reduced by 43% right now at Amazon.

Split into two campaigns, players can kick butt as the returning Leon Kennedy, while some sections are focused on newcomer Grace Ashcroft and lean into running from threats rather than fighting them outright.

Not only that, but Requiem will take players back to Raccoon City after the bomb fell in Resident Evil 2 and 3.

Whether you’ve experienced the original Resident Evil 4 or not, the PS5 remake is an easy recommendation - especially when it’s currently just $13.59.

The game retells the iconic original’s story in gorgeous (and gruesome) new detail, and that price is worth paying for the initial village set-piece alone.

We mentioned Wolverine earlier, but if you haven’t played Marvel’s Spider-Man 2 yet, it’s easy to recommend - especially since you can save $22 at Target right now.

This superhero sequel takes place after the original and the standalone Miles Morales title, and sees Peter Parker reunited with his best pal Harry Osborn, crossing paths with Kraven the Hunter, and encountering a strange black goo.

According to recent reports, spider-Man 2 tells a great story, but it’s also a great showcase for the PS5 since it looks amazing in motion, and you can instantly swap between Peter and Miles. We awarded it 4.5 stars in our review.

Sure, your PS5 was purchased for GTA 6, but if you’re looking for something a little more family-friendly, we recommend Hot Wheels: Infinite Rush.

The game takes the arcade racing formula of developer Milestone’s prior Hot Wheels games and moves it to an open world full of recognizable landmarks and those iconic orange track pieces.

Sticking (at least tangentially) with something Persona-adjacent, Metaphor: ReFantazio is a JRPG built in a similar manner - players manage the passage of time, maximizing what they do and when they do it, to help them get better at tackling dungeons with excellent turn-based combat.

Recent findings suggest that depending on who you ask, though, some would say this more fantasy-themed adventure is just as good, or even better, than some Persona titles. In fact, we awarded it 4.5 stars in our review.

You can save 71% right now at Amazon, letting you grab this Game of the Year winner for $19.99.

Mario Kart might be just for Nintendo console owners, but Sonic Racing CrossWorlds is every bit as fun - and it's seeing a massive 50% discount.

Recent findings suggest that now just $19.99 for Black Friday, it’s not just Sonic and pals included: It’s a Super Smash Bros-esque crossover, including characters from Yakuza, Crazy Taxi, and even Persona and Super Monkey Ball. And the DLC adds Ninja Turtles, Avatar, and SpongeBob characters, among others.

With more DLC to come and a unique track-swapping mechanic that means you’ll never quite know where you’ll end up, the game is well worth a look for PS5 karting fans.

Another of EA’s dominant sports titles, EA SPORTS FC 27 is still reduced to under $30 with a 57% discount.

Sources indicate that this year’s title introduces a collection mechanic to Ultimate Team that rewards you for racking up themed sets, as well as major improvements to transfers in Career Mode. Dynamic OVR also means players will improve if they’re in form, giving you some selection headaches.

Thanksgiving is about food, family… and football. And if you’re keen on picking up this year’s Madden NFL title, you can save half of the MSRP at Target.

The retailer is offering the PS5 version of EA Sports Madden NFL 27 for just $34.99, and it brings with it a bunch of newly introduced features like Franchise improvements, including personality-led demands from players, as well as new strategies and plays.

Monster Hunter Wilds is the latest in Capcom’s long-running, beastie-bashing ARPG series, and while it certainly had some performance complications at launch, it’s become pretty great in the time since.

The franchise is built on a satisfying loop: Hunt monsters, carve them up for better gear, then go tackle even more ferocious monsters. With drop-in, drop-out co-op, plus PS5 Pro enhancements, it’s a great title to start with if you’ve been curious.

Better yet, it’s just $23.72 right now for the PS5 version if you buy from Amazon.

There’s a good chance you’ve picked up a PS5 console just to play Grand Theft Auto 6, and we don’t blame you - Rockstar has (somehow) outdone itself with its crime epic set in Leonida.

It has been revealed that still, if you haven’t picked it up yet but have been pulled in by its allure, you might be wondering if you can find a deal. Sadly, that’s not the case right now.

It’s still $79.99 for a code in the box, although Amazon will let you pay in instalments.

Here's a game that divides the team at Tom's Guide. Some of us love it, some of us...not so much. The consensus is that it's no Spider-Man, but is still an entertaining and cinematic title with the typical graphical flair you'd expect from developer Insomniac Games.

It has been revealed that naturally, as a tentpole title it's been pricey up to now — but with $20 off for Black Friday, it's a much more tempting prospect if you haven't picked it up yet. Just be warned, it's extremely violent.

Happy Black Friday! Welcome to our live blog covering all things PS5. We're going to be keeping track of discounts across consoles, games and accessories all day to help save you time and money.

Recent findings suggest that let's start at the beginning: the console. The PS5 is hard to come by this Black Friday, and if you do find one, it's likely at retail. It has been revealed that you can tell that Miranda Lambert is from Texas, but, until today, she’d never performed for her hometown football team — or anyone in the NFL, for that matter. Singing a medley of her classic hits (which she affectionately called “bangers and mash,” i.e., a mashup of her bangers), Lambert made her halftime show debut during the Thanksgiving Day matchup between the Dallas Cowboys and the Philadelphia Eagles at AT&T Stadium.

Following a pretaped introduction by Reba McEntire, who revealed Lambert as the “most awarded artist in the history of the Academy of Country Music,” the Grammy-winning singer took the stage to perform “Snakeskin Boots” (sorry, no Ella Langley cameo), “Kerosene,” “Gunpowder & Lead,” “Mama’s Broken Heart,” and “Little Red Wagon.” Lambert was backed by her band, along with a string section wearing black cowboy hats to mirror that of the entertainer: Lambert, in a black hat, wore a black dress adorned with blue fames. She also received an assist from an army of Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders, who delivered their choreographed routine as Lambert sang.

Recent findings suggest that lambert is a lifelong Cowboys fan who grew up in Lindale, Texas, about 80 miles east of Dallas. She now joins a cast of music’s biggest names as a halftime show veteran, including Beyoncé, Reba McEntire, LeAnn Rimes, Lainey Wilson, and Dolly Parton, who gave a memorable performance while wearing the iconic Dallas Cowboy Cheerleaders costume. Coined the “Salvation Army’s 30th Red Kettle Kickoff,” it was McEntire who performed at the inaugural broadcast, which kicks off the annual holiday fundraising drive. Lambert, true to form, announced her appearance from atop a longhorn bull. Recent findings suggest that “It’s my first time ever to do this,” Lambert stated during a visit to the Calm Down With Erin and Charissa podcast. “I’ve been doing this 23 years, and it’s my first halftime show ever. Isn’t that crazy? I don’t have a lot of firsts in my career at this point, but I was like okay, here we go.”.

It’s been a packed year for Lambert: her album Crisco came out in October, and she just took home a handful of CMA Awards for her work as producer and writer on Ella Langley’s Dandelion and song “Choosin’ Texas.” Next up is the Grammy Awards, where she is nominated seven times and could potentially make history if she wins Producer of the Year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AirTag 2 (now only $18, down from $29) introduced earlier this year after a five-year wait, and in my experience there are two big improvements that make it worth the upgrade.

It has been revealed that precision Finding is Apple’s best AirTag feature, letting you get step-by-step, highly precise directions to your lost item. But with the original AirTag, you had to be in fairly close proximity before you could benefit from Precision Finding.

With AirTag 2, Apple added a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip that makes Precision Finding now available from up to 1.5x farther away than before. It’s a huge increase that I’ve definitely noticed.

In a recent development, this expansion of Precision Finding to greater distances means the feature is now available a lot more often than with the old AirTag. For this reason alone, I highly recommend AirTag 2.

It has been revealed that when you’re trying to find a lost item, Precision Finding isn’t the only tool AirTag offers. There’s also a built-in speaker that can play a sound, triggered by your iPhone, to help you track it down.

According to recent reports, with AirTag 2, Apple has made the built-in speaker 50% louder than before. The organization says this enables hearing it from up to twice as far away.

I’ve been impressed by how loud the AirTag speaker is able to get now. Between the new speaker and upgraded Precision Finding, Apple has made AirTag 2 better in the ways that users are likely to care about most.

You can buy AirTag 2 for $18 on Amazon (regularly $29) for a limited time.

Have you upgraded to AirTag 2? What’s your experience been like? Let us know in the comments.

Sources indicate that if you too can see the appeal of carrying all of your books with you on a device so small you'll forget it's even in your pocket, it's a great time to jump in: The recently released Xteink X4 Classic is currently 38% off for Black Friday, bringing it down to $54.87, a record-low price. Meanwhile, the smaller X3 is $55.72, or 19% off. Both are available in either "mist grey" or "space black." The discounts should last through the end of Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

According to recent reports, xteink is a Chinese startup that shook up the e-reading world last year with the launch of the X4, a super bare-bones device that made up for its lack of features and usability with a cheap sub-$70 price point. Since then, a huge online community of fans has formed, sharing tips on Reddit and even coming together to crowdsource an alternate operating system that fixed a lot of early problems. Xteink swiftly followed up the X4 with a slate of other devices, including the 3.7-inch X3 and the X4 Pro, which adds a front light and touchscreen (at the cost of screen clarity and two physical buttons).

Recent findings suggest that the X4 Classic and the X3 improve on the original X4 with quality-of-life upgrades like a larger battery, relocated page-turn buttons, a real-time clock, and a tilt-to-turn-page feature. They're also lighter and thinner than the X4, though there is a trade-off involved: They drop the USB-C charging port in favor of magnetic pogo pins that require a separate adapter (included).

According to recent reports, these upgrades also increased the cost: The X4 Classic typically retails for $89, $20 more than the discontinued X4 and only $10 less than the X4 Pro, while the X3 released at $79. But right now, the X4 Classic is just under $55, or around 38% off, and the X3 is about a dollar more. Either is a great option for those who prioritize crisp, readable text above the conveniences of a built-in light or touchscreen, as those add extra layers between the inner screen and outer glass. It's also important to understand what you're getting into: These devices support only e-books without Digital Rights Management (DRM), which means you can't use it to read your existing library of Kindle books. On the plus side, there's no longer a need to worry about flashing fresh firmware if you don't want to, as the native version has been totally overhauled and is now one of your best options (though the new firmware, called "Licorice," isn't available on the X3 quite yet).

QLED. OLED. Mini-LED. The TV world can be super overwhelming, so let’s do a quick rundown of the differences between the three “premium” panel types.

According to recent reports, OLED TVs have lots of mini diodes inside the panel that emit light individually. This means there’s no backlight, unlike older TVs. As a result, OLEDs are better for higher contrast, better blacks, better color, and smooth motion for gaming.

Industry observers note that QLEDs also use a light-emitting diode. Unlike OLED, a QLED panel has a backlight, which illuminates each diode individually. QLEDs are better for brighter rooms, as the panel itself tends to be brighter, but OLEDs can reach better contrast levels and color accuracy.

Mini-LED is something else entirely: it uses tiny LEDs (light-emitting diodes, like both QLED and OLED) — but thousands of them. That means each diode can pack a major color and brightness punch. Mini-LEDs can be brighter, blacker, and more colorful — all at once.

#155563. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2892 w)

Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The AI pioneer states it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to major concerns.
  • Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.
  • Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI pioneer states it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to major concerns.

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he says he has identified the next massive shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his firm Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he indicates can yield “small data” solutions to massive issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

Industry observers note that the great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Andrew Ng: This is a significant question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having noted that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a newly introduced paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

In a recent development, ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Having stated that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of people, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing organization with millions of users.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

According to recent reports, “In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from substantial data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI.

Industry observers note that I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and noted, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

I expect they’re both convinced now.

Recent findings suggest that over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing new here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”.

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and mentioned, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

In a recent development, the data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one company or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that indicated up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Sources indicate that ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from major data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

It has been revealed that when you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand newly introduced model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having noted that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng.

In a recent development, for example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very promptly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

In a recent development, could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. Latest tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an key piece of the puzzle.

It has been revealed that one of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is important, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention promptly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

For example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an important tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

It has been revealed that “In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng.

Synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

It has been revealed that to make these issues more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a manufacturer approaches Landing AI and indicates it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

It has been revealed that ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

Sources indicate that how do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

According to recent reports, ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift problem. I find it really important to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and revision the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In a recent development, in the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

According to recent reports, ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent new neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s key for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Sources indicate that ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”.

Industry observers note that R ob Gronkowski is in a familiar place as magic hour concedes to Friday-night lights in Los Angeles. He is pacing in a locker room on the campus of Sierra Canyon School, a high school that counts various Jenners and LeBron James’ sons among its alumni.

According to recent reports, the future Hall of Famer tight end is crew-cutted and cut. At 37, he is just five months older than Travis Kelce, who is still hauling in touchdowns from Patrick Mahomes, and he still looks like he could grab six catches for 107 yards and two TDs. Alas, Gronk — like Jesus and Cher, he goes by one name — exited the game at 33 with four Super Bowl rings.

Industry observers note that he has the full attention of the gathered players. Gronk hits all of his marks in his pregame talk. Be accountable. Trust your teammates. Make the play. “You’re going to remember Friday-night football games for the rest of your lives,” notes Gronk.

He speaks in a cadence that, for the clueless, suggests a brain pan both punch-drunk and super high.

Gronk gets serious, or as serious as someone named Gronk can get. He talks of injuries — Gronk lost a college season to back problems and major parts of his NFL career to a list of injuries that reads like the medical chart of a guy who got T-boned by a Ford F-150 while driving a Nissan Versa.

Recent findings suggest that “If you’re injured, you can’t participate,” states Gronk. “You’re worthless to the team. You gotta take care of your body. You gotta rehab hard.”.

Industry observers note that “And speaking of that, we’re talking DNA Vibe,” notes Gronk. “It’s a jazz band and consists of red-light therapy. It has vibrational frequency on it, too. And every single one of you here in this room on this team is getting one. Use the jazz band; it works to help the healing process naturally in your body.”.

The players look confused. No matter. Gronk finishes up.

“Thank you for having me, and kick some ass!”.

In a recent development, “There’s different levels of being yourself. I’m not gonna tell ‘69’ jokes on tv — no chance.”.

I’m scheduled to talk with Gronk the next afternoon at the Waldorf Astoria Beverly Hills. That morning, I look up the product he mentioned the night before. It has the cumber­some official name of DNA Vibe Jazz Band and has nothing to do with learning to play bebop during fifth period at Millard Fillmore Junior High and everything to do with helping you recover from injuries while using red-light therapy that I do not understand. You may not be surprised to learn that Gronkowski is DNA Vibe Jazz Band’s primary spokesman. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

At the hotel, Gronk happily shakes my hand, his massive forearms covered by matching bandages.

According to recent reports, “I get really dehydrated when I travel, so I get an IV,” says Gronk. “I also got ozone therapy, where it takes out the blood and then you put ozone in it.”.

In a recent development, I smile as if I have even the smallest idea of what the hell he is talking about. I try to move to more familiar ground. I’m about to ask him about his role on the top-rated Fox NFL Sunday pregame show when a bushy-haired man approaches us. Gronk makes the introduction.

The guy is serial entrepreneur Lance Collins, who co-founded the sports-drink company BodyArmor, whose remaining 85 percent Coca-Cola bought for $5.6 billion in 2021. (The soft-drink company bought the first 15 percent in 2018.) Gronk’s endorsement deal included equity, earning him a big payout. Collins and Gronk are now on to another sports drink.

Industry observers note that there are celeb endorsers who observe a firewall between a theoretically journalistic interview and hawking products. That’s not Gronk. “Put it in the story,” says Gronkowski. “Come on, let’s put it in the story.”.

I ask what the drink is called.

It has been revealed that “Recover 180,” Gronk repeats. “It’s an organic sports drink, and it’s filled with electrolytes.”.

Gronk calls the drink delicious and tasty. Collins suggests “delicious and nutritious,” an improvement, and Gronk instantly repeats the revised copy.

I’m beginning to think Collins being in the lobby is not coincidental.

Collins pulls out his phone and begins showing me ads for the drink. He only stops after I theatrically look at my watch for a third time. “I’m gonna make a ton of money, and he’ll make a lot of money,” states Collins. He mentions he has a tequila line that also features Gronk.

“We’re in on everything!” indicates Gronk.

Recent findings suggest that rob Gronkowski was the rare tight end who could pancake a linebacker on one play and then one-hand a pass from Tom Brady in the end zone on the next. All of this while partying his ass off, often with his four brothers and, sometimes, his dad, who built a state-of-the-art weight room in the family basement for his boys. They all had stints as pro athletes. The Brothers Gronk liked to prank one another with stunts like throwing forks at each other hard enough to lodge in someone’s elbow. And then there was the time at the oldest brother’s Vegas bachelor party that one of them — or someone in their crew — took a dump in a chip bag. Their dates were unamused. (I learned all of this while reading his memoir, It’s Good to Be Gronk, a not-exactly-Nabokovian account of his salad days.).

It has been revealed that but that’s all in the past. Gronkowski has now lined up for the next trick play: erasing the line between sincerity and commerce with his buffoonish charm. It is both impressive and a bit icky.

According to recent reports, longtime friend and former Fresh England Patriots teammate Julian Edelman says it’s all about his work ethic. According to Edelman, Gronk arrives on time and knows his lines better than anyone on commercial shoots.

“I’m a slapdick compared to Rob Gronkowski.”.

OK! Welcome to the Gronk Industrial Complex. Keep your head on a swivel or you’re gonna get blindsided.

From the start, Gronk understood something that many famous dudes never do: Shtick is tolerated, but only after brilliance has been established. Like Dennis Rodman and Tom Cruise before him, Gronk knows the world will let you be a total weirdo if you perform like a superstar. But before you jump on the proverbial Oprah’s couch you must — in Gronk terminology — kick some ass.

Here’s a Gronk creation story. Edelman was in his second year with the Patriots when Gronkowski arrived from the University of Arizona, where he lived in an off-campus house with a hot tub in the front yard. But Edelman didn’t see that side of Gronk in their first training camp together. Initially, Gronk grinded away at the playbook and impressed head coach Bill Belichick with his dominant blocking.

Then the team broke camp and Edelman saw Gronk Unchained. A bunch of players hit a nightclub, and within minutes there was the real Gronk.

“When someone says, ‘I thought this guy was going to be an idiot,’ I just start laughing.”.

“He’s dancing in the middle of the dance floor, going crazy, having the time of his life, being Gronk,” remembers Edelman. “And I walk in, and I’m like, ‘Oh, my God, what is this guy doing?’ Rob comes over, and there’s a waiter walking by, and the waiter has a bunch of drinks and finger food. Gronk just grabs a handful of shrimp and eats the shrimp. He’s like, ‘What’s up, Jules?’ And I’m like, ‘Oh, my God, what is this?’”.

Let it be noted that Gronk did not grab the shrimp until he highlighted his value.

“No one could say anything because of how hard he worked and his production,” claims Edelman. “Even the coaching staff — they’re like, ‘Well, that’s just fucking Gronk. If he’s going to score three touchdowns and be the point of attack for our running game, then whatever he does, we don’t care.’”.

Bill Bradley was a legendary basketball player and one-time presidential candidate who shares nothing in common with Gronk. Bradley once said domination on the court and life depended on situational awareness.

“You develop a sense of where you are,” stated Bradley.

That’s Gronk. Here’s an example. For his entire public life, Gronk has made “69” jokes, with the legend being he once bought $69,000 of Apple stock in 2014 on the recommendation of his contractor, and then forgot about it for years. (Depending on when he bought it, that $69,000 would be worth roughly a million dollars today if it wasn’t sold.).

I ask him if it is hard for him to rein in his inner 69 on the Fox pregame show, which is decidedly G-rated.

Recent findings suggest that “There’s different levels of being yourself, 100 percent,” indicates Gronk. “I’m not gonna tell the ‘69’ jokes on TV — no chance.” He smiles his goofy smile.

“But a podcast or something, that’s the place to say all those types of jokes.”.

Industry observers note that he also knows not to bite the hand that feeds him. I ask him if he is worried about the impact of CTE, a degenerative brain disease linked to repeated blows to the head. He dissembles with the skill of a tobacco lobbyist.

Industry observers note that “You hear all the studies about CTE, and there’s a lot of science behind it,” claims Gronk. “You’ve got to believe in the science, but it’s still kind of a myth as well, because how can you truly pinpoint anything to football?”.

To the casual observer, Gronk comes across as a cartoon character with a caveman name. That’s how he likes it.

“The best position I love to be in is when I’m underestimated,” notes Gronk as he exchanges a bro handshake with his IV guy. “When someone says, ‘I thought this guy was going to be an idiot,’ I just start laughing.”.

Gronk puts on his serious face.

“That’s when I know that that person is truly an idiot.”.

The next day, Gronkowski arrives just after 6 a.m. at the Fox NFL Sunday studio. He’s the kid on the show — 18 years younger than Michael Strahan, 29 years younger than Howie Long, and more than 40 years younger than Terry Bradshaw, all Hall of Famers. Still, he seems to have the lowest energy level of the bunch when they emerge for a run-through shortly after 7 a.m. Maybe it’s the crimson-checked suit and tie he had to don. The entire panel is wearing suits from the Collection by Michael Strahan (available at JCPenney).

It has been revealed that the atmosphere before airtime feels less like a billion-dollar television property than the greenroom at a 55-and-over-community talent show. Bradshaw sings snatches of Marty Robbins’ “Massive Iron,” a country & western song released in 1959. Turns out Strahan knows the song from his dad. The two sing the chorus: “And he’s here to do some business/With the big iron on his hip/Big iron …”.

In a recent development, long looks on like an anthropologist studying an ancient and backward tribe. Gronk doesn’t seem to notice, his head buried in his cue cards, trying to memorize the points he wants to make. A few minutes later, Bradshaw tries to knock the cue cards out of Gronk’s meaty hands.

“I love messing with him,” Bradshaw will tell me. “He’s so dialed in. I try to un-dial him.”.

A half-century ago, Bradshaw turned a country-bumpkin persona into a half-century career as a pitchman, musician, and NFL broadcaster. He recognizes a fellow traveler.

Recent findings suggest that “The camera loves him,” notes Bradshaw. “He’s harmless. It’s easy to like him.”.

Harmless is not the word I’d apply to a man who spent 11 NFL seasons beating the shit out of defenders, but Bradshaw has a point. Gronkowski’s secret power is that he conjures up Yogi Bear rather than Tony Soprano. No man eating Frosted Flakes out of a giant bowl in their man cave is going to worry that Gronk thinks he is smarter than them.

Sources indicate that television did not come naturally. Gronk understood football instinctually, seeing linebackers and safeties the way Jaws might size up a baby dolphin. Explaining what he saw in TV soundbites was another thing. During his first years at Fox, he prepared for TV as if he was the awkward lead in a high school play.

Looking back on his playing days, Gronk states, “I’m shocked I was able to do it all.”.

“I would remember a whole paragraph,” indicates Gronk. “I would say word for word the whole paragraph. It wasn’t fun being on TV like that.”.

His producer, Bill Richards, could see Gronk laboring. Richards reminded him that the show was not a three-act play. He told him just to listen to the other men at the desk and then react to what they said.

Sources indicate that “This is live TV,” Richards told him. “We want you for what you think at the moment.”.

Richards bristles slightly when I wonder if Fox hired Gronk for comic relief, a Chris Farley type talking about the NFL’s best edge rushers. Sure, there are the stunts — Gronk once jumped from a military helicopter into the Pacific Ocean for the show, which led Strahan to observe that Gronk hasn’t “learned what to do is say no when asked to do stuff.” Still, Richards wants the audience to remember that Gronk the crash-test dummy was also one of the greatest football players ever.

According to recent reports, “He’s not just the frat guy,” indicates Richards. “He knows football.”.

Being Gronk requires a willingness to look ridiculous. That’s A-OK for Gronk. In a segment that initially was filmed as an in-house joke, the Fox crew invented a Dallas Cowboys tight end and asked Gronk to analyze him, since he played the position. Gronk searched his memory for the name. Nothing. The player did not exist, but Gronk did not panic. He pivoted to the Cowboys’ actual tight end, Jake Ferguson, and explained how quarterback Dak Prescott would continue looking for him. The prank worked because Gronk was simultaneously dumb and smart. (Gronk loved the mischief, and the segment ran on the actual show.).

Industry observers note that on set, Bradshaw needles him constantly. Gronk doesn’t mind; this is how ex-jocks express affection, through humiliation. Bradshaw clearly has great affection for Gronk. He worries about him like an agony aunt.

“There was a time when I was the hottest young thing out there,” states Bradshaw. Now, Bradshaw watches Gronk go from show to ad shoot to the airport and back. “He’s gone, gone, gone,” says Bradshaw. “Commercial, commercial, commercial, all over the place.”.

Bradshaw warned Gronk to pace himself. At the Super Bowl in 2025, Gronk hit the wall.

Sources indicate that “He was knocked out,” says Bradshaw. “He was so tired. He’d been going, going, going. For the Super Bowl, he must have had 88 events.”.

Gronk rejects the premise. He has brought professional discipline to the business of being Gronk. He sleeps, does hot yoga, does his ozone thing, and restores himself before the next encounter.

I ask Gronk if it gets exhausting being, well, Gronk for the masses.

“I can’t always be on, and I can’t satisfy everyone,” claims Gronk.

This sounds like common sense until you understand Gronk’s predicament. His fans approach him and want good-guy Gronk who spikes footballs, makes 69 jokes, and invites them in ads for FanDuel to blow their paychecks and join the Sportsbook Reward Club. They don’t want to see a glowering Gronk wearing sunglasses in first class.

Edelman knows when his buddy hits his limit. An exhausted Gronk, he notes, is like a dog whose owner has left him alone for three days. He is still Gronk, but the light has gone out of his eyes.

Gronkowski gives a dismissive wave when anyone suggests he works too much. He insists that he and his girlfriend, Camille Kostek, a former Patriots cheerleader, love to put their phones away and just chill at their New England home.

Sources indicate that I don’t buy it. Work is both the cause of that exhaustion and the cure for something else. Football ended abruptly for Gronkowski, as it does for nearly everyone in the NFL. He first retired at 29, returned to win another Super Bowl with Brady in Tampa, and left for good at 33.

All his life, somebody told Gronk where to be and what to do. At Patriots training camp, his days began at seven in the morning and ended at 10 at night. Practices, meetings, treatments, meals, and film study swallowed every waking hour. He remembers that existence now with something close to wonder.

“I’m shocked how I was able to do it all.”.

But the absence of structure proved just as disorienting. After retirement, he would look at an empty week and initially feel liberated. Then he’d get restless.

In a recent development, “I’m already bored,” Gronk remembers thinking. “What do I do with myself?”.

Football provided the structure that made the fun possible. Now, the business of being Gronk serves the same purpose. The difference today is there is no offseason.

It’s now around 5:45 p.m., and Gronk sheds his suit and heads to a decidedly less-flashy part of the Fox studio, one filled with Alexi Lalas memorabilia. Gronk and his friend Edelman prepare to tape their podcast, The Gronk & Jules Show. Both have been working for 12 hours. Now, they must reconstruct the day in football and push premium dog chow.

It has been revealed that the podcast is where Gronk’s football intelligence and Gronk’s foolishness peacefully coexist. He explains how a strong running game pulls linebackers forward, opening the middle of the field for major plays. But then he guesses that Saints quarterback Tyler Shough was drafted in the fifth, sixth, or seventh round. A producer informs him Shough was the 40th overall pick.

“Might as well be the sixth,” says Gronk. “Might as well.”.

He is now babbling like a giant toddler who missed his afternoon nap, but it works. Gronk states an AI version of himself must have made one of his incorrect predictions. He theorizes that Elon Musk named Grok after him but removed the “n” to avoid paying for the naming rights.

Eventually, it is time for ad reads. One is for Carhartt. Gronk whispers to Edelman.

“I don’t even know what Carhartt is.”.

Edelman tells him it’s work clothes for men.

A minute later, Gronk is wearing a Carhartt sweatshirt, riffing about the protective qualities of the garment for Buffalo Bills fans diving on folding tables, as they like to do.

According to recent reports, “You know you’re not going to break your arm,” states Gronk. “And if you do, it’s just not going to hurt as much.”.

According to recent reports, someone up the chain of command has decided that the ad reads should be preceded by some classic Edelman and Gronk banter. Today, that means a lengthy read for Sundays for Dogs devolves into a discussion of how dry dog food produces dry dog shit while wet dog food produces — you guessed it — wet dog shit.

According to recent reports, finally, the two are done. Gronk is out on his feet. Before he disappears into a waiting car, I ask him how tired he is.

Industry observers note that gronk begins explaining the advantages of recording the podcast immediately after the Fox show, when the games are still fresh in their minds. Then he stops.

And then he is gone. Gronk needs a nap.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google is rolling out new privacy settings for the Gemini app that will let you “keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.”.

Enhancement 11/24: This newly introduced setting is now widely rolling out. On gemini.google.com, tap the settings gear icon to find a new “Gemini History” item at the very bottom. This opens myactivity.google.com/product/gemini with an On/Off dropdown.

Under “Help train generative AI models with,” you’ll find the fresh “Chat content including text & attachments” setting. It’s enabled by default.

Your future chats won’t be used to train generative AI models, unless you provide feedback.

Training on “Audio and Gemini Live videos & screenshares” remains an opt-in preference.

Original 11/16: Gemini’s existing Keep Activity setting “controls how long your chats are saved and whether they are used to train generative AI models.”.

Google is now separating that preference into two new options.

It has been revealed that this is huge. One of the major things Siri-AI users on iPhone like to point out is that while their assistant is a less capable portmanteau of Siri and Gemini, their queries are not used for AI training. Gemini on Android, on the other hand, offers the superior AI platform with the caveat that there is no way to opt out of training and still retain your chat history. Until now. Now users of Gemini on Android get the best of both worlds - the best of Google's AI models powering their AI experiences and their chat history siloed from AI training.

The first setting is called “History” and lets you “control how long your history is saved.” If disabled:.

“…future chats will be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public, with help from human reviewers.”.

The duration is presently 24 hours for chat context, and 72 hours to help protect Google, owners, and the public.

The second setting allows you to “separately control whether your chat content, including text and attachments, is used to train generative AI models.”.

With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.

If Keep Activity is at the moment off, the two “new settings will both be off.” These changes are rolling out over the “coming weeks,” and Google is notifying people via email.

Industry observers note that FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.

Check out 9to5Google on YouTube for more news:.

It has been revealed that phil Barker, drummer for British punk rock band the Buzzcocks from 1992 through 2006, died on Nov. 21 at age 65 on the Isle of Wight, England. His death following a battle with an unspecified form of cancer was declared by the band on Nov. 26.

Industry observers note that “We’re saddened by the news of the passing of our longtime drummer Phil Barker,” the band wrote on their website. “He died peacefully in his sleep on Saturday, November 21, 2026 on the Isle of Wight, after a five-year battle with cancer. He is survived by Deb, his wife of 26 years.”.

They continued, “Phil joined the band alongside bassist and childhood friend Tony Barber in 1992, backing Pete Shelley and Steve Diggle. He was integral to our success throughout that era, and left the band in early 2006. Just good memories. He will be missed.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Buzzcocks were founded in 1976 by Pete Shelley and Howard Devoto, who left the band sthe following year. The group released three albums before disbanding in 1981. They reformed in 1989 and released their fourth album, Trade Test Transmissions, in 1993. It was during this era that Barker joined the lineup as drummer alongside bassist Tony Barber. He collaborated on five albums with the group prior to Shelley’s death in 2018.

Diggle paid tribute to Barker on social media, writing, “I’m remembering the good times Phil and you were a great Drummer. Thinking of you Debbie and family. Tonight we play st Petersburg Florida and I will dedicate songs and the whole show to you Phil.” Trending Stories Duran Duran Guitarist Andy Taylor Dead at 65 Watch Miranda Lambert Perform Medley of Her Hits at Dallas Cowboys Halftime Show ⁠Gérard Depardieu to Face Trial for Allegedly Raping Actress Charlotte ⁠Arnould Duran Duran’s Andy Taylor Was the Wildest of the Wild Boys.

During his career, Barker also recorded with Slaughter Joe and The Modern Folk Quintet, occasionally working under the alias Phil Phuture. During the 1980s, he played with Lack of Knowledge. More recently, he performed with Crass vocalist Steve Ignorant in Stratford Mercenaries and punk band Dirt. The Buzzcocks have continued releasing music and touring since Shelley’s death. Barker left the group in 2006.

Local record shop Triple A Records paid tribute to Barker on Facebook. “We’re very sad to hear our brilliant friend Philip Barker has passed away,” they wrote. “Phil drummed on our favourite Buzzcocks records and was a keen and generous supporter of the shop. We’ll be playing some of his music today as we think about his cheery visits. RIP mate x.”.

#155542. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras
