Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3337 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.
  • In a recent development, advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated.
  • The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.

In a recent development, advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

Recent findings suggest that A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

Industry observers note that “It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn swiftly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Industry observers note that miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký.

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Industry observers note that druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

Sources indicate that an image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly indicates Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

Industry observers note that he photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

It has been revealed that he insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”.

A composite sequence of photographs demonstrates the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Václav Široký and Miloslav Druckmüller.

Industry observers note that despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

Sources indicate that to observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most crucial processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

In a recent development, space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she states, of solar eclipse photography.

It has been revealed that the European Proba-3 mission, debuted in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

Industry observers note that when Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

Industry observers note that it took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”.

In a recent development, the error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” indicates Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.).

Industry observers note that the human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller claims. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Recent findings suggest that since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

According to recent reports, the teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller states wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

According to recent reports, if you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký.

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller indicates with a grin. “It’s perfect.”.

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

Sources indicate that as the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký.

Sources indicate that those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

According to recent reports, around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

Sources indicate that “That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller notes with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

Industry observers note that the optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek.

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”.

According to recent reports, for example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as promptly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

In a recent development, “The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller says. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”.

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký.

According to recent reports, but for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Industry observers note that who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you're shopping for an iPad this holiday season, you might be a bit intimidated by Apple's price tags. The iPad mini starts at $599; the base iPad Air is $749; and the entry-level iPad Pro is a whopping $1,199. Most of Apple's iPad line certainly lives up to its expensive reputation.

In a recent development, that's where the iPad A16 comes in. This is Apple's least expensive tablet, with an MSRP of $449. But despite being Apple's "budget" option, the iPad A16 shouldn't be ignored by customers looking for the best all-around device. In fact, it's really the best iPad for most people, which is why I named it the best tablet gift of 2026. What's more, retailers are giving the iPad A16 a $50 discount ahead of Black Friday, bringing the entry-level price down to $399.

Industry observers note that the iPad A16 isn't Apple's best iPad (that would be the iPad Pro). It doesn't have the best display, the best camera, or the best processor. But it doesn't need those things: This iPad has a display, camera, and processor that are good enough for most use cases, without unnecessarily driving up the price. Simply put, it's one of the best tablets you can buy right now.

The iPad A16 has a large, 11-inch (technically 10.86 inches, according to Apple's fine print) IPS display with a brightness of 500 nits. As the name implies, it has Apple's A16 chip, the same processor as the iPhone 14 Pro and iPhone 15. That chip is about four years old at this point, and while that means it won't be as fast as Apple's newer SoCs, it still holds its own with iOS 27. It comes with two cameras: One 12MP wide camera on the back, with support for 4K video recording, and a 12MP Center Stage camera on the front.

Sources indicate that apple indicates this iPad can run for 10 hours while browsing the internet on wifi or watching video. You charge the tablet with USB-C, which supports data transfer up to USB 2.0 (which nets you 480Mb/s transfer speeds). It also comes with other perks you might expect from Apple's more "pro" tablets. You can connect the iPad to an external display, up to 4K resolution at 60Hz. It also supports two Apple Pencil models: The USB-C Apple Pencil and the first-gen Apple Pencil.

The only real consideration here is storage: This model comes with 128GB of storage, which can run out fast. It's particularly usable for users who rely on cloud storage or mostly stream their entertainment. But if your giftee prepares to store photos, videos, or music on their iPad, it's worth considering upgrading. The $50 discount applies to most storage models, as well as the cellular iPad options, except for the 512GB models: The wifi-only model has a smaller discount, while the cellular option has a $100 discount.

Recent findings suggest that sure, the iPad A16 doesn't have the fastest processor, an OLED display, support for newer accessories, or Apple's sharpest cameras. But all of the specs it does have are enough to run the things you need on iPadOS. If someone on your list is looking for an iPad for web browsing, streaming, messaging, and light gaming—and they don't need something for professional work—this device is likely more than enough iPad for them.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Sources indicate that in iOS 27, third-party apps can offer suggestions too. And when multiple apps are available with suggested actions, there’s a drop-down menu to show you all available options.

Smart Reply is a keyboard feature that automatically surfaces reply options you can utilize with a single tap.

In iOS 27, the next generation of Apple Intelligence comes with improvements to Smart Reply.

Apple notes that Smart Reply “can now draw on a user’s personalized writing style.” Essentially, rather than offering fairly generic reply options, now Smart Reply suggestions will actually sound a lot more like you.

Apple has added ‘Ask Siri’ buttons throughout Apple Mail, just like the rest of its system apps. And Siri AI brings a bunch of new powers for Mail users.

#155526. Tech Report: An annoying ‘mistake’ in macOS was actually prep for the latest MacBook Pro

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (492 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: An annoying ‘mistake’ in macOS was actually prep for the latest MacBook Pro

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (492 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You may remember that Apple made a seeming mistake in the user interface for macOS 26, meaning that attempts to resize windows would often fail.
  • Industry observers note that I was one of a number of people to note that trying to grab the corner of a window in macOS Tahoe in order to resize it would often fail.
  • It turns out that my initial click in the window corner instinctively happens in an area where the window doesn’t respond to it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You may remember that Apple made a seeming mistake in the user interface for macOS 26, meaning that attempts to resize windows would often fail. The reason for this has now become clear, and Apple has done something both fun and clever in macOS 27 to resolve it ….

Industry observers note that I was one of a number of people to note that trying to grab the corner of a window in macOS Tahoe in order to resize it would often fail. Developer Norbert Heger pointed out this is because Apple changed the radius of the corners without changing the grabbable area.

It turns out that my initial click in the window corner instinctively happens in an area where the window doesn’t respond to it. The window expects this click to happen in an area of 19 × 19 pixels, located near the window corner. If the window had no rounded corners at all, 62% of that area would lie inside the window. But due to the huge corner radius in Tahoe, most of it – about 75% – now lies outside the window.

Recent findings suggest that at the time, the radius change itself looked like an inexplicable mistake on Apple’s part, and the company did revert it. However, Macworld’s Michael Simon appears to have discovered the reason for the original change.

The new rounder corners on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR are basically a perfect match for the macOS 26 radii.

So if you move a window to the corner of the newly introduced machine, it would fit perfectly. However, since Apple reverted the corner radius, it would no longer do so. The firm solved this by a clever UI transition.

Recent findings suggest that what’s happening there is Golden Gate’s 20-point corner radius is subtly and gradually expanding when It approaches the bottom corner of the screen to match the exact corner of the display, which is much larger. I can’t be certain it’s exactly 26-point, but it sure looks like it to me. The effect is incredible. I’ve watched it like 20 times and I can barely see it changing, yet when it reaches the corner it’s perfectly expanded to match.

It has been revealed that you can see this illustrated by a GIF in the Macworld piece. While the original change annoyed me, Apple’s solution is the perfect example of the tech giant sweating the details.

According to recent reports, the senior execs responsible for the service told staff that it was the most customer-impacting incident ever experienced, and has acknowledged that not only was the problem itself unacceptable, but so too was the time taken to resolve it. Reuters got sight of a memo sent to the team.

According to recent reports, it was the most ⁠customer-impacting incident in the history of Exchange Online, M365 Core President Jason Henderson said in a memo to staff on Friday. Never before had so many customers been without email for so long, he said. “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson added.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, told a Code Red review that the affected component had experienced “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures,” according to Silver’s memo.

One reason it took so long to work out what had happened was because the diagnostic data needed was “scattered across fragmented internal systems.” The memo states 11 separate Teams chats exchanged more than 11,000 messages as they struggled to work out what exactly had gone wrong.

Microsoft is now working on five interrelated approaches to achieve a target resolution time of less than an hour for any future incidents of this nature.

#155520. How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2973 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2973 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Japan’s MMX mission aims to sample the Martian moon Phobos.
  • Japan's MMX spacecraft will fire its engines to slow down and enter orbit around Mars.
  • Sources indicate that last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japan’s MMX mission aims to sample the Martian moon Phobos.

Japan's MMX spacecraft will fire its engines to slow down and enter orbit around Mars.

Sources indicate that last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos, the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute.

NASA’s Perseverance rover captured Phobos passing in front of the Sun from the surface of Mars.ASU/MSSS/SSI/JPL-Caltech/NASA.

Industry observers note that the tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully debuted on 20 October, seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos.

Recent findings suggest that this mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet. Engineers also had to figure out how to assess and land on this low-gravity pile of loosely assembled dirt and rock, how a rover might rove across it, and how the spacecraft might take samples and return them to Earth.

According to recent reports, “I often say that landing on Phobos is like trying to land a balloon,” indicates Yasuhiro Kawakatsu, project manager of MMX at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). “It’s very difficult to drop a balloon to the ground and prevent it from tilting or bouncing.”.

In a recent development, phobos is one of two small Martian moons; the other is Deimos, named after the Greek god of dread and terror. Their cosmic origins are unknown, though there are two prevailing theories. One holds that the moons were once asteroids from the belt between Mars and Jupiter, captured by the smaller planet’s gravity. In the other theory, Phobos and Deimos formed when a large celestial body slammed into Mars, sending debris into orbit. Some models suggest the pair are the last survivors from a cluster of satellites.

The enormous Stickney crater, roughly 9 kilometers across, dominates this view of Phobos taken by NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.University of Arizona/JPL-Caltech/NASA.

Industry observers note that scientifically speaking, Phobos is considered a rubble pile, a loosely consolidated aggregate of rock and dust. Far too small to become spherical under its own mass, it’s shaped like a lumpy potato, roughly 27 kilometers in length, with only 1/1,800th of Earth’s gravity. On Phobos, a typical adult would weigh about as much as a tennis ball does on Earth.

Sources indicate that more than 10 years in the making, MMX released on Japan’s flagship H3 rocket from Tanegashima spaceport on 20 October local time. It will arrive at Mars in 2027 carrying scientific payloads from several space agencies, including NASA, and a new rover called Idefix developed by the French and German space agencies (CNES and DLR) in collaboration with JAXA.

Engineers assembled MMX’s modules at Japan’s Tanegashima Space Center before the spacecraft’s October 2026 launch.JAXA.

Sources indicate that MMX consists of three modules: a propulsion module to power its journey to Mars and apply the brakes to enter orbit around the red planet; an exploration module carrying the rover, sampling gear, and other scientific instruments; and a return module, attached to the exploration module, that harbors the capsule destined for a high-speed reentry into Earth’s atmosphere. After collecting samples on Phobos, the exploration and return modules will lift off together. The exploration module will then be jettisoned while the return module sets a course back home.

Industry observers note that if all goes according to plan, MMX will deliver a 10-gram sample to Earth in the second half of 2031. But the mission will face a series of daunting challenges to reach that end point, including navigating complex orbits around Phobos and landing on its surface while Mars periodically blocks communications with Earth.

The MMX’s modular design includes the propulsion module [left] and the exploration and return modules [right].Kyodo News/Getty Images.

“It’s the most complex mission I have ever seen,” says Patrick Michel, director of research at CNRS (the French National Center for Scientific Research) and co-principal investigator on Idefix.

An H3 rocket carried MMX into space on 20 October 2026, beginning the mission’s five-year journey to Phobos and back.The Asahi Shimbun/Getty Images.

In a recent development, once MMX reached low Earth orbit, its propulsion module’s engine fired, kicking off a nearly year-long deep-space cruise to Mars. On arrival, the spacecraft will need to fire its engines in an extended, carefully timed burn to slow down enough to be captured by Mars gravity. The propulsion module will then be jettisoned, leaving the exploration and return modules to orbit Mars.

“If something doesn’t go according to plan, MMX will fly by Mars and get catapulted into the solar system,” indicates Nicola Baresi, an astrodynamicist who coauthored a paper on specially designed orbits for MMX.

It has been revealed that from that initial orbit, MMX will transition into a specially designed quasi-satellite orbit that allows it to keep pace with the small moon but also move around it. Since Phobos is too small to orbit in the conventional sense, the spacecraft will orbit Mars alongside the moon, following a clever egg-shaped path that slings MMX alternately ahead of and behind the moon. “When you’re closer to Mars, you’re accelerating with respect to Phobos, and when you’re farther from Mars, you’re decelerating. So you essentially go back and forth,” explains Baresi.

Martian Maneuvers To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.Chris Philpot.

To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.

Sources indicate that the best existing images of Phobos, from spacecraft such as NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and ESA’s Mars Express, have resolutions of only a few meters per pixel. That’s larger than Idefix, the mission’s rover, itself about the size of a microwave oven. To map the surface in greater detail, MMX will loop in front of and behind Phobos at distances ranging from 200 kilometers to less than 20 km from the surface.

During its two-year remote sensing campaign, the exploration module will use several cameras and a laser altimeter to map the surface in high resolution and look for candidate landing sites. When Mars passes behind the Sun as seen from the Earth, causing a roughly two-week communications blackout, MMX will retreat into a larger, stable orbit. After communications resume, MMX will prepare to send its first visitor down to the surface.

Before the exploration and connected return modules attempt to land, Kawakatsu says, MMX will send a scout that in Japanese is called “the first penguin,” leaping into unknown waters. For this mission, the first to leap will be the Idefix rover, named for the canine companion to Obelix in the French comics series Asterix. The exploration module will release the rover during a low-altitude pass of between 40 and 100 meters above Phobos’s surface in 2028 or early 2029.

MMX will use its TENGOO camera [left] and LIDAR laser altimeter [right] to map Phobos’s terrain.JAXA.

It will be a tense moment that calls back to 2005, during Japan’s Hayabusa mission to explore the asteroid Itokawa. In a similarly designed drop, the MINERVA rover was released from an orbiter, but erroneously at 200 meters instead of the intended 70 meters. The rover missed the asteroid and, without propulsion, drifted off into deep space.

Idefix will get a slight nudge out of the exploration module toward its negligible-gravity target, freefalling and likely tumbling as it goes. It’s expected to touch down with a velocity of less than 1 meter per second. Unlike rovers that have landed on other surfaces with airbags or dedicated landing legs, Idefix will land without protection, apart from some extra padding on the solar panels due to their critical nature. The barely-there gravity of Phobos should allow the 23-kilogram rover to land softly, though exactly how this landing will play out is hard to predict.

The Idefix rover will travel to Phobos with its wheels tucked in and solar panels folded.DLR.

Industry observers note that “It will bounce probably several times,” says Stephan Ulamec, Idefix’s co-principal investigator and project manager at DLR. “It will come to rest somehow in some position.” Once it’s still, four retracted legs will deploy to right the rover autonomously, regardless of its orientation. It will then unfold its solar panels to charge its batteries for exploration tasks ahead.

It has been revealed that A simulation shows how Idefix is expected to tumble onto Phobos, right itself using its articulated legs, and begin exploring the moon’s surface. DLR.

Once operational, Idefix will roll at a snail’s pace, topping out at one millimeter per second. Its metal wheels have protruding blades like a paddle wheel, designed to gain traction in Phobos’s microgravity. “If we were to drive our rover faster, then it would actually be more like we were swimming through instead of driving across the surface,” says Cecily Sunday, a doctoral student involved in testing Idefix’s WheelCams at the Institut Superieur de l’Aeronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE-Supaéro) in Toulouse, France.

The WheelCams, a pair of cameras placed on the underside of the rover, will observe the wheels and their tracks during Idefix’s planned 100-Earth-day primary mission. The images will help researchers study the size and distribution of grains in Phobos’s regolith and how cohesive they are. How much or how little the grains stick together will greatly impact how Idefix moves. Sunday likens this to the difference between driving on dry and wet sand. “Think of trying to build a sandcastle with dry sand,” she notes. “You can’t. Add water, and suddenly you can.”.

The Idefix rover was mounted between the MMX spacecraft’s landing legs for the journey to Phobos.DLR.

In a recent development, the team tested the rover’s nine-bladed wheels on a variety of materials, including Phobos regolith simulants provided by JAXA and DLR, lunar simulants, glass beads, quartz sand, and clay pebbles. “We characterize the mechanical properties of each simulant precisely, then test across the full range, with varying grain size, angularity, and even color, so we can map what we see in the WheelCam images back to actual surface properties,” Sunday says.

Despite the microgravity and Phobos’s rubble-pile nature, Sunday indicates Earth-based tests can approximate the rover’s motion on the surface of the small moon fairly well. While Phobos’s reduced gravity lowers the rover’s effective weight, there is also reduced pressure between the grains beneath its wheels. “As long as you’re moving very, very slowly and using the same materials and the same weight of the system, they should be representative,” Sunday says.

With four paddle-like wheels and deployable solar panels, Idefix is designed to crawl across Phobos.Ardan Fuessmann/Imago/Alamy.

Idefix’s interactions with its latest home will offer “sub-millimeter resolution and information on porosity, on grain size, on surface strength, on how hard is the material,” Ulamec notes. “It fills a gap between remote observations from orbit and detailed observations of the return samples back on Earth.”.

What Idefix finds on this rocky, rugged world will help determine how and where JAXA attempts to land the main spacecraft. Michel claims the touchdown will provide ground truth for understanding of Phobos. When NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft touched down on the asteroid Bennu to collect a sample, its sampling arm surprisingly sank nearly half a meter into the loose material. But Ulamec doesn’t think Idefix will sink deep into Phobos, noting that Bennu is very different and much smaller, with a diameter of 500 meters.

It has been revealed that once Idefix has investigated the surface, MMX will face an even greater challenge: landing its much larger exploration module on Phobos. The spacecraft will make a controlled descent to roughly 10 meters above the surface, then drop the remaining distance in free fall. With so little gravity to pull it downward, even a small sideways motion could cause the lander to tip or bounce away. A successful, upright landing would mark the start of up to two hours on Phobos for the crucial sampling phase.

Sources indicate that the MMX mission draws on the experience and technologies of Japan’s two Hayabusa sample-return missions, which landed on the asteroids Itokawa and Ryugu. But this mission has many more moving parts. MMX’s exploration module will use two sampling devices—a coring sampler developed by JAXA and a pneumatic sampler provided by NASA and fabricated by Honeybee Robotics, a subsidiary of Blue Origin. Data from these tools, and those carried by the Idefix rover, could answer questions about the origin of Phobos and how the Mars system has evolved.

Industry observers note that the coring sampler uses a robot arm and a cylindrical corer designed to reach at least 2 centimeters below the surface. The arm can maneuver to find the best site for digging. “That by itself is a challenge because we’ve never done it,” Michel says. “You never know what can happen at the very sampling site itself, where you might have a boulder and the arm cannot move.”.

Probing beneath the top layer will be valuable because solar radiation, galactic cosmic rays, and micrometeorites have battered and weathered the surface. The material below should offer a better record of the moon’s origins, and JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grams of it.

MMX will carry both the Idefix rover [bottom] and a robotic coring sampler [top] designed to dig beneath Phobos’s weathered surface.JAXA.

Sources indicate that the pneumatic sampler takes a different approach. Mounted on one of the lander’s legs, it will inject pure, non-reactive nitrogen gas into the surface and capture the grains stirred up. This sample could illuminate the changes Mars and its moons have undergone over time. The dual system also adds redundancy in the face of Phobos’s unknowns. “If the surface of Phobos proves to be very hard, [the coring sampler] may struggle to penetrate the ground. [The pneumatic sampler] would not experience this glitch and still be able to gather material,” Kawakatsu states.

Industry observers note that one of the most intriguing aspects of MMX is the additional possibility of collecting material from the planet below. It’s likely that Phobos has been peppered by Martian ejecta thrown into space by meteor impacts, so MMX also provides an opportunity to return the first Martian samples to Earth. Michel estimates that the samples could contain “a few hundred grains coming from Mars.” Scientists can distinguish those grains from native Phobos material by analyzing their oxygen isotopes.

Sources indicate that that possibility raises a planetary-protection question. A direct Mars sample-return mission would have to follow strict rules to ensure that potentially living biological material from Mars doesn’t contaminate Earth. But those protocols don’t apply to MMX, even if its sample does collect grains of Martian soil. A panel of experts concluded that any microbes blasted off Mars wouldn’t survive the violent impact and ejection or the intense radiation exposure on the way to Phobos. This saved MMX from implementing expensive and time-consuming quarantine and containment protocols for the returning sample.

After landing on Phobos, MMX will have roughly two hours to collect samples from the moon’s surface before lifting off again.JAXA.

During the brief surface operation, the robotic arm will deposit the samples in a storage unit, from which they’ll be transferred into a capsule aboard the return module and sealed in a vacuum. After that, lift off.

Once back in Mars orbit, the exploration module will resume its observations of Phobos and make several flybys of Mars’s other diminutive moon, Deimos, to gather data on its surface, structure, and composition. In November 2030, during a favorable alignment of Mars and Earth, MMX will begin the homeward leg of its trip. The return module will separate from the exploration module and power the voyage home, its sole objective to bring the dust of Phobos to Earth.

MMX’s sample return capsule will carry material from Phobos through Earth’s atmosphere in 2031.JAXA.

Finally, in 2031, the 60-centimeter-wide sample capsule will plunge into Earth’s atmosphere at roughly 12 kilometers per second. Assuming it survives the extreme heat of reentry and lands safely in Australia, scientists will begin to tease out clues about Phobos and the early solar system. JAXA’s Institute of Space and Astronautical Science will receive and curate the samples, which will also be shared with mission partners.

Recent findings suggest that “We have macroscale measurements from the spacecraft, microscale measurements with the rover, and then sample analysis,” Michel claims. “So we can relate the three kinds of scales together because we have all of them.” The insights gleaned from orbital images, close-up images of the regolith, and the chemical analysis of the samples could have wider implications for our understanding of our solar system.

Sources indicate that “MMX is a mission to understand the Mars system and shed light onto how terrestrial planets like the Earth, and maybe Mars, develop a habitable environment,” Kawakatsu indicates. “We strongly suspect that our terrestrial planet region formed dry, and water and organics were scattered inwards from the icy-rich outer solar system.” Mars, he says, sits at the gateway between the inner and outer solar system, making its moons valuable witnesses to the processes that shaped potentially habitable worlds.

A price drop always stands out more when the product in question already has a reputation for delivering above its size, and that’s the case with the Bose SoundLink Plus. It hasn’t been on the market for long, but it’s already earned strong reviews—CNET labeled it “the Goldilocks of Bose Bluetooth speakers.” And right now, for Black Friday, it’s down to $179, which is the lowest price we've seen.

It has been revealed that bose positions it right in the middle of the SoundLink lineup, and you feel that balance in how it’s built. It’s compact enough to clip onto a backpack using its built-in nylon strap, and tough enough to handle getting knocked around, and sealed against dust and full water submersion with an IP67 rating. Battery life can last up to 20 hours, depending on the volume, which is sufficient for full-day outings. On the connectivity side, there’s Bluetooth 5.4 with AAC and AptX Adaptive support, as well as the ability to keep two devices paired for smoother switching. What you don’t get is a microphone, an aux port, or any voice assistant support, which is worth considering if you prefer wired options or use speakers for calls.

As for its sound profile, it leans into mid- and high-bass, which gives electronic and pop tracks a lively pulse, though at higher volumes, you may notice some compression (which is common in speakers this size). It also doesn’t reach into true low-bass territory, so anyone who wants thumping sub-bass may not get it here, but the punch it does deliver feels clean for its size, notes this PCMag review. And while you won't get the width and separation of a stereo mix since the SoundLink Plus plays audio in mono, its directivity is good—meaning its sound remains clear from different listening positions, so you don't have to sit directly in front of it to get a good experience.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Rust library for building communications applications. SIP, RTP, WebRTC, QUIC/WebTransport/WebSocket conversations, Media over QUIC, and voice-AI agents share one call model, and the whole stack is in the box: no external SIP server, media server, or RTP engine to install and wire together.

Sources indicate that five-minute start · For carriers · Which crate? · Pick a path · How it fits together · What ships · Interop evidence · Changes · Upgrading from 0.3.

In a recent development, rvoip is a library, not a server you deploy next to your application. Signalling, media, codecs, NAT traversal, security, and the conversation model are all Rust crates in this workspace, so a call goes from your code to the wire without a separately installed SIP proxy, media server, or RTP engine. The examples below run on a laptop with nothing installed but Rust; the same crates carry the release-gated interoperability evidence against Asterisk, FreeSWITCH, Jambonz, Kamailio, and OpenSIPS. Carriers evaluating standards coverage, performance, and reliability should start with For carriers.

One AWS c8i.4xlarge (16 vCPU, 8 cores, Intel Xeon 6, 32 GiB) running a single rvoip process, measured with the RFC 7501/7502 benchmark:.

At 2x capacity, rvoip keeps admitting calls at its max CPS, refuses the excess with fast 503 responses, and recovers cleanly once the load drops.

Full method and per-trial data: RFC 7501/7502 benchmark report.

Industry observers note that upgrading an existing application from 0.3? The 0.4 migration guide has before/after code for every breaking change.

2. Make a call. Bob answers, Alice dials, Alice hangs up. Everything runs on loopback, so this works on a laptop with no PBX, no account, and no network setup.

3. Or run the same program from the checkout.

From here, examples/ walks forward one step at a time: real microphone audio, registering to a PBX, hold/DTMF, transfers, SRTP and TLS, an IVR, a B2BUA, then browser and voice-AI gateways.

In a recent development, the workspace contains 47 crates. You import one of them; it pulls in everything it needs. The rest are internal layers you never name in your own Cargo.toml.

Deployment backends (Keycloak, LDAP, Redis, Postgres vCon storage, audit and SIEM sinks, SAML, SCIM, WebAuthn, STIR/SHAKEN, IMS AKA) are separate rvoip-* extension crates you add only when you operate that backend. The extension catalog lists them.

Industry observers note that for JavaScript UCTP control, see the experimental browser/Node WebSocket client. It is available as source with TypeScript declarations; the package is not yet published to npm. Application-profile dispatch is a separate opt-in server extension that stock servers do not enable.

Four API surfaces, from simplest to most control. Most applications use the first one.

Register an account on a PBX and place a call through it:.

Answer calls and react to key presses, the shape of an IVR or auto-attendant:.

Recent findings suggest that security and transports are configuration, not different APIs: SDES-SRTP in 07-secure-call-srtp, TLS in 08-tls-transport, DTLS-SRTP, G.729, AMR-NB/WB, and Opus behind Cargo features. The full surface is documented in the SIP crate README.

RvoipApp declares transports, roles, and routing through one builder and runs SIP, WebRTC, and UCTP listeners on the shared Orchestrator:.

In a recent development, start from 12-customer-escalation-sip-webrtc: a browser chat escalates to a SIP agent's phone. For SIP into Amazon Connect, see 13-sip-to-amazon-connect.

In a recent development, hosted agent. rvoip-vapi speaks Vapi's bidirectional raw-audio WebSocket directly. Your SIP or WebRTC caller is bridged to the agent through the Orchestrator; the agent joins as its own AI participant with typed events, control messages, and supervised teardown. Start from 14-vapi-agent, one server that accepts either kind of caller. Attaching an agent to a caller you already hold:.

Your own pipeline. rvoip-harness gives you ASR, TTS, dialog, and recording provider traits, and rvoip-vcon emits signed vCon records of the conversation. 11-ai-harness-demo runs the whole loop with deterministic providers, so you can see the shape before you plug in a real model.

Recent findings suggest that every transport turns into the same objects, so an application written against the conversation model does not care whether a leg arrived over SIP, a browser, or QUIC. That is what lets one Orchestrator bridge them.

Words you will meet in the API:.

Adapters depend on the shared ConnectionAdapter trait; the core never imports a transport. The design docs go deeper, starting with INTERFACE_DESIGN.md and CONVERSATION_PROTOCOL.md.

Developer preview means implemented and published, but API-unstable or outside that attestation. Planned items appear only in the roadmap. It has been revealed that all 14 extension crates ship at 0.5.1. They stay optional so protocol crates depend on provider contracts, never on a deployment backend.

How they attach: voip-3 on the facade brings in the harness, vCon, and the identity surface; vapi and sip-stir-shaken are their own facade features; everything else is a direct dependency.

The contracts they implement live in rvoip-auth-core, rvoip-consumers-core, and rvoip-identity.

Shark and Dyson are two of the biggest names in vacuums — but which one is better? Which one makes the best vacuum? I've tested Dysons, Samsungs, Ultenics, and I've previously owned Sharks. So let's get to the bottom of the best-value vacuum cleaner, especially considering it's Black Friday — A.K.A. the best time to buy upcoming tech.

Today, I'm going to help you decide between six of the most popular Shark and Dyson vacuums, starting from just $189. What's a HEPA filter? Do you need a laser eye? What about suction power? What does RPM actually mean?

In a recent development, I'll help you get to the bottom of it all — and hopefully you'll leave knowing precisely which vacuum cleaner to invest in this Black Friday. So long, dusty carpets and crumbly floors!

Unfortunately, Shark doesn't list its suction power, but all of these models automatically monitor floor type and adjust power for hardwood and carpeted surfaces.

The Shark Power Pro Reveal Plus is the cheapest option on this list; it automatically adjusts suction power for hardwood and carpet, has an LED headlight to illuminate every speck of dust, and lasts for up to 40 minutes.

The Shark Power Detect Pet Plus Clean & Empty lasts for a huge 70 minutes on one charge, adjusts suction power for hardwood and carpeted floors, and even automatically empties itself with the emptying station.

The Shark Power Detect Speed Plus Clean & Empty is only discounted in oatmeal (pictured), lasts for 60 minutes on a single charge, and, like the Power Detect Pet Plus Clean & Empty, automatically empties and charges itself with the included station.

Dyson's vacuums tend to be pricier than Shark's, but Dyson publishes each model's RPM and air wattage so you know exactly how powerful the vacuums are before you buy.

With 40 mins of battery life, 100 air watts of suction, and a 120,000 RPM motor, the Dyson V9 is a powerful and lightweight vacuum for everyday cleaning.

A level up from the V9, the V10 offers 60 minutes of battery life, 150 air watts of suction, and even has a 125,000 RPM motor. The Konical Variant is also $329 and has a green laser to illuminate dust.

The most expensive model on this list, the Dyson V15 Detect boasts 60 minutes of runtime, a green laser to illuminate dust, 240 air watts of suction power, and a 125,000-RPM motor.

Shark Power Detect Pet Plus Clean & Empty.

Shark Power Detect Speed Plus Clean & Empty.

It has been revealed that the best-value model on this list is far and away the Shark Power Pro Reveal Plus. Right now, this stick vacuum is just $179, which is $90 cheaper than Dyson's cheapest, the V9 Motobar.

In a recent development, although Shark doesn't publish its air wattage, it would be a fine vacuum for everyday cleaning. The battery lasts for 40 minutes on eco mode; usually, stick vacuums go for around ten minutes on full power. This Shark model also has an LED light, which is a feature I look for on every vacuum. Now that I've used a vacuum with an LED light, I can't ever go back — it's so much easier to spot pesky dirty patches with a light.

Sources indicate that neither of the other Shark models offer an LED light, which is disappointing to see — but they do both have automatic bin emptying and charging. If you often forget to empty or charge your stick vacuum, you might want to check out these two models (Power Detect Pet and Power Detect Speed).

Sources indicate that if you can afford it, I'd also recommend the Dyson V10 Cyclone. If you get the Konical Variant, which is $329, it has a green laser light to illuminate all patches of dirt.

The priciest option on this list is the Dyson V15 Detect, $598, but has the highest-rated air wattage for the most powerful suction.

Personally, I would buy the Dyson V10 Konical variant as I can't live without the green laser. At $329, 150 air watts of suction and 125,000RPM motor power is a sweet deal.

A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then shows how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that with iPads running the same chips as Macs, many have wished Apple would give us the option of running macOS on them instead of the somewhat clunky iPadOS windowing system. Apple’s previous arguments against converging devices have been somewhat weakened by the launch of the touchscreen MacBook Pro.

A new report indicates that Apple already has iPads running macOS internally, and that work on a giant iPad continues, but don’t hold your breath for a public launch of either ….

Sources indicate that as iPad hardware has grown more powerful over the years, the software has struggled to keep up. We saw split-screen capabilities first, with full windowing finally coming to the devices in iPadOS 26 last year.

The UI is still rather clunky compared to macOS, however, leading a significant number of people to wish that Apple simply offered the option of using the more powerful operating system on its tablet devices.

Industry observers note that I would be comfortable with 11" and 13" devices running macOS. Actually, I don’t require them to run macOS itself, but I do need them to run macOS apps. I wish the iPad could match a MacBook’s productivity. Running macOS on an iPad seems like a reasonable idea. The MacBook Air is now the better price choice, while those needing a powerhouse will always choose a MacBook Pro or Studio.

Some suggest that running macOS on iPad would reduce Mac sales, but I disagree. I own a nearly full-spec MacBook Pro 16" and expect to keep a machine like that, yet I also purchased a MacBook Air for lighter travel. I would prefer an iPad over the Air, but I cannot choose it because it lacks the apps I require. If it supported them, I would buy the iPad Pro with all accessories, and Apple would gain more revenue from me. I appreciate the concept of owning an iPad, but currently it lacks the value needed to justify paying more for a device that simply does less than a MacBook Air.

In a podcast Q&A, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says that Apple is already doing this internally, but there’s no sign of any aims to make it available outside the company.

Recent findings suggest that apple has iPads internally running macOS, and they’ve had that for some time. The fact that they have the underlying architecture of Apple Silicon that’s the same on the iPad and the Mac gives them the flexibility in order to test these types of things.

In terms if they’re actually going to do it – would they bring macOS to the iPad itself – at this point I don’t think that’s going to happen anytime soon. I’ve checked into this and there’s no ongoing operating system project right now in terms of a brand fresh operating system for the iPad – there is no work being done to consumerize macOs on the iPad.

Gurman states Apple seems set to continue to make piecemeal changes over time to bring iPad capabilities closer to those of the Mac but is showing no signs of full convergence.

He reiterated that work on a long-rumored giant-sized folding iPad continues.

In a recent development, the other thing I want to say is that I’m really excited for this potential of Project J312. That is, this giant 19-inch, 20-inch foldable iPad. And it’s basically like a gigantic iPhone Duo with no display on the outside.

However, he notes there’s no guarantee it will ever launch, saying the timings have already slipped from 2027 through 2028 to 2029, but both cost and yield concerns may still kill the project. If it does launch, it’s expected to cost anywhere from $3,000 to $5,000.

  • Which you go for depends on a few key factors, relating to the design options and some select features that are only on the newer models.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I was excited for Garmin Fenix 8 Pro deals this Black Friday, and knew the Fenix 8 would also be on sale, but I did not expect Garmin to cut the price of the Fenix 9 Pro too, because it only came out a couple of months ago.

I’ve tested all three watches extensively, running marathons with the Fenix 8 and Fenix 8 Pro and using the Fenix 9 Pro for the past couple of months after its launch, and all three have their merits in the sales.

Which you go for depends on a few key factors, relating to the design options and some select features that are only on the newer models.

Below I’ve highlighted what I think the key differences are between the watches, to hopefully help you make a call on which to buy.

The main reason to get the oldest Fenix of the trio is value, because it comes in $100 cheaper than the Fenix 8 Pro on sale, even when opting for a sapphire titanium model.

However, it’s not the only reason, because the orange Garmin Fenix 8 on sale is actually one of the best-looking Garmins ever made, in my opinion, and also a little bit thinner than the newer Fenix models.

According to recent reports, the Fenix 8 offers the best value of the three latest Fenixes on sale, and only misses out on a few key features compared to the newer watches. You don't get LTE and satellite connectivity or quite as bright an AMOLED display, but it still nails the essentials of sports tracking and navigation, and does so for $100 less than the Fenix 8 Pro.

As you’d expect, you miss out on some features by getting the Fenix 8, most notably the LTE and satellite connectivity available on the newer Pro models.

It also has a slightly less bright AMOLED display, which I can’t say I’ve noticed too much in my testing, and lacks the green flashlight setting and faster maps on the Fenix 9 Pro.

Garmin is actually rolling back most of the software features that arrived on the Fenix 9 Pro to the Fenix 8, though, and in general it matches the latest watches well for key sports tracking, training analysis, battery life, and navigation features.

I really don’t think you lose out on too much by getting the Fenix 8 myself, and there are three size options to pick between, along with the choice of an AMOLED or MIP display.

The main reason I’d choose the Garmin Fenix 8 Pro over the Fenix 8 is its connectivity features, which can be a lifesaver if you regularly venture off the grid or like to leave your phone behind during activities.

Getting those features while saving $150 compared with the Fenix 9 Pro makes the Fenix 8 Pro a tempting option for adventurers.

Aside from the more attractive, all-titanium design, green flashlight, and faster maps on the Fenix 9 Pro, the Fenix 8 Pro really does match up well with the newer watch on features, and you can get it for $150 less in the sales.

However, the Fenix 8 Pro only comes in AMOLED (or MicroLED, but that’s still wildly expensive) and 47mm and 51mm sizes, so those looking for a 43mm or MIP watch will have to opt for the Fenix 8 or Fenix 9 instead.

If you have to have the latest and greatest smartwatch on your wrist, it’s the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro, and the fact that it’s reduced at all is a pleasant surprise this Black Friday.

The main upgrade on the Fenix 8 Pro is the all-titanium design of the Fenix 9 Pro, which I have to say is incredibly attractive and a bigger enhancement than I expected.

All models of the Garmin Fenix 9 are reduced by at least $100 for Black Friday, including the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro with InReach, which is the watch I'm using as my main tracker right now. If you want the latest and greatest Garmin watch, this is the time to buy it, because it's the first time it's been discounted anywhere.

You also get a green flashlight mode, which I do now use more often than the white mode as it doesn’t ruin your night vision, and faster panning and zooming with maps.

As it’s the newest watch, the Fenix 9 Pro will also be getting software updates further into the future than the Fenix 8 and Fenix 8 Pro, though Garmin has shown more willingness to roll back upgrades to older models recently.

You can save $100 on any model of the Fenix 9 Pro, which has MIP and AMOLED options in its lineup, plus three sizes, and there’s actually one Fenix 9 model that’s reduced even further, which is the 43mm Fenix 9.

This sneaky little deal on one color of the 43mm Garmin Fenix 9 makes it the cheapest model of the latest watch available by $50. It misses out on some upgrades you do get on the Fenix 9 Pro, but given that the Fenix 8 Pro only comes in 47mm and 51mm sizes, this is the best 43mm Fenix you can get for $849.

The standard Fenix 9 doesn’t have the all-titanium build or extra connectivity of the Pro models (or the green flashlight mode), so I think the Fenix 8 Pro is better value at the same price, but this is the cheapest you’ll find Garmin’s latest flagship anywhere.

These are the best over-ear headphones I tested in 2025 (or ever, really). Right now, you can get the WH-1000XM6 headphones for $348 (originally $459.99), their lowest price ever during the early Black Friday sale from Amazon.

Recent findings suggest that the XM6 headphones improve on what were already excellent headphones. Sony upped the count of microphones from eight to 12 when compared to the XM5, which improves more than just how well you sound to someone on a phone call. The microphones are used in almost all of its features, like ANC, Adaptive Sound Control, and the headphones' Ambient Sound mode. They hear your surroundings to adapt their features accordingly. If you switch from a noisy room to a quiet one, the XM6 can switch from ANC to "aware mode" (if you have Adaptive Sound Control on).

It has been revealed that these headphones have a lot more features that you can nerd out on in their companion app. The audio quality is second to none, with the fully customizable EQ giving you plenty of options to get the sound how you like it. I really like being able to see what codec you're listening to in the app's main menu. That way, there's no guessing if you're getting the best audio quality or not. They will give you 30 hours of battery life with ANC on and 40 hours of juice with ANC off. There's an AUX (3.5mm) jack for wired listening, which is a nice touch for audiophiles who still rock iPod Classics (or is that just me?).

Recent findings suggest that the XM6s were not just the best headphones of 2025, but are still the best ones of 2026 and likely to be the best ones for years to come. For $348, you'll be securing the best for a record-low price.

Fans had a lot to say about this season of Dancing with the Stars — and not just about who should or shouldn’t have gone home before the Nov. 24 finale.

Julianne Hough broke out of her comfort zone this fall by donning “super extravagant and wild and playful” gowns while emceeing with Alfonso Ribeiro, she told Glamour. But her body-hugging, attention-seeking frocks sometimes upstaged the celebrities, which didn’t land well with the show’s hyper-critical fans.

In an interview with the fashion and beauty outlet, Hough acknowledged that her collaboration with celebrity stylist Brad Goreski had her initially thinking his selections were “too colorful … too much.” But that doesn’t mean she jibed with the negative feedback. Related Stories News 'Dancing With The Stars' Season 35 Finale Scores Series' Best Performance Among Young Adults In 15 Years News 'Dancing With The Stars' Finale Recap: Who Takes Home The Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy?

Industry observers note that “Apathy is the enemy,” she told Glamour. “The reason things exist and have charge and stay visible [is] people either love it or hate it. They still want to talk about it.” Watch on Deadline.

For his part, Goreski welcomes the feedback.

Sources indicate that “Any conversation, good or bad, around fashion is great. I think people weighing in — they like the hair but not the dress; they thought it was a bad outfit; they think she should fire me — is totally fine, because we’re really excited by what we’re doing, and we put a lot of thought and energy into it,” he told the outlet.

It has been revealed that “I think Jules ultimately brings the looks to life, and I’m glad that there’s another part of the show that people talk about,” he continued. “Not every person’s going to love every look. I know that from being a stylist for 15 years. And that’s OK.”.

Hough, who previously competed and judged on the show, started co-hosting DWTS in the fall of 2023. She and Ribeiro just finished emceeing a successful and very emotional season of the ABC variety show; the Nov. 24 finale scored 9.2 million total live + same-day viewers across ABC and Disney+, making it the most-watched episode of the season.

In a recent development, the Hoka Speedgoat 7 is the latest version of Hoka's popular trail-running shoe and offers a comfortable ride and secure grip across a wide variety of terrain. The colors and sizes still left in the sale are limited, so you'll need to move fast to grab this deal.

Recent findings suggest that this springy, carbon plate trail shoe makes every off-road run more fun, and if you are tackling epic ultramarathons and want a fast and comfortable ride, the Hoka Tecton X3 is one of the best shoes available.
