It has been revealed that when Saatva CEO Ron Rudzin first proposed selling luxury mattresses online, he was met with disbelief. “They thought I was crazy,” Rudzin told us. “They said, ‘Sell mattresses and no one touches them before they buy?'".

In a recent development, but 16 years later, Saatva has proven that you can shop for a high-quality bed without the obligatory five minute lie down in a bricks and mortar store. And the mattress that has catapulted Saatva into the mainstream? The Saatva Classic, a handcrafted hybrid that marries traditional bed design with a modern approach to mattress shopping.

In an exclusive interview for Tom's Guide, Byron Golub, Saatva's Senior Vice President of Product, talks us through the design and creation of Saatva's number one mattress and explains why 'classic' never goes out of style.

The Saatva Black Friday sale is serving up the best prices we've seen since Labor Day, and we don't expect them to drop any lower ahead of the Presidents' Day sales in February, making now a great time to buy. A one-year sleep trial, a limited lifetime warranty and free white glove delivery are included with every Saatva Classic.

Our Saatva Classic mattress review score: ★★★★★.

Recent findings suggest that “The Saatva Classic began with a straightforward but ambitious premise," explains Golub. "The American consumer deserved access to the kind of sleep experience typically reserved for the world’s finest hotels — without the traditional retail markup that put luxury mattresses out of reach for most people.”.

To achieve that balance of 'luxury' and 'affordable', founders Ron Rudzin and Ricky Joshi had to cut out a part of the mattress buying process that, until now, had been considered integral.

They got rid of the mattress store – Saatva was going online-only.

Industry observers note that in 2010, this was a bolder premise than it sounds today. But by losing the inherent costs of a brick-and-mortar mattress store, Saatva could pass on the savings to the customer.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

And, in doing so, hopefully cut down on what Golub describes as the familiar frustration of an industry that was “opaque, overcomplicated, and overpriced.”.

Officially introduced in 2010, Saatva, which derives from the Sanskrit word meaning truth and purity, started with just one mattress.

This luxury hybrid-innerspring drew from the traditional design of hotel mattresses and would go on to become the flagship Classic.

“The Classic introduced as Saatva’s founding product and was among the first luxury mattresses sold direct to the consumer online — at a time when buying a mattress without lying on it in a showroom was still a novel concept,” states Golub.

“The result was a mattress that could compete with what you’d find at a five-star property, built to support healthy sleep from the ground up.”.

With the Classic mattress, Saatva hoped to merge three key concepts:.

Spinal alignment was a central design requirement from the start, which led to an early focus on zoned support.

The design process resulted in a multi-layered mattress that relied on traditional innerspring support to deliver "hotel-grade" comfort but for the "everyday sleeper.".

It has been revealed that the Saatva Classic comes in two heights, 11.5" and 14.5", and is crafted from a combination of coils and comfort foam. Each layer contributes to the overall sleep comfort.

From top to bottom, here's a detailed look at how a Saatva Classic is constructed:.

Recent findings suggest that the Classic is available in three feels. You can opt for a Plush Soft (3/10 on the mattress firmness scale), Luxury Firm (5-7/10) or Firm (8/10). The basic construction of the Classic remains the same regardless of firmness but the foams in the Eurotop have a different ILD (Impression Load Deflection) based on the feel. Saatva foams have an ILD of between 18 and 30, and the exact foam and fiber blend changes depending on the feel. The Classic is also available in two mattress heights: 11.5" and 14.5". The taller model has two extra turns in the base coil unit, to add height.

The Classic's 3-inch Euro pillowtop is encased in an organic cotton blend fabric, grown without pesticides and GMOs, backed to a low-melt polyester for durability. Tape edges give a gold damask finish.

Fiberglass-free, the Classic uses a plant-based flame retardant of thistle and wool pulp, bonded with small amounts of polyester. The surface is finished with Guardin® antimicrobial botanical fabric treatment, containing thyme, geranium, lemongrass, mint and more.

‘Lumbar Zone Quilting’ is used in the central third of the mattress, to add extra support at the base of the spine. This sewing technique places the tufting in close configuration, creating a tighter finish that comes pre-compressed, to avoid your body sinking.

Sources indicate that sitting beneath is a ½” gel-infused visco-elastic memory foam lumbar crown with an ‘active spinal wire’ — a wire frame sized to the perimeter of the lumbar crown — below. Increased reinforcement at the lumbar, this unique feature is patented by Saatva.

Golub explains that the design process of the Classic is centered on the guiding principle of restorative sleep. “Every element of the Classic was interrogated through that lens," he says.

"Not just comfort in the moment of lying down, but the kind of deep, uninterrupted sleep that leaves you genuinely restored the next morning.”.

It’s a bold ideal but one the brand has tried to realize practically through a focus on lumbar support. This design element is key to the Classic’s continued success — both on the market and in our Sleep Lab.

The center third of the mattress, where the heaviest part of the body rests, demands the most attention.

According to recent reports, I've tested the Saatva Classic multiple times and the first thing that always stands out is a sense of relief. From head-to-toe, the Classic's support enables you to let go of tension and simply relax.

Rudzin describes targeted support as the "most important thing about all Saatva beds.".

"Spinal alignment was a central design requirement from the start," continues Golub, "which led to an early focus on zoned support.

"That's the understanding that the body needs different levels of firmness in different areas, and that the center third of the mattress, where the heaviest part of the body rests, demands the most attention.”.

It has been revealed that in the Classic, four design elements form this vital support core. These are:.

This focus on support has earned the Classic endorsement from the American Chiropractic Association. Golub explains this is an independent assessment of the Classic's construction, awarded to finished models.

According to recent reports, while lumbar support might be a guiding principle of the Classic, its luxury design is equally vital to its success. And this hotel indulgence isn't just found in the finish, but woven through the construction process.

Because each mattress is made fresh for the person who ordered it, Saatva can use materials and construction methods that wouldn’t survive long-term storage.

Sources indicate that “Every Saatva Classic is built to order," explains Golub. "Production begins only after a customer places their order, through a network of factories across the United States.".

Golub believes this 'off the line' delivery is essential to achieving a high-quality mattress.

"It matters to the design in a very direct way: because each mattress is made fresh for the person who ordered it, Saatva can use materials and construction methods that wouldn’t survive long-term storage.".

Industry observers note that he notes that higher-quality foams, hand-finished upholstery, and other details might degrade if left sitting in an inventory. (While boxed mattresses have proven themselves to be a convenient way forward for the sleep industry, Saatva’s commitment to traditional flat delivery adds to the appeal of the Classic.).

Industry observers note that "It also aligns with Saatva’s commitment to sustainability," says Golub. "Building to order means no overproduction, no excess inventory, and no waste from products that never find a home.".

According to recent reports, and Golub notes the "service experience" is considered part of the product by Saatva. Free white glove delivery, including set up and old mattress removal, is as integral to the product as the tufted top.

And for a brand that emphasizes lumbar support and back pain relief, it’s a bonus that someone else carries the bed up the stairs for you.

Since launch in 2010, Saatva has made some significant changes, including expanding its line-up to encompass all-foam, latex and even smart beds.

The brand also opened its first Saatva Viewing Room in 2019, offering customers a chance to get hands-on with the Saatva mattress line-up, while a team of Saatva Sleep Guides are on hand to answer any questions.

Howeve, the basic design of the Saatva Classic has remained largely unchanged.

“The architecture that defined the Classic on day one — the dual coil system, the Euro pillow top, the Lumbar Zone reinforcement, our signature mattress cover made with organic cotton — remains intact,” explains Golub.

Even so, the mattress you buy in today’s Saatva mattress sales isn’t the same Classic you would have picked up in 2010. Golub explain that over the years Saatva has focused not on redesign, but on improving the caliber of the components and the refinement of the craftsmanship.

According to recent reports, for example, in 2018 Saatva introduced its Lumbar Zone Quilting and gold damask borders. In 2023, the brand merged with Bedding Industries of America, its primary supplier, to gain more control over the quality and composition of each made-to-order mattress.

"But the bones of the product are exactly what they were at launch," claims Golub. "Which is a point of pride: we got the fundamentals right.”.

The Cutthroat Business of Shipwrecks

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1019 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jstor

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 1627, treasures started to wash up on the beaches of France: diamonds, ebony, precious porcelain, spices, ivory, ambergris, and bezoars.
  • According to recent reports, the disaster rapidly threatened to become an international incident.
  • It’s easy to understand why a beachcomber who found a diamond in the sand might want to hold onto it, but there was a legal basis for their claims.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1627, treasures started to wash up on the beaches of France: diamonds, ebony, precious porcelain, spices, ivory, ambergris, and bezoars. Two Portuguese ships, so huge they were referred to as “floating cities,” had shipwrecked off the coast of Bordeaux, spilling luxury goods into the waves.

According to recent reports, the disaster rapidly threatened to become an international incident. The owners of the cargo (unsurprisingly) wanted their goods back—but the coast dwellers claimed that anything that washed up on shore was theirs by the ancient droit du naufrage, the “right of wreck.”.

It’s easy to understand why a beachcomber who found a diamond in the sand might want to hold onto it, but there was a legal basis for their claims. The “right of wreck” was a long-lived and widespread custom, one that shaped the very architecture of seaside towns: in his travels through Norfolk, Daniel Defoe wrote that the “country people had scarce a barn, or a shed, or a stable…but what was built of old planks, beams, wales and timbers, &c. the wrecks of ships, and ruins of mariners and merchants’ fortunes.”.

That remarked, in legal terms, the right of wreck was a little more complicated than “finders keepers.” In many places, it wasn’t actually the person who stumbled on the shipwrecked goods who held the right to them; rather, they became the property of the local lord. In the earliest iterations of this idea, poor shipwreck survivors could find themselves roughly stripped of all their goods—as King Richard I of England found when his fleet was unlucky enough to wash up off the coast of Cyprus, circa 1191. His fiancée and his sister were taken as captives by the emperor of the island, who also helped himself to all the treasure they’d been traveling with. (This didn’t end well for the emperor, who lost his throne in the ensuing war.).

Neither wealthy merchants nor traveling kings were particularly enthusiastic about the idea that an accident at sea could mean forfeiting all their cargo. On the other hand, powerful landowners were eager to preserve their right to the occasional random windfall. As international trade increased, the right of wreck was slowly reshaped by centuries of legal wrangling. Courts battling over who could keep what ended up creating, for instance, highly specific legal definitions for terms like “flotsam” (goods that just happened to float to the surface after a wreck) and “jetsam” (goods intentionally tossed from a ship to make it lighter).

It has been revealed that the resulting patchwork of rules meant that every shipwreck was a complex negotiation between competing interests. Usually, the owners of the shipwrecked goods were entitled to their property back, in exchange for some kind of fee. Whether that was a ransom or a fair reward for helping salvage the goods is a matter of perspective.

Recent findings suggest that in 1236, King Henry III of England issued an edict stating that if “man, dog, or cat” escaped the shipwreck alive, finders were obligated to hold on to the wrecked goods for three months, allowing the survivors to claim them in that time. There is a bit of an issue with that rule: it’s easy to see how it could create an incentive for shore dwellers to do away with shipwreck survivors in order to claim their goods (whether those survivors be man, dog, or cat).

In a recent development, legends of these dark deeds swirled for centuries, but there’s little evidence they really happened. Still, people could be rough in their efforts to “salvage.” In Estonia, for instance, where the local lords were entitled to rewards if they helped to save ships in distress, people developed a habit of launching into enthusiastic “rescue” operations, whether or not there was any real danger.

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

Industry observers note that A particularly good wreck could spark a feeding frenzy. An account of the wreck of the Golden Grape in 1641 gives a sense of the chaos:.

According to recent reports, the first arrivals on the beach contented themselves with staving in barrels and filling linen bags and pockets with raisins or, stripping off their waistcoats, used the sleeves as bags. But soon bands of men appeared from the various villages… Some gangs or men took away a score or two of barrels of raisins or the same number of jars of oil, but they were lucky if they did not have to share their booty with a stronger gang before they could gain a place of safety.

Not everything washes ashore, of course; many of the treasures lost in wrecks sank under the waves. There were fortunes to be made, but in a time before diving equipment, the trouble was how to reach it. In the early modern era, for the most part, even European sailors could hardly swim. But Africans living by the sea in Senegambia and the Gold Coast were highly skilled swimmers and divers—leading them to be targeted by enslavers, who knew their specialized skills could be turned to the recovery of underwater riches. As historian Kevin Dawson writes in “History Below the Waterline: Enslaved Salvage Divers Harvesting Seaports’ Hinter-Seas in the Early Modern Atlantic”:.

The African-honed expertise that enslaved underwater divers carried throughout the Atlantic world allowed them to promptly recover several tons of gold, silver, and other items from shipwrecks, especially old Spanish treasure hulks. Possessing proficiencies held by few in the world, divers exchanged their unique ability to rapidly produce capital for semi-independent lives of privileged exploitation.

It has been revealed that their skills were so irreplaceable that they were able to negotiate for better treatment than most enslaved people, including a share of what they salvaged. Though, of course, a share isn’t much when you’re doing all the work.

#155482. Industry News: Pimalaya goes stable: Himalaya v3 and the pimdir standard

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1912 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Pimalaya ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Pimalaya goes stable: Himalaya v3 and the pimdir standard

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1912 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pimalaya

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It took months, but here we are: the whole Pimalaya CLI family is released at once, at the top of the first stable version of the pimdir standard.
  • Most of them are majors, and they all break something for somebody.
  • According to recent reports, in Another year with NLnet I stated this year was about consolidation and about a standard for PIM on disk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It took months, but here we are: the whole Pimalaya CLI family is released at once, at the top of the first stable version of the pimdir standard. Here the list:.

Most of them are majors, and they all break something for somebody. This post explains why, how, and where it goes from here. It is long, feel free to jump to the tool you care about.

According to recent reports, in Another year with NLnet I stated this year was about consolidation and about a standard for PIM on disk. This release is the result of both.

The thing is, every piece is now connected:.

Releasing them one by one meant releasing tools that disagree with each other: one version of the store here, another version of the output there. So I decided to bring every tool to release level first, then to release them all together. It took way longer than I wanted, but this way what you install today is one coherent family.

The other reason is the contract. The CLIs are not only used by humans anymore: they are used by scripts, by frontends (the Vim plugin, the TUI, the Android app), and by AI agents through MCP. All of them need a stable, versioned contract: the same JSON shapes, the same error codes, the same exit codes. Majors are the right moment to fix it, and from now on it should not move anymore without a upcoming major.

Few things made this release possible.

According to recent reports, specs before code. Every repository has a cairn/ folder holding its living spec, its change proposals and a dated log. Every behaviour change goes through a proposal, then gets folded into the spec. This way the truth is written somewhere, and not only in my head.

One shared kit. The pimalaya-cli and pimalaya-config libs hold everything the CLIs have in common: the output contract, the error codes, the REPL, the MCP server, the configuration loading. In fact most of the work of this release was moving code from the CLIs into this kit, and deleting the copies.

It has been revealed that one unified API, as a union. Before, the commands shared by every backend were the intersection of what the backends could do: if one backend could not do it, nobody could. Now it is the union: each backend registers the capabilities it really serves, with the same observable result as the others, and a command an account cannot serve fails before even connecting, with a clear capability-missing code.

Measured gates for pimdir. Audits always find something, so "no fresh finding" never ends. Instead, I built a test generator that produces stores, remote states and an oracle from a seed, and ran campaigns of 4,180 jobs against io-pimdir: crashes injected at every step, the search index checked against a full rebuild after each event, the sync engine replayed against scripted servers. The rule was simple: 2 campaigns in a row without any spec break, then freeze. Campaign 1 found one, campaigns 2 and 3 were clean, a late fix restarted the count, then campaigns 4 and 5 were clean. Freeze.

Live tests on real providers. Every CLI was tested against real accounts: Google, Microsoft, Fastmail and iCloud, plus few Chinese providers for Himalaya (QQ, 163, 139). A last "live night" just before the release found few bugs that went straight into the libs.

Libs first, apps after. The libs were released between the 13th and the 25th of November, the apps then moved to them without any patch or git pin. Everything you install comes from crates.io.

In a recent development, pimdir is a local-first standard for personal information: mails, contacts, calendars, tasks and files in one portable store, kept as a replica of every source, and searchable with one query language. A store is one SQLite file plus a content-addressed blob directory, the same on every OS and architecture. I already explained why such a standard is needed in Another year with NLnet, and how the Android app became its first full implementation in Pimalaya for Android enters closed alpha.

It comes in 3 parts, versioned separately:.

They are released together because a store holds sync state that follows the sync part, and the query language binds every program that offers search.

According to recent reports, what v1 means: schema version 1 never changes, every schema change is a migration, and a minor version only adds test cases. You can implement it in any language that speaks SQLite, use the I/O-free core of io-pimdir (like the Android app does, on the platform SQLite), or use its std client.

Few days before the freeze, I compared it with notmuch, which is the reference in this area. They do not do the same job (notmuch indexes mail files it does not own, pimdir owns the bodies, syncs them and holds other domains), but the search can be compared. On a store of 1 million messages from the Enron corpus, pimdir was ahead of notmuch on 50 of the 51 query measures and tied the last one, imported the million faster, and used a third of the memory. Stemming, regex and per-thread queries are still missing, they are on the list.

Recent findings suggest that one warning for the early adopters: a store written by a draft version is refused, never migrated. Sync it till nothing is pending with the last draft binary, move its directory aside, then let a release create and sync a upcoming one.

This is the change many of you will not like, so let me explain it properly.

Recent findings suggest that every CLI had a configuration wizard: you typed your email address, it discovered the servers, asked for the password, stored it in your keyring, and wrote the TOML for you. It is gone, from every CLI.

It has been revealed that the direction. The CLIs are now low-level tools: plain text to glance at, JSON for scripts, frontends and agents. Comfort (tables, colours, relative dates, guided setups, rich composition) belongs to frontends. In fact this is not upcoming: it is the same split that started the whole project, back when the logic left the Vim plugin. The CLI was always supposed to be the backend a frontend needs. This release just goes all the way.

I know some of you used the wizard to get started, and that copying a sample feels like a step back. If the welcome or the samples are not clear enough, it is a bug: please open an issue, I would rather fix the docs than bring back a second setup system per CLI.

Himalaya is now a low-level CLI over a unified mail API: the same commands on every backend, the protocol-specific ones next to them, plain text for a glance and --json for the rest.

Backends: IMAP, SMTP, ManageSieve, JMAP, the Gmail API, Microsoft Graph, Maildir (with a newly introduced maildir++ layout for Dovecot and Courier stores), mbox, and pimdir. The README has recipes for Proton Mail (through Bridge), Fastmail, Gmail, Outlook, Posteo and iCloud.

What is gone: the wizard, the m2dir backend (superseded by pimdir), the table and colour options, HIMALAYA_CONFIG. Unknown configuration keys are now refused, JSON keys are camelCase, and the v2 search syntax needs to be rewritten. The migration guide lists everything, with a full table for the queries.

Sources indicate that neverest is rebuilt around the pimdir store: every account syncs into one shared store, which the other CLIs read, search and queue their writes into. It syncs mails, contacts and calendars over IMAP, Gmail, Microsoft Graph, Google Calendar, Google People, CalDAV and CardDAV.

Industry observers note that JMAP sources are not supported yet (it is a draft), so Fastmail syncs over IMAP, CardDAV and CalDAV for now. Coming from v0.x? Your configuration and state are not carried over: start from the config.sample.toml, then run neverest sync --init.

The first stable release of Cardamum: a low-level CLI over a unified contacts API, with the same commands on CardDAV, JMAP, Microsoft Graph, Google People, vdir and pimdir.

Recent findings suggest that card search speaks the pimdir query language on every backend, account capability highlights what an account serves without connecting, and you get the REPL and the MCP server like the others. Editing a card is left to a composer such as tcard. The wizard and the discover route are gone.

Same story for calendars: the same commands on CalDAV, JMAP (new), Google Calendar, Microsoft Graph, vdir and pimdir.

Latest: event search, recurrence expansion, attendees and alarms, online meetings (--online-meeting), invitation replies through pimdir, and an agenda that draws a month or a year like cal(1) does. Editing an event is left to a composer such as tcal. The wizard, the tables and colours, and the todo and journal commands are gone: tasks and journals will move to dedicated tools (Unfog and Journal), not released yet.

Carillon is a local watcher that fires hooks on what changes in your mailboxes, address books and calendars, over IMAP, JMAP, Maildir, CalDAV, CardDAV, Microsoft Graph, the Google APIs and the pimdir store. It uses push where the server offers it (IMAP IDLE, the JMAP event stream) and polls elsewhere. A hook runs a command, reveals a desktop notification, or both.

Recent findings suggest that new in v1: a pimdir backend, on-alarm-trigger for the alarms of events and tasks, on-birthday-trigger for birthdays and anniversaries, a per-hook timeout, and a report of what moved while an IMAP or Gmail session was lost. Hooks now take the same shape as Comodoro's.

It has been revealed that ortie manages OAuth tokens for the other tools. v3 aligns it on the rest of the family: ready-made Google, Microsoft and Fastmail accounts to paste, token revocation, an auth listen to catch a redirection handed off from another machine, account checks, a REPL, and an MCP server that never hands the token to the agent. The wizard and the hooks are gone (the storage write command does what a hook did).

Comodoro manages timers: one server owns a timer, any number of clients drive it, over a local socket or TCP. v3 joins the same standard: comodoro watch feeds a status bar without polling, hooks get the cycle name and duration, plus the welcome, account checks, a REPL and an MCP server. Comodoro is now a binary only: the library is gone, and the open JSON-RPC protocol is the contract for third parties.

None of the above would exist without the libs below, all released in November on crates.io:.

They are all I/O-free, as usual: feel free to build your own tools at the top of them.

Each README lists the ways to install: prebuilt binaries from the GitHub releases (or the install.sh script), cargo install --locked, Nix, and the APT, DNF and Homebrew repositories at pkg.pimalaya.org. The packages are landing there over the coming days, and the nixpkgs and home-manager updates are on their way.

Sources indicate that special thanks to the NLnet foundation and the European Commission's NGI initiative, for the financial support through NGI Zero Core and now the NGI Zero Commons Fund. This kind of slow, deep work is only possible thanks to them.

Industry observers note that and thank you to everyone who reported bugs, tested betas, or simply waited patiently while everything was being rebuilt. Any feedback is welcomed, on GitHub, on Matrix or on Mastodon. Let me know how it goes!

Recent findings suggest that whatsApp just declared that it is rolling out scheduled messages, which it states is one of users’ most requested features. Here are the details.

From WhatsApp’s blog post announcing support for scheduled messages:.

You can write a message when you think of it and send it anywhere from 10 minutes to 14 days later, in both your 1:1 and group chats.

It has been revealed that to schedule a message, press and hold the send button and pick the date and time you want it to arrive. It will look like any other message to the person receiving it. You can see all future messages you have lined up, and delete them beforehand if you change your mind.

Even if your phone is off or out of battery, your scheduled message will still show up at the time you chose, and it remains end-to-end encrypted like all your personal messages, so no one else can read it, not even us.

WhatsApp says this feature is “rolling out globally over the coming weeks.” So you might not see it right away, but even if you don’t, it should show up on your account soon.

Scheduled messages work not only for text, but also when sending media like photos and videos.

To get access to scheduled messages, make sure you’ve updated to the latest WhatsApp app upgrade, which was just released today.

In other WhatsApp news, earlier today we reported that stickers with audio are coming soon, including user-created options.

Pocket Cinema+ is presently founder-backed but received a grant through STARZ’s #TakeTheLead initiative, which supported one of the first series on the slate. To date, actors used in the series have been relatively unknown or newcomers.

The idea is for the slate to include English and French-language genre series, starting with a horror, and they’re targeting budgets in the $60k-$100k range.

“Our editorial focus is genre-driven microseries, with an ambition to develop a wider range of stories and filmmaker perspectives within short-form entertainment,” the duo told us.

Report: Apple gains ground as Latin American smartphone shipments plunge 24% in Q3

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that according to a newly introduced Counterpoint Research report, Apple increased its share of Latin America’s smartphone shipments in Q3 2026, recording the smallest decline among the region’s top five brands.
  • In a report released this week, Counterpoint Research states the ongoing memory crunch led to a 24% year-over-year drop in smartphone shipments during Q3, “the second-lowest quarter since 2015.”.
  • Per the report, Samsung maintained its lead with a 35% shipment share, despite a 15% year-over-year decline in total shipments, well ahead of second-place Motorola, which captured 18% of shipments after a 23% drop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that according to a newly introduced Counterpoint Research report, Apple increased its share of Latin America’s smartphone shipments in Q3 2026, recording the smallest decline among the region’s top five brands. Here are the details.

In a report released this week, Counterpoint Research states the ongoing memory crunch led to a 24% year-over-year drop in smartphone shipments during Q3, “the second-lowest quarter since 2015.”.

Per the report, Samsung maintained its lead with a 35% shipment share, despite a 15% year-over-year decline in total shipments, well ahead of second-place Motorola, which captured 18% of shipments after a 23% drop. Interestingly, Motorola’s share actually increased one percentage point from a year earlier.

Rounding out the top five were Xiaomi, with a 14% share and a whopping 34% decline, Apple, with a 9% share and a 10% decline, and Honor, with an 8% share and a 27% decline.

Despite the decline in overall shipments, Apple’s shipment share increased by 2 percentage points from 7% a year earlier, moving the company from fifth to fourth place in the region.

Other brands collectively accounted for 16% of shipments, down from 19% a year earlier, with their combined shipments falling 37% year over year.

Here’s Counterpoint on Apple’s performance for Q3 in Latin America:.

Apple was the most resilient, with the smallest decline among the top five brands (shipments down 10% YoY), and rose one position to No. 4 in the region. Apple absorbed the impact of price increases better than its rivals, helped by strong product availability. Apple debuted the iPhone 18 Pro series at the end of the quarter. For the first time, Chile joined Brazil and Mexico in the first launch wave.

In a recent development, as for regional factors that contributed to the decline, Senior Analyst Benjamin Corona noted that Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia faced additional challenges beyond the global memory shortage, ranging from political uncertainty to inflation and tighter household budgets. Smartphone shipments fell 22%, 26%, and 28% in those countries, respectively.

Looking ahead, Counterpoint indicates it “expects the decline to ease in Q4 2026 as prices stabilize and seasonal demand returns,” adding that “memory-related price pressure should moderate by Q2 2027, but supply constraints will likely continue through the end of 2027.”.

#155463. An introduction to uncertainty in machine learning

An introduction to uncertainty in machine learning

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4149 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Chrhenning

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every model makes an assumption about uncertainty, often without saying so.
  • Essentially, all models are wrong, but some are useful.
  • Most of machine learning is based on probabilistic modelling, even if it does not always seem like it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every model makes an assumption about uncertainty, often without saying so. Where data is rare, that assumption decides the answer. This introduction explains where uncertainty comes from and how to judge when it needs to be faithful to be useful.

Essentially, all models are wrong, but some are useful.

Most of machine learning is based on probabilistic modelling, even if it does not always seem like it. So most models carry some uncertainty, whether we chose it or not, and in many decisions it pays to take that uncertainty into account, as the examples in this post show.

In my experience, uncertainty in machine learning is a confusing topic to get into, so I wrote this introduction to give an intuitive overview. It is not comprehensive, but it should give you a good enough mental model to choose assumptions that make your uncertainty estimates useful for decision making, even though, as Box put it, the model itself will always be wrong.This post is based on a talk I gave at the University of Alicante. The slides are online. For a more thorough introduction, see Chapters 2 and 3 of my PhD thesis .

Generally speaking, uncertainty is incomplete knowledge, and probability is how we describe it: a distribution over the possible outcomes indicates how plausible each one is, given what we know.

It helps to separate two kinds of uncertainty:.

It has been revealed that the line between the two depends on what we measure. A coin flip follows classical mechanics. If we do not measure how the coin is thrown, the best we can say is 50/50, and the uncertainty is aleatoric. If we do measure it, physics tells us how it will land, and the uncertainty becomes epistemic: now we have to learn the physics, which takes data. Richer inputs can reduce aleatoric uncertainty, but they give the model more to learn, and whether that pays off depends on how much data and prior knowledge we have.Some inputs are out of reach. For example, weather is chaotic, so tiny differences, as small as the flap of a butterfly's wings, can grow into different weather a few weeks later. Since we cannot observe every butterfly, part of the uncertainty in a forecast stays aleatoric, however much we measure.

A prediction is not a decision. When we decide, we often weigh the possible outcomes by how likely they are and what they would cost us, including rare outcomes that could hurt us badly. A single number hides this picture. It also cannot tell us when to hand a case to a human or to collect more data before we decide. The examples below show where modelling uncertainty matters.

It has been revealed that all of these need the uncertainty to be useful. To see when it is, it makes sense to look at where it comes from.

As a running example, we look at steering angle prediction. The input is the image from a car’s front camera, and the output $y$ is the steering angle. Such datasets can be recorded cheaply from human drivers. Take a car approaching a point where the road splits. In the left lane, drivers mostly go left. In the right lane, they mostly go right. In the middle lane, which points straight at the divider, about half go left and half go right.

The car’s position across the lanes is implicit in the camera image. To keep the figures simple, we use it directly as a one-dimensional input $x$ in the figures below.The rest of the image, such as where the road goes, matters just as much for the prediction. We implicitly assume that the model knows it, since it cannot be compressed into a simple one-dimensional variable that keeps the explanations easy to follow.

What we want to learn is the conditional distribution $p^*(y \mid x)$: for each position, how likely each steering angle is. As is common in statistical learning theory, we assume that the data come from a fixed joint distribution $p^*(x, y)$, and the recordings from human drivers are samples from it.

The ground truth $p^*(y \mid x)$ is just one of many possible conditional distributions.Strictly speaking, the truth is only defined where $p^*(x) > 0$. Many hypotheses agree with it on the road but differ off the road, where no data can tell them apart. We call each conditional distribution of $y$ given $x$ a hypothesis, and together they form a space. As we will see, learning amounts to searching a subset of this space.

That subset is the model, a family of hypotheses indexed by parameters $\theta$. A common choice for regression is a Gaussian whose mean is a neural network $f_\theta(x)$ and whose variance $\sigma^2$ is fixed:.

The truth need not lie inside the model. For the lane split, it does not: a single Gaussian has one peak, but in the middle lane the truth has two.

Training picks the hypothesis that best explains the data. It minimizes the negative log-likelihood (NLL), the average of $-\log p_\theta(y_i \mid x_i)$ over the training examples. For the Gaussian with fixed variance, this is the familiar mean squared errorI walked through this connection, from the KL divergence to the mean squared error, in an earlier post.:.

So a network trained with mean squared error already has an uncertainty model, even if nobody chose it on purpose.

Industry observers note that how far is the trained model from the truth? The expected NLL splits into two terms:.

In a recent development, where both expectations are over the true data distribution. The first term is the KL divergence, which measures how far the model is from the truth and is zero only if they match. The second is the entropy of the truth, its aleatoric uncertainty, which does not depend on the model. Minimizing the NLL therefore moves the model toward the truth. But we never know the entropy of the truth, so the NLL alone cannot tell us how far away we still are.This is why we are usually blind to model misspecification: a low NLL does not tell us whether the truth lies inside the model. I will get back to this later. Moreover, even the KL divergence would not be enough, since it is an average over all inputs. In real driving data, lane splits are rare, so a model can be close to the truth on average and still steer into the divider. Knowing which inputs matter takes domain expertise, which is ultimately the modeller's responsibility.

It has been revealed that back in the middle lane, the single peak has a dangerous consequence. The mean squared error is minimized by the average steering angle, and the average of left and right is straight ahead, into the divider. No choice of parameters avoids this, because every hypothesis in the model has a single peak. In an earlier post, I looked at this example in more detail, and we studied it in a paper on misspecification, the case where the truth lies outside the model .

According to recent reports, the fix is a model that contains the truth. For this example, a mixture of two Gaussians, whose weights, means and variances are all outputs of the network, is enough to contain the truth.

Industry observers note that understanding the problem well enough to make this choice is the modeller’s job. But a richer model is not free: it contains more hypotheses, so the data has to do more work to single out the right one.This is the familiar bias–variance tradeoff. For example, a fully connected network can represent everything a convolutional network can. Yet for images we use convolutional networks, because they leave out hypotheses that do not fit images and so need much less data. Their assumptions seem stronger than necessary, though: with enough data, vision transformers, which assume less, do better.

Recent findings suggest that since the mixture contains the truth, enough data brings it close, including in the middle lane. Only then is its spread the aleatoric uncertainty: with the given information, even a perfect model cannot say which lane a particular driver will take.As with the coin flip, what counts as aleatoric depends on what the input contains. If $x$ were random noise, it would carry no information, and the best fit would ignore it and learn the distribution of steering angles independent of the input, $p(y)$. A rear camera image is more deceptive. Steering changes slowly (it is strongly autocorrelated), so the view behind the car indicates how the driver steered a moment ago, and repeating that is usually a good guess. The validation error decreases as expected during training, yet the model can never anticipate a turn, because the road ahead is not in the input. I discuss this gap between predicting and forecasting in an earlier post.

In a recent development, but in practice we do not know the truth, so we cannot check the fit like this. How do we know how much we still do not know?

Recent findings suggest that so far, training gave us a single hypothesis. But with only 20 data points, many hypotheses explain the data about equally well, and by picking one of them, we ignore that the data cannot tell them apart. Bayesian inference instead keeps all of them.Bayesian inference is not the only way to capture epistemic uncertainty, but it is a principled one, and the one I know best.

Sources indicate that before seeing any data, we decide how plausible each hypothesis in the model is. This is the prior $p(\theta)$, a soft inductive bias. It captures what we know, or assume, before training, and everything the model does not know is measured relative to it.Choosing a prior can feel arbitrary, and often it is. Think of a CNN, which rules out hypotheses that do not suit images. A prior does not rule them out, but it makes them less plausible from the start. I discuss how the prior shapes what a model does not know in an earlier post. Data then shifts the weight to the hypotheses that explain it, giving rise to the posterior:.

Industry observers note that where $\mathcal{D} = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ is the data. The likelihood, written $p(\mathcal{D} \mid \theta)$ for short, measures how well hypothesis $\theta$ agrees with the data.

To predict, we average all hypotheses, each weighted by its posterior probability. This is the posterior predictive:.

Recent findings suggest that with more and more data, the posterior concentrates on a single hypothesis: the one in the model that is closest to the truth.Closest in KL divergence. This holds under regularity conditions, including that the prior puts enough weight near that hypothesis . If the model contains the truth, that hypothesis is the truth itself. If not, as in the sketch below, it is only the best the model has to offer.

Recent findings suggest that this picture splits uncertainty into three sources, using the terms of Hüllermeier and Waegeman . What sets them apart is what reduces them:.

Industry observers note that the last point matters in practice. A misspecified model can still have a confident posterior: it is confident about the least wrong hypothesis it contains.

Both models above show more uncertainty where data is missing. That is approximation uncertainty, and both capture it. To also question the model itself, a full probabilistic treatment would weigh models too, but that is hard in practice. What we can do is compare a few candidate models. For this, Bayesian inference offers the evidence, $p(\mathcal{D} \mid \mathcal{M}) = \int p(\mathcal{D} \mid \theta) \, p(\theta \mid \mathcal{M}) \, \mathrm{d}\theta$, the probability of the data under model $\mathcal{M}$, averaged over its prior.The notation can be misleading, since it suggests that we treat the model as a random variable. We do not have to, so a semicolon, $p(\mathcal{D}; \mathcal{M})$, might be a preferable notation. Note also that $\mathcal{M}$ now includes the prior: the same hypotheses with a different prior form a different model. Here it clearly prefers the mixture.The evidence has a built-in Occam's razor : a more flexible model spreads its prior over more possible datasets, so it pays a price unless the data need that flexibility. Here, the two lanes do. But it only ranks the models we try, and if none of them contains the truth, it will not tell us.

Sources indicate that like the KL divergence earlier, the evidence is an average over all data. In real driving data, lane splits are rare, so their effect can vanish in the evidence, and the simpler model may even win. Domain knowledge would tell us otherwise. This is why choosing the model remains the modeller’s job, and comparing models is a tool for it, not a replacement.

It has been revealed that so far, we have taken the prior as given. But the prior is part of the model. In theory, with enough data, its choice stops mattering, as long as it does not rule out the right hypotheses. In practice, we rarely have that much data, and a poor prior, like any poor inductive bias, can hurt a lot. I discussed this in more detail in earlier posts on uncertainty and on continual learning.

According to recent reports, in short, the posterior is uncertain where the data and our assumptions leave room for disagreement. Low uncertainty therefore does not mean we have seen data there. Generalization works exactly this way: far from the data, the inductive bias makes the hypotheses agree. If the bias is good, the model is confident and right. If not, it is confident and wrong.

In a recent development, sometimes we want a statistical guarantee, ideally one that does not depend on our modelling choices, since those can be arbitrarily wrong. Conformal prediction gives such a guarantee. Instead of a single prediction, it outputs a prediction set that contains the true output, say, 90% of the time. This is called 90% coverage. It wraps any trained model, and as long as the data are exchangeable, the guarantee holds no matter how wrong the model is .

Industry observers note that conformal prediction comes in many flavors. We look at the simplest and most common one, split conformal prediction. Its recipe has four steps:.

If the calibration and test data are exchangeable, the set has at least 90% coverage. This holds on average over inputs, not for any particular input, such as one at the lane split.

But the guarantee does not say whether the sets are useful. For that, we want low scores in the histogram above, since a small $\hat q$ gives tight sets. A poor model has higher scores and gets wider sets, with the same coverage.

According to recent reports, the guarantee only needs a calibration set. Useful sets also need the same modelling work as before. I wrote more about this in a recent post on conformal prediction.

So far, the goal was a faithful uncertainty: a predictive distribution close to the truth. But uncertainty is meant to be used, and decision theory says how. The model provides a belief $p(y \mid x)$. Whoever acts provides a loss $L(a, y)$, the cost of action $a$ if the outcome turns out to be $y$. We then pick the action with the lowest expected loss:.

In the lane split, the action is a steering angle. The belief states which angles drivers take: left or right, never straight. The loss says what we want. If our destination is to the left, steering left has a low loss, steering right a higher one, and steering into the divider is worst of all. Under the true belief, the decision follows the left lane. A belief with a single peak in the middle rules out neither lane and picks straight.

It has been revealed that how faithful does the belief need to be? It depends on the decision.Since the belief is approximate anyway, we can fit it with the loss in mind, so that it is useful for the decision . In the rest of this section, we walk through two practical examples, visual quality inspection and holding reserve for wind power, where the answers differ.

Many factories use cameras to check every part that comes off the line. Mistakes are costly here, since a missed defect may reach a customer, lead to a recall or, in the worst case, put people at risk. To keep things simple, we consider a binary classifier in this section.In practice, a yes or no is rarely enough. We may also want to know where the defect is, its outline, which component it affects and why the model flagged it. It takes the camera image $x$ and outputs the probability $p(\text{defect} \mid x)$ that the part is defective. With stakes this high, should this probability not be faithful, or even come with a guarantee?

According to recent reports, to answer this, we look at how the probability turns into a decision. We reject a part if $p = p(\text{defect} \mid x)$ is above a threshold. If we reject, we pay a cost $c_{FP}$ when the part is good, which happens with probability $1 - p$. If we ship, we pay a cost $c_{FN}$ when it is defective, which happens with probability $p$. Rejecting is cheaper on average when $c_{FP}\,(1 - p) < c_{FN}\,p$, that is, when.

What this derivation hides is that it takes $p$ at face value, so it assumes the model is calibrated: of all parts scored 0.1, about 10% should be defective. In this example, though, calibration matters less than it seems, for two reasons. First, calibrated against whom? Inspectors disagree on borderline parts, and since labels are expensive, each part is usually labeled by only one of them. So the labels can only tell us whether the model is calibrated against whoever labeled the data, and on borderline parts, another inspector would have labeled differently. Second, $c_{FN}$ includes recalls, lost customers and reputation, so it is rarely known. It is not even a single number, since a customer may never notice a faint scratch, while a deep crack can make the part fail. So the threshold is a guess anyway.

Sources indicate that what about a guarantee, such as “at most 5% of defects escape”? The guarantee we got from conformal prediction earlier does not give this. It holds on average over all parts, and since defects are rare, it can be met while missing most of them. We need coverage for defects alone. Conformal prediction can give this too, if we set the threshold using defects only. Then at most a fraction $\alpha$ of defects, here 5%, score below it .

Recent findings suggest that this guarantee has a price. Labeled defects are rare and expensive to collect, and we need many of them for a stable threshold. Worse, a defect is anything that is not normal. The guarantee holds only for defects that are exchangeable with the ones we collected, and the next one may look like none of them.Indeed, defects are so rare that practical solutions often teach the model with defect-free images only, an approach I worked on at Ethon (see here and here). Finally, the guarantee fixes the threshold, however many good parts it rejects.

If the model rejects too many good parts and we raise the threshold, we give up the guarantee and are back to costs we cannot measure.

Sources indicate that so in this example, we need neither calibration nor a guarantee. Since $c_{FN}$ is unknown, an operator tunes the threshold by hand, and for that, only the order of the scores matters: they should grow with the severity of a flaw. Small scratches are rarely called defects and deep cracks almost always, and in between, inspectors disagree. A model calibrated against a large pool of inspectors would give such a score, but these labels are too expensive. Getting the order right without them is hard modelling work: we have to build the right inductive biases into the model, for instance during pre-training.

In a recent development, wind power depends on the weather, so a grid operator never knows exactly how much will arrive. To cover a shortfall, meaning less wind power than planned, the operator keeps backup power on standby, called the reserve. Unlike inspecting parts, no person could forecast the shortfall by hand, so the model learns it from past data alone. It takes inputs $x$, such as the weather forecast and recent measurements, and outputs a distribution $p(\text{shortfall} \mid x)$ over the shortfall. If the shortfall exceeds the reserve, we have a shortage, and each missing unit costs $c_{\text{short}}$, and each unit of reserve that goes unused costs $c_{\text{idle}}$.In practice, $c_{\text{short}}$ is much larger. A shortage must be covered within minutes, by fast and expensive plants, by buying power at short notice or, in the worst case, by cutting off customers. Idle reserve only costs what it takes to keep a plant ready. Unlike $c_{FN}$ in visual inspection, both costs can be roughly estimated, for instance from market prices, so for the sake of argument, we take them as known.

The best reserve is the $\tau$-quantile of the predicted shortfall, with.

It has been revealed that the costs pick the quantile.Why the $\tau$-quantile? Say we hold a reserve $r$ and add one more unit. If the shortfall turns out larger than $r$, the unit is used and saves $c_{\text{short}}$. Otherwise, it sits idle and costs $c_{\text{idle}}$. So the unit pays off when $c_{\text{short}}\, P(\text{shortfall} > r) > c_{\text{idle}}\, P(\text{shortfall} \le r)$. As $r$ grows, the left side shrinks and the right side grows, so we add reserve until both are equal. With $P(\text{shortfall} > r) = 1 - P(\text{shortfall} \le r)$, this gives $P(\text{shortfall} \le r) = \tau$, which is the $\tau$-quantile. Since these costs change by the hour, so does $\tau$.

To see what this asks of the model, we again take a Gaussian model for simplicity. On most days, the forecast is roughly right, and the shortfall is small. But on rare days, the wind dies down unexpectedly, and the shortfall is large. So in the tail, the truth is not Gaussian. Since shortages are costly, $\tau$ is high, and the reserve sits far out in the tail of the predicted distribution, so the model has to get these rare, large shortfalls right.

In a recent development, if we blueprint for a shortage 1 in 10 times ($\tau = 90\%$), the two dots almost coincide, and the Gaussian works well. Now say we plan for 1 in 100 ($\tau = 99\%$). The Gaussian sets the reserve at the blue dot. But how often this reserve falls short is decided by the truth, and at this reserve, the orange curve lies well above 1 in 100. Shortages come more than twice as often as planned. Unlike in visual inspection, the probabilities are used at face value here,Why not adjust the reserve by hand, as the operator did with the threshold? In inspection, there is one threshold to tune. Here, $\tau$ changes by the hour, so every quantile would need tuning, and shortages are too rare to notice when one is off. and since $\tau$ changes by the hour, the whole distribution must be faithful, tail included.

In a year of daily data, a 1-in-100 shortfall shows up only a few times, and anything rarer than once a year not at all. So where we need the uncertainty most, in the tail, we have the least data, and the assumptions built into the model decide the answer. We have to choose them from what we know about wind and weather.

According to recent reports, every model in this post made an assumption about uncertainty, whether we chose it or not. Making it faithful took real work: a likelihood that can represent the truth, enough data to find it, and inductive biases that hold up where the data runs out.

That work is not always needed. Our own uncertainty is not faithful either. We humans misjudge probabilities in well-known ways , yet we handle most everyday tasks just fine. In this post, too, we saw tasks where uncertainty did not have to be faithful, and others where it counted. So before investing in faithful uncertainty, ask what you gain from it. And even when it does not have to be faithful, I believe it helps to know what faithful would mean. Then we know what our uncertainty gets wrong and can judge whether that matters for the decision.

Recent findings suggest that ice storms cause long outages because several exposures act together. Ice adds weight to conductors, hardware and structures. Wind pushes on the larger iced surface. Trees and limbs bend into the line and add impact and uneven load. Conductors may also gallop and lose clearance. This paper explains how these loads combine and why the complete line must be assessed, not a single component. It reviews a monitored winter test of three conductor systems. It also summarizes utility records from a major regional ice storm. Finally, it outlines how to choose corridors, proposal restoration and keep crews and the public safe around covered conductors.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Read the Gmail server's tool list and you'll find that it can search your mail, read threads, create a draft and file things under labels.
  • If you've built an email assistant on the Gmail API, or you run a coding agent with a Google Workspace plugin, you have about two months to work out which side of the rule you're on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that on 24 November, Google made its eight Workspace MCP servers generally available and published a upcoming clause in its API terms. From 1 February 2027, any tool that "is or is driven by an AI Agent" must reach Gmail, Drive, Calendar and the rest of Workspace through those servers.

Read the Gmail server's tool list and you'll find that it can search your mail, read threads, create a draft and file things under labels. It can't send a message, reply, forward, or change a draft after creating it. Those tools exist, but Google's quota page claims they "require partner access and aren't generally available".

If you've built an email assistant on the Gmail API, or you run a coding agent with a Google Workspace plugin, you have about two months to work out which side of the rule you're on.

The upcoming Workspace AI Tools Addendum to the Google APIs Terms of Service puts it in one sentence:.

The GWS Access Tool must use a Google MCP where the GWS Access Tool is or is driven by an AI Agent, an AI Harness or an AI model or service employing an AI model.

Industry observers note that the next sentence forbids disguising an agent to avoid the classification. Breaking either lets Google "restrict or remove the GWS Access Tool's access" or suspend your account.

According to recent reports, there's a technical side too. From the same date, agents that call the REST APIs directly are held to Standard-tier quotas, whatever tier the project has paid for. REST keeps working for them, slowly and in breach of the terms.

It has been revealed that apps that don't involve AI carry on as before. A nightly backup job, a CRM sync or a deterministic script on its own OAuth client is, in Google's words, "not affected by this change".

The addendum also adds data rules that matter to anyone building an agent with memory:.

Recent findings suggest that the 30-day cap is the one product teams will feel. An assistant that builds a long-term index of your inbox to answer questions about last year's contracts has to rebuild it monthly or drop it.

Coverage is uneven. Docs, Slides and Tasks are close to everything the REST API offers. Gmail and Drive are much thinner.

Sources indicate that the Gmail gap is the one that breaks real workflows. An agent that drafts a reply, gets feedback from you and revises it before you hit send can't do the revision step. It has to create a second draft and leave the first one behind.

Drive's gap is similar: an agent can create a report but can't move it into the right folder or share it with the team.

In a recent development, google hasn't stated who qualifies for partner access or when the partner-only Gmail tools will reach everyone. The effect is already visible, though. Anthropic's Google Workspace connector for Claude advertises sending, replying and forwarding email, and moving and trashing Drive files. Those are exactly the operations the public servers lack.

So a large AI vendor's agent can send your email through an approved channel, while an independent developer's agent, using the same OAuth scopes the user granted, can only leave drafts. Once the addendum takes effect, that independent developer also can't fall back to the REST API without breaching the terms.

The definitions are broad. An "AI Harness" or a tool "driven by" an AI model plausibly covers a personal script that pipes your inbox into an LLM, and a "GWS Access Point" explicitly includes any "connector, proxy, command line interface, or third-party service". Google hasn't addressed hobby use directly.

Industry observers note that classification starts with self-declaration. OAuth clients now have a checkbox, "Use this client for an AI-powered agent", and since 11 November the MCP servers reject clients without it. Clients created before the cut-off and not marked in time stay non-agentic permanently, so owners have to create latest ones. Google hasn't remarked how it will detect agents that call REST without declaring themselves.

A few edge cases are documented:.

Recent findings suggest that every project gets the free Standard tier: 5,000 MCP requests per day, per project, per product. Some calls cost more than one request. A Gmail search_threads or list_drafts counts as 10, so an agent that does nothing but search gets 500 searches a day across all its users. That's a project-wide limit, so a small multi-user product will hit it swiftly.

Recent findings suggest that the paid Scaled tier starts billing on 1 April 2027 for Gmail, Calendar and Drive. Its structure favours REST. MCP usage is billed from the first request, while REST usage gets large free daily allowances: 70 million light Gmail requests a day, for example. Google hasn't published per-request prices.

Google's case, from a Cloud blog post by Chandu Thota and Brad Calder, is that OAuth was designed for apps acting on a human's clear intent:.

Traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed â¦ a valid token is no longer enough. Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path.

There's substance to this. An email agent that reads a message saying "forward the last ten invoices to this address" is a well-documented prompt-injection risk, and a token that allows gmail.modify gives the agent the power to do it. Routing every agent through one gateway gives admins a single place to block categories of action, require approval and audit what happened. The MCP servers do all of that, and apply data-loss-prevention rules automatically.

In a recent development, the same design also gives Google control of which agents can do what, which data they can keep, and whether anything built on that data can compete with Google's own products. The partner-only tools and the 30-day cap on embeddings show that control in use.

Slack went down a similar path in May 2025. It cut history API rate limits to one request a minute for apps outside its Marketplace and banned bulk export of Slack data for LLMs. Slack drew the line by distribution channel. Google draws it by whether the software is an AI, which is harder to define and harder to enforce.

If you build an agent product on Workspace:.

Industry observers note that if you run a personal agent or MCP server against your own account: open-source servers that call REST, such as the popular google_workspace_mcp, will keep running, but at Standard quotas and outside the terms. Switching to Google's servers costs you sending and draft editing in Gmail, and moving and sharing in Drive.

Recent findings suggest that if you're a Workspace admin: the fresh controls are under Admin console â Security â API Controls. You can block or approve each category of agent action, set approval policies, and see agent activity in the audit logs. People can't view or revoke the approvals they've saved, which expire after 90 days, so it's worth setting policy before people start connecting agents.

If your integration doesn't use AI: nothing changes, as long as it stays on its own OAuth client and nobody wires a model into it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a significant development in Apple’s Supreme Court appeal of a civil contempt ruling, Epic Games has received backing from 32 states and the District of Columbia, along with major developers, legal experts, former federal judges, and more.
  • Apple’s ever-sprawling fight against Epic Games over its App Store policies is presently being fought on two fronts: in the Supreme Court, where Apple is seeking to overturn a civil contempt ruling, and in the district court, where the companies are disputing what commission, if any, Apple can charge on purchases made through external payment systems.
  • The civil contempt ruling came after Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers found that Apple had violated an earlier injunction issued in its App Store dispute with Epic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a significant development in Apple’s Supreme Court appeal of a civil contempt ruling, Epic Games has received backing from 32 states and the District of Columbia, along with major developers, legal experts, former federal judges, and more. Here are the details.

Apple’s ever-sprawling fight against Epic Games over its App Store policies is presently being fought on two fronts: in the Supreme Court, where Apple is seeking to overturn a civil contempt ruling, and in the district court, where the companies are disputing what commission, if any, Apple can charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

The civil contempt ruling came after Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers found that Apple had violated an earlier injunction issued in its App Store dispute with Epic.

In a nutshell, after she ordered Apple to allow developers to direct owners to alternative payment methods outside the App Store, the company responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them.

Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn the civil contempt ruling, basically arguing that the original injunction did not explicitly prohibit the commissions and other restrictions it imposed on external purchases.

After the Ninth Circuit upheld the contempt finding and denied its request for rehearing, Apple took the case to the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear its appeal.

Importantly, the Supreme Court will only consider the legal standard used to uphold Apple’s civil contempt ruling, not the separate question of what commission, if any, the firm can charge on purchases made through external payment methods.

That will still be determined in the district court, where proceedings have continued despite Apple’s attempts to put them on hold pending the Supreme Court’s decision.

With oral arguments scheduled for January 11, 2027, the case has recently seen a flurry of activity, including Apple’s opening brief in September and Epic’s response earlier this month.

Recent findings suggest that apple also received support from several organizations in September, including the Washington Legal Foundation, the International Center for Law and Economics, the Computer & Communications Industry Association, and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. The US government also submitted a brief supporting neither party, arguing that the contempt finding was unjustified over Apple’s 27% commission, but warranted over its restrictions on button designs.

Which brings us to the latest developments: a series of amicus briefs filed in support of Epic Games.

Last week, a total of 9 amicus briefs were filed in support of Epic Games, including one led by Utah and joined by 31 other states and the District of Columbia.

This particular brief notes that “the district court correctly held Apple in contempt for continuing to engage in anticompetitive conduct barred by a prior injunction,” adding:.

According to recent reports, “The court found that Apple engaged in unlawful anti-steering restrictions and required Apple to lift those restrictions. Apple then lifted them in name only, imposed newly introduced (and substantially similar) strictures on developers that mirrored the old ones and produced the same result. Worse still, Apple did all this in bad faith: Apple knew its behavior was wrong and actively hid that fact from the court, including by providing false testimony. Under any reasonable reading of the district court’s injunction, Apple’s conduct is worthy of civil contempt.”.

The states also argue that “Injunctions in competition cases cannot afford complete relief without addressing the ongoing effects of anticompetitive behavior,” and that “[c]onstruing competition injunctions narrowly defeats their purpose and prevents meaningful redress.”.

Similar arguments appear throughout the other briefs, which include submissions from Spotify, Match Group, and Microsoft, as well as nonprofit organizations such as the American Antitrust Institute (AAI), Public Knowledge, and the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF).

In their joint brief, Spotify, Match Group, and Microsoft argue that they “have first-hand experience with the effects of Apple’s conduct and evasion efforts,” adding that “Apple’s newly introduced restrictions were no different from the unlawful rules they replaced.”.

Industry observers note that as for the brief filed by former federal judges, they warned that “[i]n cases like these, where enjoined parties seek to circumvent an injunction through reliance on its literal text, courts must have the power of contempt to deter and remedy evasion. Otherwise, courts would be forced into a game of whack-a-mole, trying to anticipate every possible means of evading an injunction […]”.

Arguments by the Little Tech Association, AAI, Public Knowledge, and the EFF all follow a similar line, with some also addressing how Apple’s restrictions on external payment links could affect consumer choice, pricing, and competition.

In a recent development, netflix has snapped up The Melody Of Love and is launching the music-driven Chinese fantasy drama in the U.S. and internationally on its platform on 29 Nov.

The show hails from Chinese production company Stellar Pictures, which made fantasy series Love Between Fairy and Devil and Love Game in Eastern Fantasy, both of which are also available on Netflix.

The Melody Of Love is a 40-part series starring Li Yitong and Chen Xinhai. Set in a fantasy world shaped by the power of music, the drama follows a legendary musician living under a concealed identity and a mysterious musical spirit who has lost his memory. Forced into an unlikely alliance to protect their kingdom, the two gradually fall in love. Related Stories News Netflix Posts Racy Thanksgiving Message On 'The Hunting Wives' Season 2 Premiere Day News 'Steps' Director Alyce Tzue On "Punk Rock" Inspirations For 'Cinderella' Reimagining.

Zhao Yilong directs the series. It bows on Netflix on the same day it has its domestic premiere in China, on Hunan Satellite TV, Tencent Video and Mango TV. There has been strong interest locally, with the release announcement generating hundreds of millions of views on Douyin, the Chinese counterpart to TikTok. Watch on Deadline.

“Over the past few years, we have seen our stories find audiences in markets that were once unfamiliar with Chinese fantasy,” stated Wang Yixu, Founder and Chairman of Stellar Pictures.

Sources indicate that “With The Melody of Love, we wanted to explore a different creative direction through Chinese musical traditions. We hope more Chinese stories like this can travel beyond borders and be seen and loved by audiences around the world.”.

As well as Netflix, The Melody Of Love will also be on Tencent’s international streaming service WeTV internationally, as well as Rakuten-owned streamer Viki in selected territories.
