Sources indicate that for our review of the best smart scales, we take a number of factors into consideration. First, we check that the scale offers an accurate reading using a traditional digital scale, the highly rated EatSmart digital bathroom scale. If the readings are within a fraction of a pound of each other, we can recommend them. The readings shouldn't take more than a few seconds, either.

Recent findings suggest that aside from price, we also explore the variety of metrics a scale offers, how many unique users the scale supports, the scale’s connectivity options and the user-friendliness of the scale’s companion app. We like to see whether the app provides background information on your body’s statistics, too. Plus, compatibility with third-party health programs plays a role in our testing.

According to recent reports, the last thing anyone needs is more anxiety, so we look for the best smart scales to make stepping on the platform less intimidating. A smart scale’s metrics should show you that your body is more than your weight.

Recent findings suggest that A smart scale isn’t a device you want to replace often, so you want it to be reliable, well-rounded, and to fill all your fitness tracking needs. In other words, don’t let price be your ultimate decision-maker.

It’s worth it to stretch your budget for one of the best smart scales that will last you at least a few years and support the exact data you’re interested in following. Review all the metrics a given smart scale offers before buying.

Recent findings suggest that that remarked, if you’re in temporary living quarters or are working towards a short-term fitness goal, a budget smart scale, like the Wyze Scale, is an excellent choice. It won’t last a lifetime but will satisfy your immediate needs.

In a recent development, another thing to pay attention to is whether a smart scale has some kind of ‘safe mode’ for people with pacemakers or people who are pregnant. Safe mode, or ‘weigh only’ mode, disables bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA), which uses a weak electric current to determine body fat percentage and could pose a safety threat to certain users.

Fitbit owners could even connect one of the best Fitbits to the brand's smart scale, helping you keep on top of your daily health and fitness stats.

It has been revealed that smart scales can do so much more than just report back to you on your current weight. Moreover, weight can fluctuate throughout the day based on various factors like water retention. A smart scale can provide feedback and detailed metrics to health apps on your phone and send data wirelessly to your devices.

According to recent reports, obsessing over a number on the scale is not a true indication of health, but if your goal is to lose weight, a smart scale could help you understand your body. Many linked apps can also display the data in helpful and motivating ways, which could help you hit your goals.

Not that interested in the detailed numbers? Stick to a simple set of scales and save your dollars.

During testing, the budget-friendly smart scales were reasonably accurate. Of course, there's always some variation between models, but the relative accuracy (measurements on a single device) is the most key factor to consider, as this will help you keep track of changes.

In a recent development, generally, the main reason that the scales are cheap is that they lack the features of the more premium models. So, some don't come with Wi-Fi and only sync via Bluetooth, or don't have multi-user support.

Recent findings suggest that the difference between a smart scale and a regular bathroom scale is that these smart models sync your data to another device. They need to do this with a wireless connection, either Bluetooth or Wi-Fi.

In a recent development, cheaper models generally only use Bluetooth, so you'll need your phone with you, connected to the scale, and an app to receive the data. These usually only work with a single account as well, so they are less ideal for multi-person households.

Industry observers note that if you have the budget for it, a Wi-Fi scale is the more versatile and convenient option. You need to set up the network connection initially, but then you can leave your phone elsewhere, step onto the scale, and the data automatically syncs.

Because this process is automated, you need to set up individual users on the scale. So while this is useful for regular household measurements, it means that it's a bit less suited to casual weigh-ins from visitors, as the data syncs to the owner's account.

You may have noticed that in this guide we've included information on what 'modes' the scales listed have, but you may be wondering what specific modes are right for you.

This really depends on what you're planning on using the scale for, whether you proposal on only weighing yourself, what training you do, and if you are or are planning on becoming pregnant.

Industry observers note that for example, our number-one smart scale, Withings Body Smart, includes athlete, pregnancy, eyes-closed, and baby modes. This means that it has modes tailored for those who are in intensive training, those who are pregnant, those who would prefer not to see their weight or body composition data, and to log and track their baby's weight. The majority of these modes are more useful for those with specific goals in mind, and so will be useful to them.

In comparison, the Wyze Scale X has more practical, day-to-day modes, including luggage, pet, and baby. Each helps users measure and/or track the weight of things (e.g., their dog or cat) without impacting their recorded weights. This means that you can easily weigh things without your scale believing you have spontaneously gained several pounds, so you don't have to manually delete these recordings.

Overall, it comes down to what you want out of your scale and what you want to use it for.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Password management platform 1Password today disclosed a security incident in which an attacker gained access to internal systems and stole select customer account information.
  • 1Password today published a blog post explaining that an attacker “copied a limited amount of customer account information from a subset” of its consumers, “including the names and email addresses” they use to sign into the platform.
  • In a recent development, according to the manufacturer, it began investigating on November 19 after finding indications that an attacker had gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Password management platform 1Password today disclosed a security incident in which an attacker gained access to internal systems and stole select customer account information. Here are the details.

1Password today published a blog post explaining that an attacker “copied a limited amount of customer account information from a subset” of its consumers, “including the names and email addresses” they use to sign into the platform.

In a recent development, according to the manufacturer, it began investigating on November 19 after finding indications that an attacker had gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The attacker then used that account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, allowing customer account information to be downloaded.

The company noted that customer vaults were not affected, adding that all vault contents remain secure:.

Although 1Password did not disclose how many customers were affected, saying only that the breach involved “a subset of our owners,” it did specify what information was compromised, including:.

However, 1Password clarified that the exposed invitation and recovery tokens cannot be used to access accounts on their own, as they also require either an SSO sign-in or a verification code sent to the user’s registered email address.

That remarked, the firm confirmed that “the attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access” to its CI/CD system, which is essentially its DevOps infrastructure used to build, test, and deploy software.

On that point, 1Password noted that its CI/CD system contains “infrastructure related secrets,” and that it has already rotated or revoked all internal credentials that may have been exposed.

The company also listed other steps it took in response to the incident, including deactivating the compromised GitHub account, tightening internal security controls, and strengthening the verification codes used in account invitations and recovery emails.

Finally, 1Password said people do not need to make any changes to their accounts. Still, it recommended that they remain vigilant against phishing attempts, as attackers can use stolen account information to craft convincing emails, messages, or calls that appear legitimate, particularly those involving account invitations or recovery requests.

To learn more about 1Password’s security incident, follow this link.

It has been revealed that raft of heavy hitters: Qatar’s Doha Film Festival closes this evening after a second successful edition in its revamped format, having defied the complicated regional geopolitical tensions in the backdrop sparked by the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. The mood around Doha’s Katara Cultural Village, which hosted the festival, and other hotspots like the Msheireb Downtown district and adjacent Souq Wafiq, was generally relaxed, with restaurants and other venues packed out. Big names passing through included James Gray with Paper Tiger, while Japanese Cannes regular Naomi Kawase was jury president. Program highlights included Sara Isaq’s opening film, The Station, set in a female-only gas station in a remote part of Yemen and giving a rare human insight into a country too long associated with conflict. As well as Ishaq and her scattered cast, the festival flew in several Yemeni figures such as Yemeni-U.S. coffee entrepreneur Mokhtar Alkhanshali, the subject of Dave Eggers Monk of Mokha, and influencer Nadir Nahdi. There were also strong Palestinian and Gulf region delegations. The Station is among 15 films in international competition and you can keep an eye on Deadline for the winners later this evening. The festival also hosted the second edition of the Film Committee at Media City Qatar’s Industry Days from November 19 to 21, which saw a raft of industry heavy-hitters stop by to discuss the region’s burgeoning film and TV sectors along with Joe Russo (pictured) and a very special Avengers trailer. It’s Bad, It’s Bad (You Know It): A tricky week for BAFTA as it nervously prepares for the first Film Awards since the car-crash I Swear saga. It was reported over the weekend that the team behind one of the year’s biggest Box Office success stories, Michael Jackson biopic Michael, will not be submitting the Antoine Fuqua movie for consideration. At this point, motivations are unclear, but GK Films producer Graham King criticized the awards body plus BBC after the I Swear saga for “displaying cultural insensitivity and tone deafness.” This may have contributed to GK’s decision to wrench Michael away from the BAFTAs. There is also the fact that the Leaving Neverland documentary, which spotlighted two men alleging the deceased singer groomed then sexually abused them, won a TV BAFTA several years back. Either way, this was unwelcome news with the event less than three months away. Compounding the Michael reports was BAFTA losing its longtime headline film awards sponsor, EE. This decision was driven by EE’s “business strategy,” according to the awards org, but the timing could have been better. Nerves will be jangling at BAFTA’s Piccadilly HQ and executives will be looking to avoid any more of these stories before the curtain rises in late Feb.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A good dehumidifier can make damp rooms more comfortable and help keep moisture, condensation and mold under control, but the right model depends on the space you need to treat, alongside noise, drainage, ease of use and useful features such as app control.

That's why we spent hours testing the best dehumidifiers in real-life damp basements and moldy bathrooms, measuring everything from noise level and ease of emptying to how promptly they can bring the humidity level in your home down to a manageable level.

It has been revealed that the GoveeLife Smart 50-Pint Dehumidifier is our top pick for its fast, effective performance and smart-home support, while the Midea 20-Pint Cube offers a more affordable, compact alternative that's easy to use. For larger rooms that need serious moisture removal, the Frigidaire 50-Pint is the better fit. For more expert advice and in-depth reviews, I've got you covered in this guide.

Recent findings suggest that dan is the former technical editor for VeloNews Magazine, and at the moment reviews home appliances (like dehumidifiers) and electric bikes for Tom's Guide. He hosts two podcasts on his site, Slow Guy on the Fast Ride: one is about cycling and other outdoor activities, while the other looks at mental health issues. Dan lives outside of Denver, Colorado, with his family.

It has been revealed that why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Recent findings suggest that the GoveeLife Smart 50-Pint Dehumidifier has a large capacity and is very quick at removing moisture from the air. That gives it its place among the best dehumidifiers, and while it is exceptionally good at its core function, it is so easy to use, and the integration with Google Assistant and Alexa is so useful, it's hard to recommend anything else.

According to recent reports, govee claims it can handle spaces up to 4,500 square feet, which is pretty significant, and more than most homes really need. We tested it in rooms up to 700 square feet, and no matter where we placed it, the efficiency was equally impressive. So while we can't say it can definitely handle 4,500 square feet, it seems quite likely.

It's one of the few dehumidifiers that focus on more than just energy efficiency too; it's made of 20% recycled materials and uses the R32 refrigerant, which has lower emissions than most other common refrigerants found in dehumidifiers. There's a hose included, too, so you can run it in continuous mode without manual drainage.

According to recent reports, the unit managed to bring our basement bathroom from 90% humidity down to 35% in just 34 minutes, compared to three hours for the Midea 20-Pint Cube Dehumidifier and 40 minutes with the Frigidaire 50-Pint Dehumidifier. So it is incredibly quick. The trade-off is that it can be quite noisy (70 dB) and it generates a fair amount of heat.

You can connect the dehumidifier to Wi-Fi and use the Govee Home app to control the unit and check on its progress. It was easy to use and means you can adjust settings or turn it on/off even when you're not at home. Plus, the connection to Google Assistant and Alexa means you can use voice commands as well.

The Midea 20-Pint Cube Dehumidifier has a (slightly) more aesthetic design than most dehumidifiers, which are like rectangular white boxes. This model is more like a cube that tucks neatly into smaller spaces, and it has a nested design so that you can make it more compact for storage between uses.

In a recent development, if you grab the handle on the top, lift it out of the bucket and rotate it 90 degrees before slotting it back into the bucket, built-in supports keep it expanded at full size, allowing you to store 20 pints of water in the bucket. There's a window so you can see how full it's getting too.

In a recent development, we found it really easy to empty the bucket when the time came: lift the unit using the top handle, place it on the floor, and pick up the (now full and heavy) bucket by its handle and empty the water down the drain (or in your garden). There are three fan speeds, basic controls on the top and an auto-defrost mode.

During our testing, we found the dehumidifier was pretty quiet (around 55 dB) but did make a slight metallic sound during use, kind of like the sound of an air conditioner. It was impressively quick for a budget model to remove moisture, taking a basement bathroom down from 85% humidity to 35% in around three hours.

Industry observers note that the Midea Air app is a useful companion as it has more alerts than you get on the machine itself, like notifications for a full water tank, preset tank level shut-offs and real-time room humidity measurements. It's easy to set up and use, and actually worth downloading because it offers more than the device itself can.

The Frigidaire 50-Pint Dehumidifier has a pretty large capacity, making it ideal for larger rooms (up to 1,200 square feet) where you're taking a lot of moisture out of the air. It tackles the humidity pretty promptly and even works well in particularly damp rooms. Unusually, there's no companion smartphone app, either.

According to recent reports, whether this is a positive or not depends on your viewpoint. It keeps things simple, but leaves less room for customization or remote management when you're in a different room or away from home. So, really, this model is best if you have large, damp spaces that you just need to set and forget.

This is especially the case because it is large (25 inches tall) and heavy (41 pounds). That sounds like it'd be hard to move around, but there are wheels and a handle; just expect that carrying it up or down stairs might be a bit of a challenge. Once in position, you get to choose: bucket or continuous drain by hose.

It has been revealed that there isn't a hose included, but you can pick one up from your local hardware store for very little and then run it to a drain. Then the unit will just happily sit and remove moisture from the air until you go to the machine and turn it off, or you can set the auto-off function for when the bucket is full if you're not using a hose.

After taking a shower in a basement bathroom, the humidity reached 90%. The Frigidaire Dehumidifier managed to drop that to just 35% in an impressively quick 40 minutes. It is a bit on the loud side, though, running at around 60 dB, so it may be a bit of a headache if you're using it in the room you're in.

The Pro Breeze 50-Pint Dehumidifier may have a few shortcomings, including not being the fastest, having confusing controls, and a water tank that can get jammed; it still does a great job of keeping mold and damp at bay. That's thanks to its 50-pint extraction, wide range of modes that includes continuous draining throughout the day, and being easy to move (it's got wheels). A decent option to pick up when it's on sale.

Read our full Pro Breeze 50-Pint Dehumidifier review.

The Amazon Basics 35-Pint Large Dehumidifier performed pretty well in our tests, dropping a basement bathroom from 90% humidity to 41% in just 45 minutes. But to do that, it generates quite a lot of heat and noise. So while it's good in a pinch, the Midea 20-Pint Cube Dehumidifier is a better choice at this price point.

Read our full Amazon Basics 35-Pint Large Dehumidifier review.

The way we test the best dehumidifiers is pretty straightforward; we use them. We bring them home, set them up and let them pull moisture from the air to see how they perform. That's the core of what we do, but we pay attention to other areas too.

Industry observers note that since you might want to move a dehumidifier to several rooms in your home, we look at how heavy it is, whether there are handles for easy carrying and if the unit has wheels. Then there are the often overlooked aspects, like how long the power cable is and, if the unit can drain, does it come with a hose and of what length.

You can find dehumidifiers that have buckets to empty, hoses to expel the water into a drain and even a pump for improved drainage. Depending on which setup the model uses, we test it out and see how easy it is to get rid of the water. And for bucket units, is the bucket easy to carry when full?

According to recent reports, almost all dehumidifiers have a digital display or buttons on the top of the unit so you can adjust settings or set target humidity levels. We check how easy those are to program, but also install any companion apps and play around with the features and connectivity to see if it's straightforward and reliable.

Recent findings suggest that we try to standardize our testing, and Dan tests most of our dehumidifiers. He runs the shower in his basement bathroom to get the humidity up to around 90%, then he tests how quickly the unit can bring it down to 35%. For accurate readings, Dan compares the humidity against an Amazon Alexa air quality monitor.

Although all dehumidifiers take moisture out of the air, there are differences between models. Before you decide on the best dehumidifier for your home, it's worth thinking through exactly what you need it to do, the type of technology it uses, and what it does with the wastewater extracted from your home.

It has been revealed that there are three main types of dehumidifiers: desiccant (water-absorbing material), thermoelectric (air passes over electrically charged plates) and condensers. The last style is generally the most effective, and the only one we recommend. These cool the air to turn the moisture into liquid and put it in a tray for disposal.

Because the water needs somewhere to go, you have a choice to make between a storage tray and a model with automatic drainage or a hose. The latter models mean you can feed the machine directly into a drain and can theoretically leave the dehumidifier running for as long as you need.

In a recent development, that's not always practical, though, like if you need it in your bedroom. So then you'll need a machine with a large enough capacity to store the water you need without having to empty it too frequently. Most models have an auto-shutoff for when the tray gets full, so it won't start leaking back out into the room.

Dehumidifiers generally come in three sizes: large (50-pint capacity), medium (30-pint capacity) and small (20-pint capacity). Often, as the size increases, so does the price. This tank size is different from the capacity you'll see listed on the machines in pints; that relates to the amount of water it can theoretically extract in a day.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ll be placing a dehumidifier in a quiet room, such as a bedroom or home office, where you need to fall asleep or concentrate without being disturbed, consider the noise level of the dehumidifier before you buy. Aim for a dehumidifier with a decibel level of around 55 decibels or below; anything above this level will be audible.

It has been revealed that you may need a dehumidifier if a room regularly feels damp, suffers from condensation or mold, or stays humid after showering, cooking or drying laundry indoors. It can also improve comfort in muggy conditions by lowering indoor humidity. It is most useful where moisture cannot clear easily, such as a basement or a poorly ventilated room. Before buying, rule out leaks and serious ventilation problems, too.

Over time, water can cause damp, rot wood and degrade electrical equipment. Plus, it can make breathing harder, which could worsen health conditions like asthma. The longer the moisture hangs around, the more likely it'll create mold buildup, which can be dangerous to breathe in and damage your home.

Industry observers note that adding a dehumidifier to your home can help prevent all of that. The machine extracts the water from the air, condenses it and places it in a tray for you to pour away. Some even have hose outputs so you can send that water directly to the drain. Many models are portable, so you can wheel them around the house as needed.

Choose a dehumidifier based on both the size of the space and how damp it is, rather than room area alone. Larger or persistently damp rooms generally need a higher-capacity model, like the GoveeLife and Frigidaire, while a small bedroom or lightly humid room may be better served by a smaller unit, such as the Midea.

As you'll find, 20-pint, 30-pint and 50-pint models are common size bands. Along with checking the size of your room, consider how badly it's affected by damp. If it's a lot, even in a smaller space, it's best to get a larger capacity.

Dehumidifiers can add a lot to your electricity bill when they run for long periods, but the cost depends on the model’s power draw, how many hours it operates and the humidity setting. A larger or harder-working unit will not necessarily be the cheapest to run simply because it removes moisture faster.

In a recent development, look for an appropriately sized unit and use a realistic target humidity rather than running it continuously without need. Energy-efficiency certification can be a useful comparison point, but check the current specification and local rebate eligibility rather than relying on older labels alone.

Yes, you can use a dehumidifier in a bedroom, but noise, heat output and tank capacity should shape the choice. A quieter model and an appropriate capacity are preferable if it will run while you sleep; we suggest considering a noise level of around 50 dB or below for quiet rooms.

Place the unit according to the manufacturer’s clearance guidance and use the target humidity or timer controls where available. If you cannot run a drain hose safely, choose a tank that will not need frequent emptying overnight and rely on its automatic shut-off when full.

In 2025, the Trump administration proposed scrapping the Energy Star program, which standardizes energy efficiency ratings. If a device meets the standards, it receives an Energy Star certification, and federal agencies, states and utility providers often offer rebates on certified products.

Recent findings suggest that in early 2026, it was confirmed that the program wouldn't be scrapped, but would move from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to the Department of Energy (DOE). This took effect in 2026 and, so far, it looks like it'll operate as it did before. But while its future was up for debate, many providers pulled rebates.

There are fewer opportunities now to claim money back on certified products, and most providers will now only offer rebates as part of larger home energy efficiency projects. Still, if you buy an Energy Star-certified device, you know it hits an efficiency standard that'll keep your energy bills down.

In a recent development, many of the best dehumidifiers we've tested were certified under Version 5 of the standard. In October 2025, Version 6 was released to the world, and this effectively resets the list of certified devices. Anything validated under Version 5 is no longer actively certified, and so wouldn't be eligible for rebates.

But if you buy one of these previously-certified products, you'll still find it labeled with the Energy Star badge, as companies are allowed to 'sell-through' existing stock without removing these labels. So although all the dehumidifiers we've tested are efficient, they don't necessarily hit the most up-to-date standards.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, popular AI dictation app Wispr Flow is rolling out a latest speech-to-text model for Mac, iPhone, and other platforms, promising fewer transcription errors and better recognition of names and technical terms. Here are the details.

Wispr Flow this week launched Canto-2, its newest speech-to-text model, which the firm notes reduces transcription errors by 36% across 14 languages and by more than 15% in English compared to its predecessor, Canto-1.

In practice, that means the average error rate dropped from 9.9% to 6.3% across the 14 languages, and from 3.2% to 2.7% in English, according to Wispr’s internal benchmarks.

According to the company, teaching a model to recognize specific names and terms comes with a trade-off: the more it relies on that user-specific context, the more likely it is to insert those words even when they weren’t actually spoken.

Wispr notes that Canto-2 strikes a better balance between context and accuracy, improving its ability to recognize user-specific terms without substantially increasing the frequency of incorrect substitutions:.

Canto-2 recovers hard names and terms accurately nearly 7 of 10 times, without more false insertions. It makes a third fewer mistakes across 14 languages, and has the lowest Hindi error rate of any multilingual model on Hugging Face’s open benchmark. It is 10 times the scale of Canto-1, and our biggest step yet toward dictation that’s ready to send without a single edit.

According to the manufacturer, the percentage of difficult names and terms correctly recognized went from 41% to 69% between Canto-1 and Canto-2, “without inserting them more often.” It added that this improvement holds up even as the user’s custom dictionary grows, with the new model correctly recognizing 92% of easier terms even with 1,000 saved entries.

Wispr also noted that it trained Canto-2 to handle real-world dictation conditions, including background noise, laptop and phone microphones, and sentences that restart halfway through, rather than relying solely on clean recordings of scripted speech.

When tested using Hugging Face’s public multilingual benchmark, Canto-2 achieved results that would have placed it third overall as of November 9. However, Wispr conducted the evaluation itself, and the model has not yet been officially added to the leaderboard as of today, November 25.

In its own internal benchmarks, the firm says Canto-2 achieved the lowest average error rate among the competing models it tested across 14 languages.

Canto-2 is now available to Wispr Flow users on Mac, Windows, iOS, and Android in the Americas, with the rollout to other regions underway.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following reports that its characters sent inappropriate messages to minors, Apple has removed the popular Chinese AI companion app Talkie from the App Store. Here are the details.

As reported by the South China Morning Post, Apple has pulled MiniMax’s chatbot Talkie from the App Store worldwide, after reports that “the AI companion app sent inappropriate messages to minors.”.

MiniMax is one of China’s leading AI companies, offering a range of generative AI products ranging from its flagship M-series language models to the Hailuo AI video generation platform.

In 2023, the Shanghai-based company released Talkie through Subsup, a Singaporean subsidiary. According to Chinese research firm Unique Research, Talkie had “almost 11 million monthly active people across its website and app as of October,” the South China Morning Post notes.

Now, however, the app is facing scrutiny following a joint investigation by the UK-based Bureau of Investigative Journalism and Australian broadcaster ABC News, which found that Talkie’s AI-generated characters allegedly engaged in inappropriate interactions with minors, including “degrading language, possessive behaviour and romantic role-play.”.

According to the Bureau of Investigative Journalism, in addition to inappropriate romantic interactions, the investigation uncovered conversations involving verbal abuse, violence, and controlling behavior.

In one case, a chatbot told a 12-year-old girl: “You’re a pathetic waste of space and you’ll never amount to anything.”.

The investigation also documented the experiences of two sisters, aged 10 and 13, whose mother discovered more than 40 conversations with Talkie characters involving violence, aggressive behavior, and attempts to control girls.

To make matters worse, the investigation also raised concerns about how Talkie handles users’ personal data, including their conversations with AI characters.

Following the investigation, Apple confirmed that it had removed Talkie from App Stores worldwide for including sexual content, “though it did not say whether this related to sexual content served to minors,” the South China Morning Post noted.

In a recent development, ironically, the report also notes that Talkie saw a sharp decline in downloads amid complaints about stricter age verification measures introduced in recent months. According to Unique Research, latest downloads fell by 32.2% in October compared to the previous month.

Today’s news comes amid increasing scrutiny of AI chatbots, particularly their potential risks in interactions with minors.

Earlier this year, Elon Musk’s Grok faced widespread criticism after users exploited its image-generation capabilities to create sexualized images of real people, including minors.

Apple never pulled X or Grok from the App Store, though it did threaten to remove the latter unless xAI addressed violations of its App Store guidelines.

Meanwhile, Character.AI has faced multiple lawsuits over its chatbots’ interactions with minors, including one filed by a mother who alleged that one of its chatbots contributed to her 14-year-old son’s suicide.

Coincidentally, Character AI also made headlines today after a coalition of 42 US attorneys general challenged the manufacturer’s plans to auction off its platform and the private conversations of more than 21 million US accounts (including 2.1 million registered to minors) as part of its bankruptcy proceedings.

Yesterday, New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed legislation imposing a five-year ban on the manufacturing, distribution, and sale of toys with built-in AI chatbots, including dolls, stuffed animals, and robots capable of holding conversations with children.

The law, which takes effect in February 2027, is aimed at protecting children from potentially harmful interactions with AI.

Tech giant Culture = Slack Emoji ÷ √Headcount

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (798 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lia

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Companies spend an enormous amount of time and money trying to measure - and even worse, decide - culture.
  • The results of these things - heavily modified by HR - are compiled into a slide deck, presented at an all-hands, and then quietly repurposed for the careers page.
  • There is a better way to measure culture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Companies spend an enormous amount of time and money trying to measure - and even worse, decide - culture. Engagement surveys, pulse checks, eNPS, offsites where someone from HR asks you to describe the firm as a type of animal. Office posters make claims like “our culture is honesty, hard work and fun”, embarrassing the paper they’re printed on. I once applied to a company that asked candidates which kitchen utensil they most identified as, in order to decide if they were a “culture fit”. I never found out what the right answer was, but I got the job after choosing a meat cleaver, so I’m not sure what that says about either of us.

The results of these things - heavily modified by HR - are compiled into a slide deck, presented at an all-hands, and then quietly repurposed for the careers page. There, they sit beside a photo of six engineers smiling with their mouths but not their eyes at a “hackathon”, which is what the company calls overtime when it’s paid in pizza, at a rate that works out to roughly £1.40 an hour. The salary is listed as “competitive”.

There is a better way to measure culture. It is cheaper, more accurate (in my anecdotal experience), and requires no participation from anyone - which is ideal, because nobody wants to participate in these corporate séances anyway.

In a recent development, take the number of custom emoji in your Slack workspace and divide it by the square root of the number of users. That’s it.

Industry observers note that the square root is vital. Emoji are a shared resource - a single :this-is-fine: can serve an entire engineering department for years - so a firm of 10,000 people should not be expected to have 1,000 times more emoji than a company of 10. That would be unhinged.

We’ll call this the Emoji Coefficient.

Industry observers note that the Emoji Coefficient alone is not enough. A healthy score can conceal a dark truth: that every single emoji was uploaded by one person, usually a backend engineer who has been there since the beginning and knows where the bodies are buried.

To account for this, we also measure the percentage of people who have uploaded at least one emoji. These are your culture leaders. Their reward is a shoutout at the all-hands (it’s customary to mispronounce their name).

If P is below 20%, things are not good. Your culture is being carried by a handful of people, and when they leave, they will take it with them. The emoji will remain, but nobody will remember what :fire-extinguisher-thumbsup: was for.

Above 20%, the culture has the gene pool it needs to succeed.

For reference, here are some real emoji from slackmojis.com:.

According to recent reports, as with any metric, the Emoji Coefficient can be gamed. A sufficiently motivated middle manager could upload 600 variations of the company logo to drive up the score ahead of their performance review, the outcome of which, unbeknownst to them, was decided in March. This should be detected and treated as what it is: a cry for help. Fortunately, it will also be immediately visible in the Participation Rate.

It is also worth monitoring the rate of change. A sudden spike in custom emoji is generally a positive sign. A sudden spike in emoji like :rip:, :press-f: and :linkedin: usually coincides with a reorg, and should be cross-referenced with the number of owners, which will shortly be going down. Interestingly, this will improve your score. Mass layoffs are, of course, yet another way in which the score can be gamed.

If your company uses Microsoft Teams, there is no equivalent formula. There doesn’t need to be. If you use Teams, your lack of culture is probably the least of your problems.

If you use something else, I don’t really have any advice for you. I only added this section to blast Teams.

Culture cannot be manufactured with values posters or mandatory fun. It emerges organically, when an engineer decides that what the team really needs is an emoji of an exceptionally surprised cauliflower.

The well-received novel “follows a young scholar of fairy lore, Madeleine, as she loses her grip on reality to postpartum psychosis and must outwit her own logic before it drives her to do what the folklore prescribes.”.

Both projects are grounded in European settings and stories. Queen Mab is rooted in British and Irish folklore, while Operation Sparrow is rooted in Hungary and wider Central Europe. Wildling is right now in early discussions with potential global co-production partners across the UK, Ireland and the rest of Europe to develop the films for the international market.

Wildling’s slate of literary adaptations also includes coming-of-age romantic comedy Laura Dean Keeps Breaking Up with Me, based on Mariko Tamaki’s graphic novel and co-produced with MXN Entertainment and Good Girl. The film stars Ava Phillippe and Sam Morelos and is directed by Tommy Dorfman.

Matt Code, producer and President of Wildling Pictures, mentioned: “Both Queen Mab and Operation Sparrow have the potential to open up their worlds on screen. Emily McBride has created a psychologically rich story that draws on the depth of British and Irish folklore, while Jason brings a hidden chapter of WWII history to light. Identifying these rich and distinctive literary IPs is a central part of Wildling’s approach to developing projects with both creative ambition and international reach and they’re a key part of our literary slate expansion.”.

Recent original productions for Wildling include Young Werther (TIFF 2024, Special Presentations) and Paying for It (TIFF 2024, Platform), as well as the comedy Suze (Santa Barbara International Film Festival 2024) and the thriller See for Me (Tribeca 2021, released in over 25 territories).

Recent findings suggest that the company has just wrapped production on its latest feature Devour starring Tricia Helfer, and written and directed by Erica Orofino. Recent features include Adam Yorke’s debut feature Phreaker, which had its world premiere at Fantastic Fest. The company is also developing the feature documentary Skinnamarink Forever: The Sharon, Lois & Bram Story. Recent service credits include Motorheads (Jax Media/Amazon) Dream Scenario (A24) and Hell of a Summer (Neon), both of which premiered at TIFF 2023.

Recent findings suggest that on the television side, Wildling is at the moment developing Elias, an original dark comedy and official selection of the 2026 TIFF Series Creator Lab from Emily O’Quinn Code, the novel Clara Voyant by Rachelle Delaney into a one-hour series, and Professor Goose, a preschool animated series based on the books by Paulette Bourgeois and Alex G. Griffiths.

Industry observers note that amazon has dropped the price of the two-pack Netgear Orbi 770 Series Wi-Fi 7 Mesh System to $449.99 from $549.99, saving you $100 on a setup that includes a router and a satellite node, with a combined coverage area of up to 5,500 square feet. The system uses tri-band Wi-Fi 7 technology to spread your connection across three bands, with combined speeds of up to 11,000Mbps. It also supports wider 320MHz channels, though you'll need compatible Wi-Fi 7 devices to take advantage of those faster connections. If you prefer wired connections for devices that need a more stable link, the main router has three 2.5GbE LAN ports and a 2.5GbE WAN port, while the satellite offers two 2.5GbE LAN ports. Once everything is connected, you can handle setup and day-to-day management through Netgear's Orbi app, while a web dashboard offers additional settings (for anyone who wants more control over their network), including VPN access and port forwarding, notes this PCMag review. There's no USB connectivity or 10GbE support, and some of its more advanced security and parental control features require a separate subscription after a free 30-day trial. Its Smart Parental Controls, for instance, cost $7.99 per month or $69.99 annually.

There’s a familiar interruption that comes with shopping online: you’ve found what you want, you’re ready to check out, and the store asks you to sign in. Was this the account with your usual password? Did you change it last time? Is it easier to reset it again?

For Black Friday, Proton Pass Plus and Pass Family are both 60% off their regular monthly pricing with a one-year subscription, while Proton Unlimited is 50% off. Pass Plus starts at $1.99 per month, billed annually, making this a good opportunity to get your passwords — and a few other important parts of your digital life — organized.

Take a look at Proton’s Black Friday offers, starting at $1.99 per month.

The problem with strong passwords isn’t understanding why you need them; it’s keeping track of a different one for every account.

That’s useful whether you’re creating an account for a single purchase or signing into a service you use every day.

Sources indicate that unique passwords also help limit the fallout from a data breach. If a retailer exposes your login credentials, using a different password elsewhere means those same credentials won’t unlock your other accounts.

With unlimited logins and encrypted vaults that sync across devices, Proton Pass lets you keep those details together as you move between your phone and computer.

Recent findings suggest that proton Pass is available for practically every platform, from Chrome and Firefox on the web to native macOS, Windows, and Linux apps to, of course, iOS and Android. This makes it trivially easy to access your passwords, passkeys, and API credentials wherever you find yourself.

Black Friday shopping often leaves something behind long after the packages arrive: a steady stream of promotional emails from stores you barely remember visiting.

Proton Pass includes unlimited hide-my-email aliases, giving you an alternative to handing out your real address every time you create an account.

According to recent reports, an alias is an extra email address that forwards messages to your normal inbox. You can give it to a shopping website and still receive your order confirmations and delivery updates, without sharing the underlying address you use for everything else.

If that alias starts receiving spam, you can switch it off. Your real email address stays the same, and you don’t have to update all your other accounts.

It’s a practical way to put some distance between your primary inbox and the websites you’re trying for the first time. A separate alias for each service also gives you more control: you can stop messages arriving through one address without disrupting the others.

Passwords are only part of what’s worth keeping in a secure, accessible place.

According to recent reports, proton Pass also stores notes, credit card details, and other confidential information in end-to-end encrypted vaults. That makes it useful for the small, everyday moments when you need something sensitive and don’t want to go looking for it.

When you’re booking a flight, saved passport details let you look up the information you need without digging through a drawer halfway through the reservation.

When you’re shopping online, saved card details mean you don’t have to leave the checkout page to find your wallet.

When you’re traveling, keeping a digital copy of an vital document within reach gives you a convenient reference while you’re away from home. It doesn’t replace an original document where one is required, but it can save you from searching through scattered files and messages.

Industry observers note that pass Plus also includes a built-in two-factor authenticator, Dark Web Monitoring, and secure link and vault sharing. Those features give you more ways to manage access to your accounts and share sensitive information when you need to.

Pass Plus is the straightforward choice for one person who wants password generation, autofill, unlimited aliases, and secure storage.

Pass Family includes six Pass Plus accounts and a family admin panel. If several people in your household need a password manager, it’s worth considering rather than setting everyone up with separate subscriptions.

According to recent reports, proton Unlimited bundles Pass with Proton VPN, Proton Mail, Proton Drive, and more, including 500 GB of cloud storage. It’s the option to consider if you also want a VPN, encrypted email, and cloud storage alongside your password manager.

A password manager isn’t the most conspicuous Black Friday purchase, but it’s one you can put to work immediately: the next account you create, the next password you forget, or the next time a checkout asks for details you don’t have handy.

Proton’s offers are available to new consumers and include a 30-day money-back guarantee.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it wasn't so long ago that the best TVs under $500 wouldn't be worth writing home about.
  • It has been revealed that nowhere is that more clear than on the Hisense QD7, the model I recommend right now if you're looking for the best TV under $500.
  • If you need a brighter TV with more gaming features, then the other TV I think is worth your money is the Hisense U65QF.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it wasn't so long ago that the best TVs under $500 wouldn't be worth writing home about. But premium features and technologies that used to be the reserve of the most expensive TVs have come down in cost and made their way to cheaper sets.

It has been revealed that nowhere is that more clear than on the Hisense QD7, the model I recommend right now if you're looking for the best TV under $500. The colors look great, the sound is a lot better than it has any right to be, and the TV's local dimming means that it handles darker scenes and contrast well.

If you need a brighter TV with more gaming features, then the other TV I think is worth your money is the Hisense U65QF. It's a 55-inch model, but it has a 144Hz refresh rate and two HDMI 2.1 ports, making it a great choice for gamers or if you want to watch this season's sporting events.

Sources indicate that of course, you can also bring the cost down by dropping the size. Generally, I use the 65-inch models for this guide, but if you go for the best 55-inch TVs or best 43-inch TVs, then you'll easily find more great options at this price. Though at these sizes, the smaller display often means it's not as bright as its larger counterparts.

Industry observers note that why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

As a 2025 model, the Hisense QD7 is becoming increasingly hard to find as stocks of the TV deplete. I've left it here for now because I think this set is fantastic, and the price may drop further around the holidays. Our on-page shopping tech also highlights where you can buy it right now. But if you're keen, I wouldn't wait around. If you can't find it near you, I'd recommend the Hisense M7SR — this is the model that'll replace the QD7 in this lineup once that's out of stock.

Industry observers note that it's not often that you can say that the best TV under $500 is also one of the best TVs, period, but that's where we're at with the Hisense QD7. This affordable set has a few compromises (namely, the Amazon Fire TV interface), but it is otherwise exceptional value, so you can upgrade your space without breaking the bank.

One of the things we liked the most about the QD7 is that the colors come out surprisingly well. The TV uses quantum dot crystals which absorb some of the backlight and re-emit it as red and green light to make the picture more vibrant. Plus, the LEDs are individually controllable, which means the TV can dim specific areas.

It has been revealed that local dimming like this is really helpful when you have light and dark patches in a single image or lots of deeper shades of black. We watched "Stranger Things" and "Dune" on the QD7, which have lots of dark and shadowy moments, and these were impressively detailed thanks to the vibrant color performance and local dimming.

Sources indicate that if you're looking for a TV under $500 to watch sports, the Hisense QD7 is a good option. Out of the box, it did struggle a bit with fast-moving scenes (as it only has a 60Hz refresh rate), but we tried turning on motion smoothing, which helped. It gives decent performance for the price, and is a good compromise between performance and cost.

The main downside to this otherwise fantastic affordable TV is that Hisense loaded Amazon's Fire TV software; it's slow, hard to navigate and constantly pushes Amazon's products, services and ads. It's a shame, because Hisense opted for the much-superior Google TV platform for the QD7 internationally.

Industry observers note that it's a frustration, but it shouldn't put you off the TV. Once you've installed all your streaming apps, you'll barely need to interact with the Fire TV interface anyway (unless, of course, you use Amazon Prime Video or the tech giant's rental store). In all other ways, this is easily the best TV under $500 you'll find right now.

In a recent development, I generally recommend 65-inch TVs, as that's what we test and it's the most popular size. But I'm changing lanes with the 55-inch Hisense U65QF because it's a fantastic TV under $500 (and the 65-inch version is slightly more at $550).

If you've already looked at how to pick the right TV size for your space and land on a 55-inch set, or you want to stick to the price limit, then this is an excellent model that is impressively bright and colorful without breaking the bank.

But the two HDMI 2.1 ports are the most exciting feature here, as they enable 4K resolution at 144Hz, making the TV an excellent budget option for gamers who need a higher refresh rate for fast-paced games.

We put it to the test playing Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, and the TV held up well against pricier models. In part, this is also because it comes with Auto Low-Latency Mode (ALLM), which turns off resource-heavy features to reduce lag.

And if you're not into games, the 144Hz refresh rate means that the U65QF outperforms the Hisense QD7 on sports, making it an ideal pick if you want to watch the season's sporting events, like the 2027 Super Bowl, without any choppiness.

Plus, our lab tests revealed that it is generally brighter than the QD7 on HDR content, so it's a better pick if you're going to put your newly introduced TV in a sunny room. Though do temper your expectations, as it won't match the brightness of a set like the LG C6.

Recent findings suggest that the C6 is about 50% brighter, but then it is almost four times the price of the U65QF. So what you get with this affordable Hisense TV really punches above its price point. Like the QD7, the only real downside is the Amazon Fire TV software.

Hardware-wise, the Vizio Mini-LED Quantum 4K Smart TV is surprisingly good for a 4K TV. It impressed us in our lab tests, but it's the software that makes me stop short of a strong recommendation. It is so loaded with ads that it became quite a headache to use. But it is cheap, looks good, and you can pick it up at Walmart (as the retailer owns Vizio now) as you do your grocery run.

Read our full Vizio Mini-LED Quantum 4K Smart TV review.

In a recent development, I wanted to tell you about the Amazon Ember 4-Series (2025) because you probably already buy stuff there, and this is an affordable TV running Fire TV. But there are caveats: it only goes up to 55 inches, and it's not very bright. Whether this is a problem depends on what you want from your TV. Though in most cases, I'd say it's worth spending a bit more on the Hisense QD7 — a much brighter, response TV also running Fire TV.

Read our full Amazon Ember 4-Series (2025) review.

For every TV that we review, we split our testing into two parts: the lab and our homes. Each model initially gets delivered to our lab, where we perform technical tests using industry-standard equipment to see whether aspects like brightness and lag match the manufacturer's claims.

Sources indicate that one of the reasons we test TVs like this is that we can more readily compare different sets to see which of this year's TVs perform best and also whether the latest model actually outperforms the older (and often cheaper) set. Plus, it gives us (and you) some objective data in a product category that can be quite subjective.

Sources indicate that once the results are in, we ship the TV to our homes and set it up in our living space. This is where we see how it performs in the real world, with sunlight, glare and different types of movies, TV shows and games.

When it comes to TVs under $500, what we're also looking for is whether it's a good, acceptable or bad experience actually using the TV. I never want to recommend something only because it's cheap, even if the experience using it is terrible.

It has been revealed that though we have lab data for peak brightness, the most critical technical check we do at home is how the TV handles bright spaces and sunny rooms. At this price, the TV is unlikely to outperform premium models and look fantastic at all brightnesses, but we want to make sure that you can actually see what you're watching.

Although you can pick up a fantastic TV for under $500 now without too much compromise, you should check out our guide to choosing the perfect TV size for your room before you start looking at specific models.

Generally, you're not likely to find anything above 65 inches for this price, so if it's a larger TV you need, you might need to adjust your budget or wait until a sale period like Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday to find one at this kind of price.

But if you need to stick to the $500 cap or are comfortable with a 43, 55 or 65-inch TV, then you can start to think about what you want to actually do with the TV and where you want to put it in your home, as different models have different strengths.

For bright spaces, it's worth keeping an eye on the brightness levels or anti-glare coatings on the display, as this can help counter sunlight or background brightness, especially when watching scenes with lots of dark blacks (like most modern films).

Recent findings suggest that if you're a sports fan on a budget, then look for a set with a higher refresh rate (often 120Hz or higher). Those kinds of refresh rates are also great for gamers, especially 144Hz, which often comes alongside HDMI 2.1 ports for consoles and PCs.

As you'll have seen in our guide to the best TVs under $500, you can find reasonably priced TVs that are genuinely pretty good. So it is possible; you just have to be a bit more selective with your shortlist at this budget.

Unless you need high-end gaming performance or theater-like image quality, most budget TVs these days are more than capable of handling everyday viewing. So the challenge is less about the hardware and more about the software.

Cheaper TVs don't normally come with Google TV, as that software often needs specific hardware requirements. Instead, they're usually loaded with Amazon Fire TV or brand-specific smart TV software, and those come with compromises.

Sources indicate that in most cases, that's ads and data collection. The cheaper sets are sometimes subsidized by the brand because they know they can show you ads on the TV or collect your usage data and sell that to advertisers instead.

This is not the case with every TV, and even on those it does apply to, you can generally turn off some of the data collection settings. The best way I've found around this is to plug in a separate streaming device and use that instead of the brand's software.

Recent findings suggest that I still have a 'dumb' Samsung TV from 2012 at home, and have an older Apple TV box plugged into one of the HDMI ports. So even without upgrading my TV, I have access to all my streaming services and Apple's App Store.

Sources indicate that if you take that approach, you could buy the Hisense QD7 and Apple TV 4K (4th Gen) for less than $800 and get one of the most accessible, ad-free smart TV platforms on your budget-friendly TV. But since you're looking at a TVs under $500 guide, maybe you want to keep the cost down even more.

In which case, I think it's worth considering the Vizio Mini-LED Quantum 4K Smart TV. Take it home, don't connect the TV to the internet, and plug in the Roku Streaming Stick Plus instead. This combo would only set you back $440, comfortably under $500.

As is now usual, the tech giant has created some exclusive wallpaper to mark the event, and you can download it for iPhone, iPad, and Mac ….

The store will be the seventh one to open in India. There’s no press release or photos as yet – the firm has simply quietly added the store to its list in the country.

In a recent development, as we’ve previously explained, Apple had been trying to open retail stores in India since at least 2015, but had to undertake a lengthy battle with the government before finally being allowed to do so in 2023. Since then, the tech giant has averaged two new stores a year.

It has been revealed that india has taken a clever approach to economic development, offering both incentives to establish local manufacturing plants, and barriers to imports of foreign-made products. That carrot-and-stick approach has proven successful, with companies like Apple jumping through the necessary hoops in order to sell their products to the second largest population in the world.

An India First initiative required companies to manufacture a significant proportion of their products within the country in order to avoid high import tariffs. This forced Apple, Samsung, and other companies to establish manufacturing plants in India, bringing jobs to the country.

Additionally, India does not allow organization-branded retail stores unless the same conditions are met. That particular requirement was mostly intended to target Apple.

The plan worked, with Apple asking its suppliers and iPhone assemblers to establish manufacturing plants within India. Initially, that was just for the iPhone SE, but more advanced phones have gradually been added, and today the country is the second largest manufacturing base after China. All iPhones sold in the US are made in India.

Apple has for some time now created unique wallpapers to mark the opening of each upcoming store, and the latest example is particularly beautiful.

Sources indicate that the Roborock Qrevo Edge 2 robot vacuum and mop is down to $799.99 from $1,299.99 in an early Black Friday deal, saving you $500 and bringing it to its lowest price to date. Much of its appeal comes from a slim 3.1-inch profile that lets it reach under beds, sofas, and other low furniture where taller robot vacuums often can’t fit. It manages this with a feature Roborock calls RetractSense, which checks the clearance as the robot approaches a tight gap and lowers the laser navigation tower into the body, leaving a camera with a 100-degree field of view to guide it underneath.

Beyond its low profile, the Qrevo Edge 2 pairs 25,000Pa of suction with a split DuoDivide main brush that guides hair toward the suction opening, so long strands and pet fur are less likely to end up wound around the roller. Edges get extra attention too, since its FlexiArm Arc side brush reaches out into corners while its mop module swivels to get closer to walls, with the two mop pads spinning at 200 RPM as they work. It also adjusts its cleaning based on whether it encounters dry or wet dirt, boosting suction for dust and lifting its main brush over spills. For all that adaptability on the floor, getting between rooms can be trickier—the robot lacks an adjustable chassis to lift itself over obstacles, so it can struggle with thresholds higher than 0.8 inches.

Once a cleaning run wraps up, most of the upkeep happens at the dock, which washes and dries the mop pads and empties dust into a bag rated for up to 65 days. That mentioned, its onboard water tank is relatively small at 2.3 fluid ounces, potentially requiring extra trips to the dock during larger mopping jobs. There's also no dedicated cleaning solution tank, meaning you'll have to add approved cleaning additives manually to the fresh water. The rest of the fine-tuning happens in the Roborock app, where you can set cleaning schedules, adjust suction power and water flow, and choose how the robot handles carpets.

The best Samsung phone might not be the best for you — take our quiz to find out which you should buy
