⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finding the best Samsung phone is a tall order — there are so many different options available, all with the same name.
  • According to recent reports, that's why we've created this guide, so that you can more easily tell which phone is the best for you, highlighting the strengths and weaknesses of each.
  • All you need to do is answer the questions, and you'll be recommended a device that fits what you want out of your next Samsung phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finding the best Samsung phone is a tall order — there are so many different options available, all with the same name. It's confusing, to say the least, and finding out what sets each model apart from the others is, at best, annoying.

According to recent reports, that's why we've created this guide, so that you can more easily tell which phone is the best for you, highlighting the strengths and weaknesses of each. We've also made a quiz that you can use to help you find the phone that's going to fit your unique use case.

All you need to do is answer the questions, and you'll be recommended a device that fits what you want out of your next Samsung phone. It couldn't be easier. So let's get started — which is the best Samsung phone for you?

Want to learn more about the current Samsung lineup? Here's how we rank them after thoroughly testing each model.

While the S25 Ultra was the previous peak of Samsung's power, the Galaxy S26 Ultra arrives as a more than worthy successor. The S26 Ultra introduces a world-first "Privacy Display" that gives it a unique security advantage over every other model in Samsung's current catalog, and even phones by other brands.

However, the Ultra's Privacy Display does come with a negative: it is slightly dimmer (1,806 nits) and has narrower viewing angles than the vibrant, traditional panels found on the S25 Edge or the Z Fold 8.

The S26 Ultra pushes the boundaries of software with its latest AI powers. Samsung has added predictive tools like "Now Brief" and automated app actions that can handle complex background tasks, making it a much more capable productivity tool.

In the photography department, the S26 Ultra remains far more advanced than any other Galaxy phone, with its 200MP main camera and 50MP telephoto lens, which have both been upgraded with wider apertures for superior low-light performance. Samsung has also introduced Horizon Lock for video, providing a level of professional-grade stabilization that the cameras on older and cheaper models cannot match.

While the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is Samsung's thinnest phone, the Galaxy S26 Ultra still managed to be thinner and lighter than its predecessor without sacrificing its 6.9-inch screen size.

According to recent reports, regarding battery performance, the S26 Ultra’s 16 hours and 10 minutes of life easily outclasses Samsung’s foldables like the Z Flip 7 (12:24) and Z Fold 7 (10:55). It also powers up faster thanks to newly added 60W wired charging support.

Ultimately, the S26 Ultra remains a steep $1,299 investment, especially compared to the $899 Galaxy S26. But the Ultra's combination of top-tier zoom, innovative security features, and AI-driven efficiency makes it the definitive choice for power customers who find other phones simply too limited.

Sources indicate that while it's still over six inches in size (what would have been called a "phablet" not too long ago), and technically a foldable would be smaller in your pocket, the Galaxy S26 is as compact as you can get with a modern Samsung phone. And fortunately, as a flagship Galaxy S model, it's got everything you could want it to have despite its size.

The newly introduced 6.3-inch AMOLED display is significantly brighter than Samsung's older models, reaching up to 1,950 nits, which makes it far more legible in direct sunlight than its predecessors or main competitors like the iPhone 17. This makes it an ideal choice for customers who prioritize media consumption and outdoor visibility in a device that still fits comfortably in one hand.

The S26 maintains an easy-to-carry form factor while still housing the same powerful Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset found in the more expensive Ultra model (at least in the U.S.). This ensures that average people get top-tier speed and gaming capabilities without the physical or financial burden of the largest devices.

Industry observers note that the introduction of newly introduced and upgraded AI features is a major selling point too. These features allow the phone to become more aware of user habits and offer sophisticated photo editing capabilities—such as generating new elements or removing reflections—that were previously limited to more niche devices. For the everyday user, these AI tools simplify complex tasks like photo editing and device management, making the smartphone experience more intuitive and efficient.

Recent findings suggest that finally, while the S26 saw a price increase to $899, it remains the most practical choice due to its high-end software experience and innovative camera features like "Horizon Lock." This video stabilization tool keeps footage perfectly level even during significant rotation, a feature the reviewer noted as being far more useful for the average person than high-resolution 8K recording. By combining professional-grade internals with user-friendly software and a manageable size, the Galaxy S26 secures its spot as the most well-rounded option in Samsung’s 2026 line-up.

In a recent development, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is, currently the most expensive phone you can buy from Samsung. Apart from the ill-fated Trifold. What do you get for a $2,099 purchase? The best folding phone that you can buy right now, as you might expect. Samsung has stepped up its game with this model, after other manufacturers started to catch up and land higher places in best lists.

It has been revealed that the screen on the inside is the most noticeable improvement. For one, it’s incredibly bright and clear. This is one of the brightest AMOLED screens that Samsung has packed into a foldable yet, and it looks phenomenal. Movies are immersive, and games look epic. The crease is almost gone now too — you can still feel it with your finger, but it’s all but entirely invisible this time around.

Going back to games swiftly, the Z Fold 8 Ultra is a powerhouse. We threw some very graphically intensive games at the Fold 8 Ultra, and they all ran incredibly smoothly. Gamers will love it. Productivity heads will get a kick out of it too, as they pan around and multitask without any kind of slowdown at all. This is a very powerful handset.

Industry observers note that we only wish that the cameras were better, especially considering how much the phone costs. The main camera is fine, and the selfie camera takes a decent image, but the telephoto camera is straight-up bad. It might as well not be there at all — everything looks blurry and awful. If you want the best camera around, you’re better off with the non-folding Galaxy S26 Ultra.

Battery life is good, with 14 and a half hours of staying power. That’s excellent, although not quite as good as the Motorola Razr Fold.

And we need to talk about that price. On a phone contract, it might not be something you think about initially, but it will add up month by month. $2,099 is a lot of money for a phone, whether it's excellent or not.

Recent findings suggest that “Big screen” and “easily pocketable” aren’t usually things that you’d assume could be a part of the same conversation. And yet, thanks to a very clever folding screen and square shape, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is just that. A pocketable phone with a massive screen inside. It’s about the same size and shape as a passport when it's folded.

There’s not much missing here, beyond perhaps a telephoto lens. But given how bad the telephoto lens on the more expensive Fold 8 Ultra is, it's perhaps no great loss. We’d also like it if more apps were suited to the larger screen inside, but that’s not really the fault of the phone itself. Just app developers. Still, worth thinking about if you’re going to buy one.

Everything else is great. The large display inside is super bright and clear, and the crease in the middle has been handled with some very cool latest screen tech to make it almost invisible.

The outer screen is similarly bright and clear, and easy to use with one hand thanks to that squarer shape. The whole thing is mind-blowingly thin when unfolded, as well. We really shouldn’t be wowed by stuff like this anymore, but it's hard not to be impressed by a knife-like phone in the hand.

It all runs extremely smoothly as well, with the Elite chip inside handling multitasking and heavy games with ease. Gamers will love that extra screen real estate too. Productivity folks will find a lot to like too, as they hop quickly from app to app on the same screen. Very cool.

Cameras are fine, although by no means class-leading. If you’re looking for a camera to take loads of snaps, you’ll want one of the non-folding models. If you just want to take the occasional picture, you’ll be fine, mind you. Battery life is good too, with more than an extra hour of battery over the Fold 7. It’s likely that most people will be charging by the time they go to bed every evening.

In a recent development, the Fold 8 is a great phone, and this wider form factor is a master stroke that sets it apart from the larger and more expensive Fold 8 Ultra. It’s still expensive, but it hasn’t broken the $2,000 mark yet. That honor is for the flagship.

The Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8 is a very similar phone to the 7th generation that came before it. In essence, not a necessary upgrade if you’ve got the old one. But. If you’re looking for a good flip phone to buy right now, and you’re upgrading a 3-year-old phone that’s coming up to the end of its device blueprint, then there’s little better right now than the Z Flip 8.

The screens this time around are brighter than ever, making sure that you can see them no matter the outside lighting conditions. Bright sun? No problem for either display in the Flip 8. There’s also some fancy new tech in the folding display that makes the crease inside far less noticeable. Like, it’s there, but it’s far less noticeable than before.

Sources indicate that battery life is fine, although nothing to write home about. During our lab testing, we found that the phone lasted for 12 hours and 50 minutes — that’s pretty good for a folding phone, but not that much more than the previous model. Expect to be plugging in every night, regardless.

It's smooth and slick to use thanks to a very powerful chip inside. We threw a range of different games at the phone during testing, and that larger interior display looked great the whole time. The phone had little problem running everything at high frame rates. Just don’t expect to use the outer screen. You can even use the Flip 8 as a computer with DeX, if you want. You should probably stick to your laptop.

According to recent reports, this is an expensive phone, mind you. It comes in at around $1,099, which is more than other phones that have a similarly sized screen when it's open. For those with small pockets who sometimes want a larger screen, though, you’ll love the Flip 8.

The Samsung Galaxy A57 stands out as Samsung’s best value phone this year, delivering an expansive 6.7-inch display at a midrange price that’s especially compelling for buyers who want big-screen utility without overspending. The screen size brings benefits for streaming and multitasking, and the price means you don’t have to compromise on core features.

Battery life is a clear highlight, with the A57 using a battery as large as the S26 Ultra. Long-term value is another strength. Samsung guarantees six years of security updates and four years of major Android upgrades, so buyers can expect their investment to stay secure and current well past the average upgrade cycle. It's not as good as the seven-year offer you get with a flagship Samsung, but still plenty of time.

Compared to Samsung’s upmarket S26 Ultra and S26, the A57 lacks some luxuries. It doesn’t come with the S26 Ultra’s brighter display, ultra-fast performance, or advanced AI camera features. For hundreds less, you still get a roomy screen and reliable everyday camera performance — essentials most consumers genuinely need.

The Galaxy A57 is our pick for buyers who want a long-lasting phone with a massive screen and great battery life but don’t need the latest in AI tricks or flagship camera prowess. If you want a future-proof everyday workhorse at a sensible price, this is the Samsung to get. Those chasing cutting-edge AI or the brightest, fastest display may want to look at the S26 Ultra instead.

Industry observers note that in previous years, the cheaper FE edition of the flagship would easily outperform the A-edition. But this time around, the S26 FE isn't quite a step up from the S25 FE, and the A57 is a significant improvement on the A56. The S26 FE is still almost twice the price of the A57, but the gap between them is shrinking.

Sources indicate that one thing the S26 FE does have is a lot of AI features. Some are good, most are novelties, but if you need a more affordable entry-point to Samsung's tools, this is the phone to go for. Not that it always feels it (and I mean that literally). The materials in the 2026 model don't have the same premium quality.

Then again, it doesn't feel like a cheap phone, which often are quite plastic-y in your hand. Whether this is an appropriate compromise when this isn't actually a cheap-cheap phone depends on how far your budget will stretch to get access to Samsung's latest features, when the A57 isn't far behind, performance-wise.

At the time of writing, we've not been able to perform our full battery tests, so can't accurately compare it against the other models. But it seems about in line with past FE performance; good, not great. Enough to see you through a day, but you'll still need a charger handy by the evening or a few hours of heavy use.

Recent findings suggest that if I seem a little down on the Galaxy S26 FE, I'm not. It's a very good phone with a lot of what we liked about the mainline S26 at a cheaper price. But the A57 isn't a whole lot different and is quite a bit cheaper, so I have a hard time recommending this phone when there's a more bank-balance-friendly option available.

Picking which Samsung phone to buy is primarily driven by budget considerations. You won't want to look at the latest Galaxy S Ultra or Z Fold if you're not prepared to pay for it. But other factors need to be taken into consideration as well.

Focusing on battery life will mean ruling out Samsung's foldables. Most other phones on this list have strong longevity on a single charge, but unfortunately, you'll probably have to pay more to get the best available battery life.

It has been revealed that for photography, the best will normally be the latest Galaxy S Ultra model. That goes for productivity too, due to Samsung bundling the S Pen in with its Ultra models, unless you'd prefer the extra screen space and multitasking options that a Galaxy Z Fold can provide. And if you're a gamer, any Galaxy S phone will offer the best possible performance — it's just up to you to decide how much you want to pay for other features on top of that.

According to recent reports, for a smartphone to make our best phone list, it needs to excel on several tests that we run on every handset. We perform some of these tests in our labs and some in the real world. See our detailed explanation on how Tom's Guide tests and reviews smartphones for more information.

In a recent development, when it comes to performance, we rely on such synthetic benchmarks as Geekbench 6 and 3DMark to measure graphics performance. These tests allow us to compare performance across iPhones and Android devices.

We also run a real-world video transcoding test on each phone using the Adobe Premiere Rush app and time the result. (We unfortunately have to skip this test on some phones due to app compatibility issues, but we attempt this benchmark with each device we get in to review.).

Geekbench 6 (single-core / multicore).

To measure the quality of a phone's display, we perform lab tests to determine the brightness of the panel (in nits), as well as how colorful each screen is (DCI-P3 color gamut). In these cases, higher numbers are better. We also measure the color accuracy of each panel with a Delta-E rating, where lower numbers are better, and a score of 0 is perfect.

In a recent development, one of the most important tests we run is the Tom's Guide battery test. We run a web surfing test over 5G (or 4G if the phone doesn't have 5G support) at 150 nits of screen brightness until the battery gives out. In general, a phone that lasts 10 hours or more is good, and anything above 11 hours makes our list of the best phone battery life.

Last but not least, we take the best phones out in the field to take photos outdoors, indoors, and at night in low light to see how they perform versus their closest competitors.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With most AI chatbots using your interactions as training data, we’ve previously cautioned against sharing sensitive personal details with them, highlighting the much stronger privacy protections offered by Apple. If you ever needed evidence of the importance of this, the Character․ai mess provides it.

The firm recently filed for bankruptcy and is now offering all of its assets for sale, including the contents of user chat sessions. Some 42 state attorneys general are trying to block this, but it’s unclear whether they will succeed ….

Character․AI had long come under fire for its extremely irresponsible attitude to privacy and safety. Last summer, it was accused of harvesting mental health data from underage consumers, and in May of this year it faced a lawsuit after its chatbots were found to be pretending to be licensed doctors. The company filed for bankruptcy last month.

A group of 42 attorneys general are trying to block the chatbot manufacturer from auctioning off users’ chat histories and other sensitive information […] “Nothing in the agreement restricts what the buyer may do with the data after closing, including selling it,” the AGs say in a court filing […].

“Character․AI’s plan to auction off its platform, including the IP addresses and private chats histories of its users — many of them children — with zero protection for those users is appalling,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted in a statement. “If this sale goes through, users’ sensitive data would go into the hands of a buyer even though Character․AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold.”.

The chat histories reportedly include conversations in which AI characters drew both adults and children into explicit sexual conversations.

Siri AI interactions are handled on-device wherever possible. Where this isn’t possible, Private Cloud Compute (PCC) servers are used, with guarantees that no data is stored or linked to your Apple account. Apple has designed the system in such a way that its privacy claims can be independently verified by security researchers.

In a recent development, when a user makes a request, Apple Intelligence analyzes whether it can be processed on device. For more complex requests, it can draw on Private Cloud Compute, which extends the privacy and security of your iPhone into the cloud. With Private Cloud Compute, only the data that is relevant to your request is processed on Apple silicon servers, before being removed.

The data being processed in Private Cloud Compute is not stored or made accessible to Apple. It is processed only to fulfill your request, after which point the results are returned securely to your device and are not retained by Private Cloud Compute. Independent privacy and security researchers can inspect the code that runs on Apple silicon servers that enable Private Cloud Compute to verify this privacy promise at any time.

It has been revealed that apple also recently introduced a safe way to ask an AI questions about your health. Data sources used are limited to the same platforms used by healthcare professionals, with links to peer-reviewed clinical citations. Apple guarantees that your chat sessions are not used for AI training with no retention of either questions or answers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar highlights how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.What You Will Learn:How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processesHow baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affectedHow in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structuresWhen offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign materialHow correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projectsRegister now for this free webinar!

In a recent development, in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar demonstrates how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

It has been revealed that in the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session reveals how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • US bill to tighten controls on chipmaking equipment sales to China goes “way too far”, Dutch trade minister Sjoerd Sjoerdsma told parliament on Thursday, according to Reuters.
  • The minister stated the proposal could put Europe at an unacceptable disadvantage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, the Dutch minister for foreign trade and development cooperation.

US bill to tighten controls on chipmaking equipment sales to China goes “way too far”, Dutch trade minister Sjoerd Sjoerdsma told parliament on Thursday, according to Reuters.

The minister stated the proposal could put Europe at an unacceptable disadvantage. His warning targets the Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act, or MATCH Act, which the US Congress is negotiating to attach to its annual defence policy bill.

The Dutch government has been lobbying against the bipartisan proposal for months. Under the bill, US allies with major semiconductor industries, including the Netherlands and Japan, would have 150 days to bring their export controls on China into line with Washington’s. If they did not, the US would impose restrictions on their equipment makers itself.

That would land hardest on ASML, the Dutch manufacturer whose lithography machines are essential for making advanced chips, and Europe’s most valuable listed firm.

The government opposes the bill’s extraterritorial reach, Sjoerdsma mentioned, and the damage would not stop at the Dutch border, because other European countries’ chip industries would also be hit.

“We will not simply be told what to do. If the act is adopted, our message to the US administration will be to not enforce it,” Sjoerdsma said.

Recent findings suggest that he also pointed to the stakes for the region’s AI ambitions, telling parliament that Europe cannot afford to fall behind in semiconductors. Sjoerdsma mentioned he was in close contact with his European colleagues about a common response to the bill.

The remarks are a sharp turn in a relationship that has mostly bent to US pressure. The Netherlands criticised US restrictions in 2023 but still introduced its own controls on ASML’s advanced machines that year, and has tightened them several times since.

ASML’s former chief executive Peter Wennink argued in 2024 that the ever-expanding export curbs were driven more by US economics than by security. China was once ASML’s second-largest market, and the restrictions have already cut its sales there.

It has been revealed that whether the MATCH Act becomes law now depends on the defence bill negotiations in Congress, where lawmakers are deciding which provisions make it into the final text. No date has been set for a vote, which leaves the Dutch government time to press its case in Washington.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Introducing Intel One Mono, an expressive monospaced font family that’s built with clarity, legibility, and the needs of developers in mind.

It’s easier to read, and available for free, with an open-source font license.

Identifying the typographically underserved low-vision developer audience, Frere-Jones Type designed the Intel One Mono typeface in partnership with the Intel Brand Team and VMLY&R, for maximum legibility to address developers' fatigue and eyestrain and reduce coding errors. A panel of low-vision and legally blind developers provided feedback at each stage of design.

It has been revealed that intel One Mono also covers a wide range of over 200 languages using the Latin script. The Intel One Mono fonts are provided in four weights — Light, Regular, Medium, and Bold — with matching italics, and we are happy to share both an official release of fonts ready to use as well as editable sources.

To install the fonts, please use the provided builds under Releases. Please refer to your software’s documentation for how to activate and use these fonts.

Recent findings suggest that we recommend using these fonts at 7 points and larger in print, 9 pixels and larger on screen. The .ttf, .woff and .woff2 fonts provided in the official release have been manually optimized for screen display, improving clarity and legibility, especially on Windows platforms.

Outside of the default characters, there are a few extra features that are accessible in some applications, as well as via CSS:.

Programming ligatures are not active by default. To use them, activate the stylistic sets of your preference in your code editor. For example:.

You will find editable sources in the sources directory. The instances subfolder contains separate source files for each style of the typeface. Sources are provided in .ufo files, which contain complete artwork, links to OpenType features provided in separate .fea files, as well as meta information like naming and vertical alignments for each style of the typeface.

Industry observers note that these are not installable fonts, but rather the source files that produce them: UFO (Unified Font Object) is an open, human-readable font source file format; you can find the file spec here. These sources were created using RoboFont. Many other font editors will also be able to open .ufo files; we recommend using RoboFont version 4.4.

According to recent reports, for instances, you will find postscript and truetype subfolders; these contain separate source files for the .otf format and the .ttf/.woff/.woff2 files respectively. Since the format for the outline drawings differs between these sets of formats, for best results we recommend using the postscript sources to create .otf fonts, and the TrueType sources to create .ttf, .woff, or .woff2 fonts.

Recent findings suggest that after making your desired edits, you can generate installable fonts directly from the font editor using its “Generate Font” functionality. If you use RoboFont, any install options should default to the ideal settings, but here they are for reference:.

Sources indicate that if you would like to apply edits across multiple weights, a more advanced yet potentially efficient way is to edit the masters. These are special sources that describe the extreme points in the design space — the lightest and heaviest weights for both roman and italic designs.

According to recent reports, after editing masters, you will need to rerun interpolation to generate individual weights and styles within that design space. This requires the .designspace files enclosed with the masters. The designspace format is an open, XML-based format that describes interpolation spaces (format specification for reference). For a RoboFont-based workflow we recommend Skateboard for interpolation; you can also use the free DesignSpaceEditor extension to view and edit these files.

Note that masters are only available in postscript format, so they will be best for creating .otf fonts. If you need to make TrueType based builds from the masters, we recommend QuadraticConverter for best quality conversion of the curves before generating .ttf, .woff, or .woff2 files; mind that the results will not match the provided instances precisely.

In a recent development, NB: The prepared instances contain some additional data that cannot be maintained through interpolation. For best results, compare upcoming interpolations to the existing instance sources and upgrade them accordingly, specifically the information accessible through the Font Info panels.

For TrueType-based formats (.ttf, .woff, .woff2 files), the official releases are manually optimized for screen rendering. These “hinting” sources are stored separately from the .ufo files, which do not contain any TrueType hinting information. When rebuilding TrueType-based formats, we recommend using the “autohint” option to achieve reasonable, though not identical screen rendering.

If you would like to access and edit manual hinting instructions, you will find these in the separate set of source files under hinting/truetype hinting source. These special TTF files will be viewable and editable using Microsoft VTT.

If you have requests for edits or additions to the official releases, please open challenges and we will try to accomodate them.

#155422. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3530 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3530 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.
  • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.
  • According to recent reports, I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

According to recent reports, I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

In a recent development, the patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell states. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

The screen reveals my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

Sources indicate that but can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” states Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

Recent findings suggest that the N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

Recent findings suggest that if all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

According to recent reports, sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

According to recent reports, remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

According to recent reports, this system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sources indicate that sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga indicates. “It was just major enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

Industry observers note that dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In Fresh York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

It has been revealed that but telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” indicates Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Industry observers note that surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson claims. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

It has been revealed that in 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

In a recent development, noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga states.

In a recent development, still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell states. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” indicates neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Recent findings suggest that medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

In a recent development, but the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

Industry observers note that telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra notes. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

Industry observers note that in September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Recent findings suggest that neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

Recent findings suggest that in the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell states. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

Industry observers note that the procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as promptly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell claims. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In a recent development, in 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

A few months after my visit, Remedy confirmed US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

It has been revealed that sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga claims they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How rapidly are doctors picking up on this upcoming technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

Industry observers note that these ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

Switzerland confirms first AI agent cyberattacks on critical infrastructure

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (588 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, attackers are now using AI agents against companies and critical infrastructure operators in Switzerland.
  • “In all cyberattacks known to the NCSC, the use of AI agents led to the successful compromise of the victim’s IT systems,” the agency wrote.
  • Florian Schütz, the NCSC’s director, gave the first figures on Thursday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Verzasca Dam in Ticino, Switzerland.

According to recent reports, attackers are now using AI agents against companies and critical infrastructure operators in Switzerland. The country’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) confirmed its first such cyberattacks in an advisory on Tuesday. The federal agency remarked the attacks hit at least two sectors.

“In all cyberattacks known to the NCSC, the use of AI agents led to the successful compromise of the victim’s IT systems,” the agency wrote.

Florian Schütz, the NCSC’s director, gave the first figures on Thursday. He spoke in an interview with SRF, the Swiss public broadcaster. The agency has five confirmed cases, all reported in recent days, he said. Three targeted critical infrastructure operators, and two of those succeeded. Across all five, attackers got into systems four times.

That is one fewer than Tuesday’s advisory implied, when the agency remarked every known attack had worked. SRF’s report does not say why the count changed.

In Switzerland, critical infrastructure includes electricity, drinking water and telecoms suppliers, SRF reported. Attackers also hacked small and medium-sized companies, which came forward voluntarily. Schütz mentioned there were no major outages. The NCSC will not name the victims and is leaving it to them to speak for themselves. Who is behind the attacks is still unclear.

Sources indicate that the attackers used what the NCSC calls agentic offensive frameworks. These AI agents search for weaknesses on their own, pick attack tools, check the results and initiative the next step. Security teams use the same tools for penetration testing.

According to recent reports, the agents exploit default or easily guessed passwords and known flaws in systems connected to the internet, the agency remarked. They need a fraction of the time a human attacker would. When they hit a defence, they switch to another known method. That leaves companies far less time to spot an attack and respond.

Sources indicate that the number of such agents reachable online has almost doubled since October, according to the NCSC. It named ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI as examples. It did not say which tools the attackers used in the Swiss cases. The FBI has said ARTEX can break into networks in under three hours. This week, Microsoft said state hackers from China and North Korea now use it.

Recent findings suggest that the NCSC expects more fast and successful attacks. It wants companies to install critical security updates on internet-facing systems within 24 hours of release. Webmail, VPNs and other services reachable from the internet should all sit behind multi-factor authentication or passkeys. Companies should also expose as few systems as possible. The agency also shares technical indicators of these attacks with critical infrastructure operators.

“If there is no vulnerability, an AI agent cannot get into a system either,” Schütz told SRF.

In a recent development, alex Stamos, the former Facebook security chief, stated this month that AI has pushed cybersecurity into a dark age. Raphael Reischuk co-founded the country’s National Test Institute for Cybersecurity and works at consulting firm Zühlke. He told SRF he expects a major wave of attacks. Many smaller companies lack the resources to keep their systems up to date, he said. He wants the federal government to consider jointly funded support for them, as it does for drinking water and electricity.

“Companies are not taking the problem seriously enough,” Reischuk said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

It has been revealed that this shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

In a recent development, this White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

MacBook Neo vs MacBook Air: Which should you buy right now?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple’s Mac lineup is stronger than ever this year, largely thanks to the latest MacBook Neo.
  • The MacBook Neo is Apple’s most affordable laptop ever, starting at $699 (presently on sale for $599).
  • In a recent development, unlike Apple’s other Macs, the MacBook Neo is powered by an A-series chip rather than an M-series chip.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple’s Mac lineup is stronger than ever this year, largely thanks to the latest MacBook Neo. If you’re deciding between the MacBook Neo and the MacBook Air this holiday season, here’s everything you need to know.

The MacBook Neo is Apple’s most affordable laptop ever, starting at $699 (presently on sale for $599). It features a solid aluminum design that comes in a range of fun colors, including Silver, Blush, Citrus, and Indigo.

In a recent development, unlike Apple’s other Macs, the MacBook Neo is powered by an A-series chip rather than an M-series chip. It uses the A18 Pro chip originally introduced with the iPhone 16 Pro, featuring a 6-core CPU and 5-core GPU.

The MacBook Neo comes with 8GB of unified memory, with no additional RAM configuration options available. It starts with 256GB of storage, with a 512GB configuration available for an additional $100. That $100 upgrade also gets you Touch ID, which is not included in the base model.

It has been revealed that there are some other trade-offs compared to the MacBook Air. The MacBook Neo lacks a backlit keyboard, MagSafe charging, and a Force Touch trackpad. It also has more limited USB-C connectivity and supports just one external display.

Still, the MacBook Neo offers an impressive feature set. It has a 13-inch display, up to 16 hours of battery life, a 1080p FaceTime camera, and the full macOS experience.

The MacBook Air, meanwhile, was updated earlier this year with Apple’s M5 chip. It starts at $1,299, making it $600 more expensive than the entry-level MacBook Air. The MacBook Air is right now on sale with a starting price of $999.

Recent findings suggest that for that $600 upgrade, the MacBook Air offers several key advantages over the MacBook Air. The M5 chip has a 10-core CPU and up to a 10-core GPU, enabling better sustained performance than the MacBook Neo.

It has been revealed that the MacBook Air also starts with 16GB of unified memory and 512GB of storage, both double the entry-level MacBook Neo. You can configure it with up to 32GB of memory and 4TB of storage, while the MacBook Neo is limited to 8GB of memory and 512GB of storage.

Apple rates the MacBook Air for up to 18 hours of video streaming and 15 hours of wireless web browsing, compared to 16 hours and 11 hours, respectively, for the MacBook Neo.

In a recent development, as I wrote in my review earlier this year, I think the MacBook Neo is a great Mac, full stop … not just because of the great price. It can handle the vast majority of things most people will throw at it. This includes web browsing, basic photo and video editing, research, and much more.

It has been revealed that the M5 MacBook Air, meanwhile, offers more power and more configuration options. This makes it a great option for people who need more storage, RAM, and power than the MacBook Neo can offer.

According to recent reports, one of my favorite things about the MacBook Air is that it’s available in two screen sizes. The 15-inch MacBook Air is one of my favorite Apple laptops with a combination of the ultra-thin and light design and the larger screen. I think a lot of people forget it exists, but it’s an excellent choice.

To recap, I think the MacBook Neo is a great choice for everyday tasks like web browsing, email, writing, and streaming. The MacBook Air is a better fit for more demanding workflows, including photo and video editing, coding, working with large spreadsheets, and heavy multitasking.

Beyond performance, the MacBook Air offers a handful of niceties that you won’t find on the MacBook Neo. These include a backlit keyboard, a larger display with True Tone, MagSafe charging, a better webcam and speakers, and a Force Touch trackpad. It also includes Touch ID on every configuration, longer battery life, and support for two external displays.

If it’s in the budget, I think the MacBook Air is an excellent choice for all Mac shoppers. It’s plenty powerful, thin and light, and is highly configurable compared to the MacBook Neo.

Bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones are 45% off right now, down to $199 for Black Friday, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet. Colors include in Dewdrop Mint, Eucalyptus Green, and Hazelnut Taupe. Weighing around 8.1 ounces, they’re among the lightest premium noise-canceling headphones, with generously padded earcups and a cushioned headband that spreads pressure without gripping too tightly, making them comfortable to wear for extended periods. They’re also easy to pack for travel, as the earcups fold and swivel for storage in the included hard-shell carrying case. The removable earpads are another welcome touch, since you can replace them as they wear down without having to retire the entire pair.

According to recent reports, comfort aside, noise cancellation is another area where these headphones deliver, doing a particularly good job of reducing lower-frequency rumble and background chatter, though some higher-pitched voices can still come through, notes this PCMag review. As for their sound profile, it leans warm and bass-forward, with deep lows that suit bass-heavy genres, while the companion app adds Bose Immersive Audio for spatial sound and lets you create customized listening profiles—the three-band EQ is fairly basic, though, so anyone who likes fine-tuning their sound may find the adjustment options limiting.

Connectivity, too, brings some useful upgrades over the previous generation, including Bluetooth 5.4, multipoint pairing for two devices, Google Fast Pair, and lossless audio over USB-C. That same USB-C port lets you charge the headphones while you listen, and the included USB-C-to-3.5mm cable covers standard headphone jacks, including the ones on in-flight entertainment systems. That said, battery life is less impressive, topping out at 24 hours with ANC enabled, although a 15-minute charge adds around 2.5 hours of playback. Wireless audio is also limited to the standard AAC and SBC codecs, with no support for the higher-quality aptX Adaptive—a feature available on Bose’s QuietComfort Ultra Headphones.

Warsaw startup Lute raises $20M to build robot AI that learns from touch

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (580 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lute, a Warsaw physical AI startup founded in January, has raised $20M to build robot models trained on touch.
  • Lute will spend the money on touch data, model training and new customers.
  • Most robots and physical AI models rely on cameras alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Lute team with one of its robots.

Lute, a Warsaw physical AI startup founded in January, has raised $20M to build robot models trained on touch. The pre-seed and seed money was announced on Tuesday. OTB Ventures and FORWARD.one co-led the seed round, and Credo Ventures and Seedcamp led the pre-seed. Inovo VC, Borusan Ventures, ff Venture Capital and angel investor Naval Ravikant also took part.

Lute will spend the money on touch data, model training and new customers. It is hiring in Warsaw and San Mateo, California.

Most robots and physical AI models rely on cameras alone. Vision shows a robot where things are, Lute’s founders wrote. It does not show how firmly the robot holds an item, whether the item is slipping or how fragile it is.

“We believe touch is the missing signal that lets robots handle real work reliably,” chief executive Paweł Budzianowski said in a statement published by FORWARD.one.

With partners, Lute co-designed small, soft tactile sensors and built them into a portable rig. That lets it collect touch data anywhere. Zurich’s Enact is chasing the same idea, and raised $30M in October to give robots a sense of touch.

Industry observers note that lute also released its first model, Lute-0. It learns from video how a scene changes and turns that into robot movements. It is the first of a family of models Lute aims to train on touch as well as vision.

It has been revealed that in Lute’s own retail tests, Lute-0 matched or beat π0.5, the open-source model from Physical Intelligence. It handled vegetables successfully 76% of the time, against 22% for π0.5. With soft snacks, the score was 98% against 70%. Lute says it also responds twice as fast. The figures come from Lute’s internal evaluation, and TNW has seen no independent results.

Sources indicate that lute says Lute-0 was pre-trained on far less data than π0.5, and trained much faster. Its two lead investors give different figures. It used about a twentieth of the data and a quarter of the training steps, OTB Ventures wrote. FORWARD.one puts it at about a tenth of the pre-training data.

Ten months in, Lute’s models already work at what it calls Europe’s largest automotive parts distributor. OTB puts that organization’s annual revenue at $6bn. Lute also works on site with large retailers, and its models run in hospital corridors, according to OTB. The startup also partners with integrators, the firms that install robots for clients, starting with healthcare and manufacturing.

Industry observers note that on site, the robots work on their own where they can, and a remote operator steps in when one needs help. They run unattended about 90% of the time, according to FORWARD.one. Failures and fixes then go back into training, so each deployment improves the next.

“In physical AI, the slow and the perfect will both lose,” said Boy de Jonge, investment manager at FORWARD.one.

Budzianowski has a machine learning PhD from Cambridge and led the machine learning team at PolyAI. He also co-founded K-Scale Labs, which built low-cost open-source humanoid robots. Co-founder Krzysztof Walas, the chief technology officer, was an associate professor at Poznań University of Technology and advised the Polish warehouse robotics firm Nomagic. The team has 16 people in Warsaw and the Bay Area.

If you’re anything like me, you know the exact spiral that hits when your to-do list gets overwhelming. Your brain panics, you bounce between six smaller distractions to feel “productive,” and by 5 PM, you’ve somehow been busy all day while finishing absolutely nothing.

That’s why I was equal parts skeptical and desperate when I slipped on the Neurable One — a pair of over-ear ANC headphones that pack 12 EEG sensors directly into the ear cushions to read your brainwave patterns in real time.

Normally $499, Neurable has knocked $50 off for Black Friday, dropping them to $449 through November 30 — and crucially, there’s no subscription paywall locked behind the app. After testing them myself, I can confirm they genuinely work.

Save $50 on these brain-sensing ANC headphones that pack 12 dry EEG sensors into great-sounding 40mm beryllium drivers to track your focus, flag burnout before it hits, and keep you on task — with zero monthly subscription fees.

First, let’s clear up the sci-fi paranoia: these aren’t reading your thoughts. The fabric sensors knitted into the memory foam pads pick up electrical patterns from your brain (no messy gel or electrodes required) and translate them into a live Focus Tracking feed and a Brain battery fuel gauge in the companion app.

For a serial procrastinator (hi), having a live scoreboard for your attention is a game-changer. Starting a focus session turns staying on task into a literal workout for your brain: you can see the exact moment your concentration starts to drift, and the app nudges you to take Smart Brain Breaks before you hit the wall and doomscroll for an hour.

Recent findings suggest that since I started working with these on, I’m noticeably getting more done in my day without feeling fried by the evening. But the weirdest, most welcome side effect? My sleep score actually improved too — likely because I’m finally respecting my mental bandwidth during work hours instead of trying to brute force through exhaustion.

Normally, some party trick comes at the cost of forgetting to make a good pair of headphones. Fortunately, Neurable’s first all-in-house design gets the audio fundamentals right.

The custom 40mm beryllium drivers sound crisp, balanced and genuinely enjoyable for long workdays — tuned for clean, fatigue-free listening rather than bloated showroom bass.

Sources indicate that yes, the companion app’s EQ options are limited, which is going to bug the hardcore audio tweakers out there. But to my trained ears, the out-the-box audio quality is strong enough that it’s nowhere near a dealbreaker.

You also get solid active noise cancellation, a clear latency-free ambient mode and Bluetooth multipoint for hopping between your laptop and phone.

Before you do buy, I’d be doing a disservice in not pointing out a couple of downsides with these cans:.

At $449, the Neurable one is still a serious investment — and if you just want the absolute lightest travel headphones with the greatest sound quality, there are plenty of mainstream options.

But if you struggle with distraction, burnout, or juggling ten half-finished tasks at once, these are the rare wellness wearable that actually earns its keep.

Getting a great sounding pair of ANC headphones and a personal focus coach for $50 off — with zero monthly fees — makes this one of the most interesting pair of cans I’ve tested this year, and my personal favorite Black Friday deal.

Hackers breached the US Air Force’s Cloud One platform, Reuters reports

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (432 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Pentagon, headquarters of the US Department of Defense, in September 2018.
  • Hackers have broken into Cloud One, the US Air Force’s main cloud computing platform, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters on Friday.
  • Sources indicate that two of the people said the intrusion came to light in the past month or so, while the system was being upgraded.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Pentagon, headquarters of the US Department of Defense, in September 2018.

Hackers have broken into Cloud One, the US Air Force’s main cloud computing platform, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters on Friday. The breach could put a wide range of military data at risk, from personnel records to logistics and tactical information.

Sources indicate that two of the people said the intrusion came to light in the past month or so, while the system was being upgraded. Reuters could not establish who was behind it, how far it reached or whether any data was stolen.

“A breach here is a significant deal,” one of the people told Reuters.

The report adds to a run of recent breaches at US government bodies, as this week, hackers hit a system used by several spy agencies, and in October a Homeland Security leak exposed 41,000 staff.

Since the discovery, work to move the Air Force’s back-office applications onto Cloud One has been paused, according to two of the sources and a fourth person. Updates to applications already running there have also been blocked, leaving staff unable to install fixes for newly disclosed flaws. A fifth person said some customers lost their administrator rights.

Another source said the hackers used a software flaw to reach the control plane, the layer that manages the whole platform, and compared that access to a universal remote. In theory, it could show the status of military aircraft or the movement of spare parts, but it is unclear whether the hackers used it that way.

The Air Force introduced Cloud One in 2017 as a single home for its IT, built on cloud services from Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Google. Scores of applications run on it, covering pay, personnel, logistics and maintenance.

Among them is a command-and-control system that combines air defence radar feeds from across North America, Reuters reported. Another tracks bombs and missiles at more than 200 Air Force sites worldwide.

According to recent reports, SAIC ran the platform as prime contractor until Leidos took over under a $454.9M task order awarded in December 2025. According to one source, US Cyber Command has been brought in to gauge the damage, and Cyber Command did not respond either.

“[The Air Force] does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems,” the service said in a statement to Reuters.
